description: This course offers a comprehensive overview of disaster management principles and operational strategies across all phases of the disaster cycle including mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. We will explore essential theoretical frameworks, practical tools, and organizational structures for effective disaster risk reduction and crisis management. Topics include hazard identification, emergency planning, incident command systems, resource mobilization, and community resilience. Through case studies and simulations, you'll develop critical thinking and leadership skills for careers in disaster management and emergency response
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Disaster Management and Operations

description: This course provides an intensive exploration of medical care delivery in challenging and resource-limited settings, often characterized by remote locations, extreme conditions, limited infrastructure, and prolonged patient contact without immediate evacuation. Students will delve into the unique medical, logistical, and ethical considerations inherent in providing healthcare in wilderness, disaster, conflict, and expedition environments. Key topics include prolonged field care, trauma management in low-resource settings, environmental injuries (e.g., hypothermia, heat stroke, altitude sickness), improvised medical techniques, expeditionary medicine planning, public health considerations in austere environments, and the psychological impacts of operating in isolated or high-stress situations
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Medicine in Austere Environments

description: The course will cover a range of topics from historical special operations forces (SOF) campaigns and their impact on warfare to current trends in asymmetric conflict, counter-terrorism, unconventional warfare, and information operations. Emphasis will be placed on understanding the strategic utility of SOF, the ethical and legal frameworks governing their deployment, and the complex interplay between special operations and national policy. Through case studies, historical analysis, and contemporary examples, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how special operations contribute to national security objectives and address emerging threats in a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape. This course is designed for students interested in national security, military history, international relations, and strategic studies
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Military and Special Operations

prerequisites: Graduate classification

description: Multidisciplinary instruction in animal welfare science; exploration of issues including physiology, behavior, human-animal interactions, suffering and pain, ethics, health, assessment and standards and economics; experience in assessment of welfare of animals of a variety of species in virtual situations; promotion of problem solving and critical thinking skills through assessments, discussions, readings and assignments

prerequisites: Graduate classification

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Examination of the Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles specifically related to meat and poultry; microbiological and process overviews; good manufacturing practices (GMP) and standard operating procedures (SOP) development; team-building and implementation into industry operations. This class is designed for the production of food and fulfills the training requirements of USDA's HACCP regulation for meat and poultry (9 CFR Part 417), and FDA's HACCP regulations for fish and fishery products (21 CFR Part 123 and 1240) and for juice (21 CFR Part 120)

prerequisites: Approval of instructor

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Principles of food system process control; statistical process control (SPC); tools required to assure uniform communication and understanding of quality assurance systems
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Quality Assurance for the Food Industry

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Application of horses in moving cattle via riding the 58 mile cattle trail in the Green River Drift; techniques for care of stock; emphasis on riding and horsemanship; insight into relationships between ranchers and Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service; exposure to packing horses and mules; appreciation of heritage and current issues related to ranching in the Green River Valley
prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of instructor

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

title: Biological Anthropology

description: Development of archaeology as a discipline; methods and theories used in archaeology for reconstructing cultural history and cultural process
title: Archaeological Methods and Theory

prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Seafaring Life and Maritime Communities

description: Survey of the theoretical concepts used in anthropology and how to construct models used in cultural and social anthropology
title: Cultural Method and Theory

description: Fundamentals and applications of artifact conservation techniques in archaeology
prerequisites: Knowledge of basic chemistry and physics recommended
title: Conservation of Archaeological Resources I

prerequisites: Approval of instructor; graduate classification
title: Outfitting and Sailing the Wooden Ship 1400-1900

prerequisites: Approval of instructor and graduate classification

description: Seafarers and watercraft of the ancient Near East and Mediterranean until ca. 700 B.C. Types of watercraft used, routes, cargoes, voyages of exploration and economics of maritime trade
title: Preclassical Seafaring

description: Culture history of Mediterranean seafarers between ca. 700 B.C. and end of Byzantine Empire; types of ships and boats, sea law, naval tactics, harbor-works, routes, cargoes and economics of trade
title: Classical Seafaring

description: Design and construction of preserved and excavated sailing ships, the expertise of their builders and technology involved in ancient and early shipbuilding
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: History of Shipbuilding Technology

prerequisites: Approval of instructor

prerequisites: ANTH 605
title: Conservation III--Preservation of Organic Materials

description: Cultural history of seafaring in the Mediterranean region during medieval times; ship types and their uses, naval warfare, sea law, harborworks, routes and cargoes, and maritime economic institutions and practices
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Medieval Seafaring in the Mediterranean

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. An applied course on the contribution of earth sciences to the interpretation of archaeological contexts, this course consists of field, lab and lecture components. Reviews Quaternary geomorphology. Investigates site formation processes in different depositional environments and impacts on archaeological sites. Provides training in stratigraphic description and interpretation and archaeological dating methods and interpretations. Applies earth science fields and methodologies to archaeological problems. Field trips will be a required component of the course in order to complete field descriptions and sampling. TOPICS AND THEMES. The development of geoarchaeology; sediments and soils and their relevance to archaeological sites; stratigraphy; dating methods and archaeological applications; landscape reconstruction and geoarchaeological interpretations; depositional environments and site formation processes; remote sensing; geophysics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to geoarchaeology
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Geoarchaeology

description: Analysis of animal bones from archaeological sites; inference of how prehistoric peoples hunted, domesticated and used animals
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of zoology and archaeology
title: Zooarchaeology

description: Cultural history of seafaring in the Western Hemisphere from the fifteenth century to the present; ship types and their uses; harborworks, commerce, naval warfare, sailing routes, maritime practices
prerequisites: ANTH 615 and ANTH 616 or approval of instructor
title: New World Seafaring

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human courtship, marriage, reproduction, family structure and parenting through the lens of evolutionary ecology. Explores how human reproductive and parenting patterns compare with those of other primates and how they vary across cultures. Evaluates different viewpoints on and approaches to the application of evolutionary logic to the study of these topics. Critically examines hypotheses explaining human behavior through biological, cultural and ecological lenses. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include evolutionary approaches to the study of human behavior, life histories, reproductive strategies, sexual selection, marriage, parental care, infidelity, divorce, as well as explorations of cross-cultural and cross-species variation in these areas
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Anthropology of Human Reproduction

description: Survey the behavioral ecology of the nonhuman primates exploring topics such as their hunting behavior; sexual coercion; language capabilities; culture; tool use; homosexuality; dominance; parental care, ethics of field study and their conservation
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Primate Behavioral Ecology

description: Principles and techniques used in palynology, pollen morphology, ontogeny, biochemistry, dispersion and preservation; role of palynology as a research tool in plant taxonomy agriculture, medicine, paleobotany and anthropology
title: Palynology

description: Codes of professional ethics applicable to excavation and preservation of archaeological sites; ethnographic fieldwork and professional relationships with colleagues and informants; professional protocols for publication and presentation of research results
prerequisites: Graduate classification in anthropology and approval of instructor
title: Anthropological Ethics and Professionalism

description: Research design used by anthropologists to develop sampling strategies, test hypotheses and compile quantitative data
prerequisites: ANTH 602
title: Research Design in Anthropology

description: Laboratory-based course reviewing methods archaeologists use to analyze stone tools and debitage, including identification of tool-stone sources, reconstruction of technology, explanation of assemblage variability, and microscopic use-wear analysis
prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of instructor
title: Lithic Artifact Analysis

description: Methods common to anthropology for the field collection of data on cultural behavior
prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of instructor
title: Ethnographic Field Methods

description: Survey of past frontiers in First American studies important to the peopling of the Americas: review of the archaeology, geology, and dating of early sites in North, Middle, and South America; human migration hypotheses; biological evidence; and late Quaternary environmental factors
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: First American Archaeology

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology and anthropology of foraging (hunting and gathering) societies in time and space. Includes an overview of archaeology focused on foraging societies and current methodological and theoretical issues, especially the use of ethnographic and environmental data. Investigates ecologically oriented case studies of late Pleistocene and Holocene hunter-gatherers paired with the ethnographic record used to interpret these sites. Archaeological case studies will have an emphasis on land-use, site-structure and site formation analyses. Ethnographic case studies will focus on the diversity of hunting and gathering societies, change in these societies through time and discussion of forager economies, with specific attention to critiquing ethnohistoric accounts and the applicability of these case studies to the archaeological record. TOPICS AND THEMES. Forager (hunter-gatherer) variation in different environments; forager variation through time; forager social structures; forager mobility; forager subsistence; socio-political complexity in foraging societies; ethnographic critiques; archaeology of foraging societies; resource management; foragers in the modern world and change in forager societies in the recent past; archaeological site structure; lithic analysis; site formation processes; archaeological site survey; archaeological theory of foragers; site modeling and resource modeling. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: The Archaeology and Anthropology of Foraging Societies

description: Quantitative data collection and analytical methods employed by anthropologists including standardized observation, structured interviews, demography and network analysis; emphasizes hands-on assignments involving data collection among local community
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Quantitative Ethnographic Methods

description: Field instruction in the methods of archaeological excavations; recovery and cataloging of cultural, floral and faunal remains; and interpretation of these data. Locations of the field course will vary according to site. Field trips required. May be taken more than once but not to exceed 8 hours of credit toward an MA degree and not to exceed 12 hours of credit toward a PhD degree
prerequisites: ANTH 602 or equivalent
title: Field Archaeology

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology and inferences made based on these data. Develops long-term, global perspective on human-environment interactions provided by the fields of archaeology and earth science. TOPICS AND THEMES. The use of archaeological sites as paleoenvironmental archives, human impacts on ancient environments, Quaternary extinctions, long-term landscape evolution, plant and animal domestication, the Anthropocene and cultural collapse and resilience
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Environmental Archaeology

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Reviews current evidence from the fields of archaeology, genetics, biological anthropology and paleoecology for the dispersal of modern humans to the New World during the Pleistocene. Examines terminal Pleistocene cultures in Asia and the earliest sites in the Americas. Discusses various models proposed for this migration. Critically examines major archaeological sites and cultures. Stresses an interdisciplinary approach. Applies theory and method used to explain prehistoric human migration and colonization of empty lands. TOPICS AND THEMES. Pleistocene Americas; ancient DNA; paleoenvironments; radiocarbon dating; archaeological modeling; lithic analysis; ethnographic analogy; zooarchaeology and extinctions; archaeological site formation processes; critical analysis of fragmentary data; statistical analysis. This course will incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to the peopling of the Americas. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Method and Theory in the Peopling of the Americas

description: Conventional and advanced techniques used for artifact material analysis and artifact documentation; material analysis is the way that we study artifacts, both in structure and elemental composition; includes photography and artifact sketching, computer modeling, laser digitization, computer image photogrammetry, 3D printing and XRF elemental analysis
prerequisites: Graduate classification in anthropology or approval of instructor
title: Analytical Methods in Archaeology and Conservation

description: Evaluation of modern ideas about how and why archaeological, architectural, ethnographic, and natural resources should be preserved and presented to current and future societies; critical examination of the theories, methods, regulations, and ethics that guide efforts to preserve and protect cultural heritage within a context of past endeavors and future directions
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Cultural Heritage and Resource Management

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how biomolecules – DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites – persist in plant and animal remains, artifacts and sediments for thousands to millions of years, preserving key insights into long-term ecological and human history. Determines how these molecules are preserved, identified and analyzed within archaeological contexts to address interdisciplinary questions about evolution, migration, diet, disease, culture, tool production, health and environmental change. Interpretation of biomolecular evidence will draw from archaeological, historical and scientific sources to reconstruct past lifeways within their own cultural and environmental settings. Develops the ability through lectures, discussions and data analysis to assess the suitability for different biomolecular methods for addressing specific research questions and critically evaluate current scientific literature in the field. Skills learned are directly applicable to making informed, evidence-based decisions, empowering students to navigate information-rich environments with discernment and confidence. Prior knowledge in either biology/biochemistry or archaeology is required, but not both. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of the hereditary biomolecules DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites; large-scale ‘omics’ approaches, including genomics, metagenomics, proteomics, metaproteomics, lipiomics and metabolomics used to investigate complex systems; instrumentation including PCR, Sanger Sequencing, Whole Genome Sequencing (NGS and WGS), chromatography and mass spectrometry; specialized applications such as environmental DNA, microbiomes and dental calculus genetics and proteomics; biomolecule preservation and degradation; ways biomolecular techniques are adapted for archaeological considerations; integration with other lines of archaeological, textual, historic and scientific evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to archaeological biomolecules
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Ancient Biomolecules

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Medical Anthropology

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Evaluates core psychological, medical, evolutionary and anthropological theories of body image, eating disorders, fat and cosmetic surgery. Surveys and critiques theories of body image from the lens of medical anthropology and global mental health. Develops expertise in articulating the major theoretical questions, strengths and limitations of different frameworks, particularly in relation to cross-cultural variation. Critically analyzes global case studies of body image-related illnesses. Applies anthropological theories to identifying biases in the body image literature and public health consequences. Formulates anthropological solutions to conversations and concerns in the body image literature surrounding emerging trends, cross-cultural value- and knowledge-systems and the challenges of treatment. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of anthropological theories of the body; critique of current theories of body image and eating disorders; assessment of psychological and anthropological approaches to fat talk; critique and synthesis of biomedical and social justice approaches to weight and weight stigma; evaluation of limitations of eating disorders research from a cross-cultural perspective; formulation of anthropological solutions to emerging discussions in body image among men, racial minorities and sexual minorities; evaluating the cross-cultural motivations and ethics of cosmetic surgery; critiquing current treatments for eating disorders and obesity from an anthropological lens
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Anthropology of Body Image

description: This course deals with a systematic observation in educational settings with the purpose of assessing and evaluating instruction and making recommendations for its improvement. Most key components of classroom observation for emergent bilingual, English as a second language (ESL) and dual language programs include language content, communication mode, language of instruction and activity structures. The course will be organized around the following topics: significance of classroom observations for improving instructional capacity; potential impact to address the education needs of all learners with special emphasis in emergent bilingual, English learners and dual language learners; theoretical frame work, operational definitions, theoretical models and constructs for classroom observation; classroom observation and coding process; some more used classroom observation instruments; Pedagogical Observation Protocol instruments with current typical measurement practices; validation evidence, predictive validity; validation research questions on classroom observation: intra-rater reliability, inter-rater reliability of pedagogical observation protocols between human coders and machine coders, inter-rater reliability of the Pedagogical Observation Protocol among coders who are more experienced versus those who are less experienced; predictive validity under bilingual, ESL and dual language strategies, language content, language of instruction, communication mode, physical grouping and activity structure; other classroom observation instruments for bilingual and language learners; the future of classroom observation through artificial intelligence

description: Intensive work on selected topics of research in media studies; may address work in the areas of audience studies, media effects, industries, policy, international issues, media and culture, media history or theory
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Topics in Media Studies

description: Investigation of processes through which mediated messages influence our everyday lives; examination of social scientific approaches; understanding how viewers select, interpret and respond to mediated messages; includes media representations, mediated inter-group processes, news framing, political advertising, persuasive messages, entertainment media, popular culture, health campaigns, positive media psychology, new media technologies, pro-social media effects and critical media literacy
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Media Processes and Effects

description: Examines the relationships between human communication and technology, investigating the social effects of communication technologies, the quality of messages, communicative practices, and rhetorical norms that typify effective communication in technological society
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Communication and Technology

description: Examination of theories, methods and research that characterize the use of media in health contexts; focus on mass media influence on public health and/or strategic use of mass media to promote health behaviors; engagement of social and behavioral science approaches to media effects and/or critical perspectives on the study of media as social institutions
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Media and Health

description: Theories and research in health communication considering functions and outcomes of communication processes in various health contexts, ranging from interpersonal settings to public campaigns; emphasis on providing a framework for synthesizing and critically evaluating health communication research
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Health Communication

description: Investigation of a subject important to the understanding of health communication, such as persuasion and public health campaigns, physician-patient communication, or communication in health care organizations
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Topics in Health Communication

description: Provides socialization to the profession of communication, focusing on graduate students' roles as scholars and teachers; provides instruction on teaching communication, conducting and writing publishable research, and fulfilling responsibilities to one's organization and profession
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Professional Seminar

description: Directed studies in specific problem areas in communication. Student may take up to two sections of directed studies in communication in the same semester, with a maximum of 6 credits
prerequisites: Approval of department head
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified area of communication
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Special Topics in

description: Research for thesis
title: Research

description: Study of construction materials and methods emphasizing interpretation of plans and specifications, including a research component requiring investigation of current and emerging materials, methods and practices
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Advanced Construction Materials and Methods

description: Determination of quantities for various types of construction materials and works including earthwork, foundations, structural systems, mechanical and electrical systems, and building finishes; methods used for pricing of construction works including labor, materials, equipment, sub-contractors, overhead and profit; use of various types of cost data catalogs available in the industry
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Construction Cost Estimating

description: Introduction to commonly used techniques and computer applications for the planning, scheduling, monitoring, and controlling of construction projects; includes key scheduling techniques such as Gantt Chart, CPM, PERT, LSM, and EVM; practical scheduling practices such as tracking, controlling, and forecasting trends of schedules, cost control, and reporting
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Construction Scheduling

description: Building environmental systems with a major emphasis on the design and control of the heating, ventilation and cooling systems, plumbing and drainage systems, electrical, fire and lightening protection, and lighting; design opportunities, calculations, equipment selection and economics as they relate to design and construction
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Mechanical and Electrical Construction

description: Investigation of interrelationships between structural integrity, behavior and failure mechanisms in building systems. Through case studies and applied theory in construction structures, students explore real-world structural failures to understand how design, construction and maintenance decisions affect performance and safety. The course emphasizes professional responsibility, diagnostic reasoning and failure prevention in construction practice
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Structural Integrity and Failure Forensics

description: Running a construction company; strategic planning; business planning; organizational theory; competitor analysis; risk management; financial analysis; human resources; management information systems; leadership; codes of ethics; best practices
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Construction Company Operations

description: Theoretical, practical, and strategic development in the management of contemporary construction projects; advanced techniques used in scheduling and evaluating progress in construction project control; exploration of state-of-the-art management principles and practices, and development of additional insights
prerequisites: COSC 603 or COSC 475
title: Advanced Project Management

description: Foundation in Life Cycle Cost Analysis computation within the context of current issues in environmental sustainability and evidence-based thinking; lean construction as a strategy to overcome the hurdle of first cost
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Construction Economics

description: Fundamental theories and applied methods of construction accounting and construction financial management including cash flow analysis, financial planning, risk analysis, and project financing
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Construction Accounting and Financial Management

description: Advanced construction law, contracts, and risk management applicable to construction management; identification of common disputes and construction risks among the owner, design professionals, and contractor; analysis of construction contracts with an emphasis on troublesome provisions and solutions; demonstration of tools of negotiation and dispute resolution; ethics in construction
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Construction Contracts and Risk Management

description: Introduction to lean history, concepts and methods; deduction of basic training modules in lean project delivery; application of lean management in construction projects
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Advanced Productivity and Lean

description: Introduction to Life Cycle Assessment from a coupled energy-carbon-water (ECW) nexus perspective; Key LCA concepts; the LCA process; LCA standards; application of LCA approaches and software to assess the energy, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, water, and other environmental impacts of building construction industry at the material and whole building levels; study and analysis of factors relating to material and assembly choices, site logistics, on-site and off­ site construction and/or fabrication processes, additive construction (large-scale 3D printing), and construction and demolition waste to reduce the energy use, GHG emissions, and water use; analysis and comparison of LCA results of process-based and macro-economic model-based Life Cycle Inventory (LCI)
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Life Cycle Assessment in Building Construction

description: Exploration of emerging technologies for the construction industry including hardware and software systems such as BIM, RFID, Wireless/Mobile, information systems, construction specific programs, and information strategy planning; using information strategy planning by owners and contractors to effectively enhance the management of business entities and projects in construction
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Construction Information Technology

description: Theoretical, practical, and strategic development in contemporary construction systems; exploration of state-of-the-art innovations in environmental control systems, structural principles and practices; integration of innovations with information technologies, and development of additional insights
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Advanced Construction Systems

description: Introduction to the theory and application of 3-D computer models in the design/build construction process; creation, positioning in 3-D space, and linking of building components to a database record; creation of a wide range of construction related information useful in controlling project quality
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Advanced Construction Visualization

description: Data science with a focus on built environment applications; overview of statistics, data collection, data visualization, data cleaning, and machine learning; focuses on tackling research problems in construction and built environment using machine learning
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science or approval of instructor
title: Data Science for the Built Environment

description: Contribution of materials and methods to meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; overview of international, national and local programs promoting sustainable construction; characteristics of the components of successful sustainable construction projects; theories and practices through case studies
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Sustainable Construction

description: Evaluation of safety management practices and accident prevention techniques, including state and federal laws related to general and construction projects; theoretical concepts and industry practices used to model, evaluate, and improve construction worker safety through the design of the project features, construction operations, and site safety program elements; causes of construction site accidents, hazard recognition and comprehension, safety risk valuation and mitigation, and the true costs of injuries and fatalities; role of technology in enhancing safety and health management; fulfills the requirements for the ten-hour OSHA certification
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Advanced Construction Safety and Health Management

description: Fundamentals of facility asset management and property management including concepts, theories, and principles of design, construction, accounting, finance, and management of the built environment; an overview of a project throughout its entire life cycle from various perspectives including the owner, users, designers, constructors and facility management personnel
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Facilities Asset Management

description: Discussion and review of degree requirements, career opportunities, and current research activities in construction management
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Seminar

description: Approximately 400-600 hours with a construction or construction-related company that exposes the student to construction-related activities; an initial report, monthly progress reports, a final report, and a final completion letter are required
prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of graduate coordinator; approval of internship coordinator
title: Professional Internship

description: Individual problems in the area of building construction involving the application of theory and practice
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified field of construction management
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Special Topics in

description: Introduction to research, research tools, proposal writing and research reports; emphasis on research planning and design, conducting a comprehensive review of literature, quantitative and qualitative research methodologies, defining research problems in construction science, and the development of research proposals
prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science
title: Theory of Research in Construction Science

description: Research for thesis
prerequisites: COSC 690 or concurrent enrollment; approval of graduate coordinator
title: Research

description: Approved professional study of project undertaken as terminal requirement for Master of Science, non-thesis option. Preparation of a record of study summarizing the rationale, procedure and results of the completed study
prerequisites: COSC 690 or concurrent enrollment; approval of graduate coordinator
title: Professional Study

description: Overview of various counseling theories and its application in a school setting
prerequisites: CPSY 630
title: Counseling Theories for School Counselors

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Intersecting role of ethnicity, cultural background, gender and sexual orientation and how they shape the psychosocial development of children and adolescents and impact their educational trajectories; development and appreciation of cultural and ethnic differences among individuals, groups and families to enhance school counseling service delivery
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Multicultural Counseling in Schools

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Broad view of counseling techniques using a microskills approach; opportunities to observe and practice counseling techniques
prerequisites: CPSY 630 ; graduate classification
title: Counseling Techniques for School Counselors

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Development of group counseling interventions for children and adolescents in school settings

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Understanding the culturally competent career counseling theory, assessment and skills as applied to the diverse populations in schools
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Career Counseling in Schools

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Purposes and functions of a guidance program; components of a comprehensive guidance program; systems approach to implementing a comprehensive guidance program for elementary and secondary students and adults
prerequisites: Graduation classification
title: Planning and Organizing Comprehensive Guidance Programs

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Causes, course, outcomes and treatment of abnormal and maladaptive behavior; degrees of variation possible from normal adaptive behavior; biological, developmental, social, cultural and psychological perspective on abnormal behavior
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Psychopathology

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Personality evaluation using structured assessment instruments; variety of self-report personality inventories; the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory
prerequisites: EPSY 622
title: Structured Personality Assessment in Counseling

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Philosophical, psychological, and sociological concepts fundamental to counseling in schools
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Foundations of School Counseling

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Methods and procedures descriptive of the counseling process; dynamics of counselor-counselee relationship; interviewing techniques; use of test results in counseling
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Techniques of Counseling

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Theories of career development; sources, classification and analysis of educational, occupational and social information including occupational trends, post-secondary programs and financial planning; use of occupational-educational information, appropriate psychological measures and computerized guidance systems
prerequisites: CPSY 679
title: Career Counseling

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Principles, procedures and processes of group approaches to assisting individuals in their personal growth and development in education, public and mental health settings; participation as member of a personal growth required
prerequisites: CPSY 630
title: Introduction to Group Process

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Provides a foundation in theory and research at the interface of social and counseling psychology; fundamentals of social psychology theories, methodologies and perspectives; understanding the relevance to counseling psychology practice; focus on social and cognitive theories, concepts, and processes rather than specific psychological disorders
prerequisites: Doctoral student in good standing in counseling, clinical, school or social psychology
title: Social Counseling Psychology Interface

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Focuses on organizations as the target of analysis, intervention, and change; established social science concepts and principles; consideration of concepts, intervention strategies, and skills that extend beyond those used in counseling and psychotherapy; highlights consultation as a mode of change agency; considerable attention given to putting theory into practice
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Psychological Consultation to Organizations

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Supervised experience in individual counseling; cases engaged in the counseling laboratory on campus; off-campus counseling in schools and various public and mental health settings also assigned at supervisor's discretion. May be taken for credit 2 times as content varies
prerequisites: CPSY 631 and CPSY 632 ; approval of instructor
title: Counseling Practicum I

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Legal, ethical, economic and practical issues that impact the training, credentialing, placement and marketing of counseling psychologists and their services
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Professional Issues and Ethics in Counseling Psychology

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: (1-6).Supervised experience in individual and group counseling requiring advanced technical skills; continuing counseling relationships with various, selected subjects
prerequisites: CPSY 639

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: (1-6).Supervised experience in directing counseling and guidance activities of students involved in practicum and field experiences; intended for individuals preparing to become counselor educators or supervisors
prerequisites: CPSY 664 ; approval of instructor
title: Practicum in Counselor Supervision

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Comprehensive and intensive study of major theoretical positions in counseling and psychotherapy; implications for research and practice in public and mental health settings
prerequisites: CPSY 631
title: Theories of Counseling and Psychotherapy

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Effective communication skills in cross-cultural counseling or helping relationships in public and mental health settings; integration of theoretical knowledge with experiential learning; psychosocial factors and lifestyles of cultural groups; effect on counseling relationships
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Multicultural Counseling

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Supervised experience in professional public and mental health settings in counseling psychology; wide range of practical experiences and activities that are closely supervised by departmental faculty. May be taken up to 30 hours
prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of instructor
title: Field Practicum

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Limited to advanced doctoral students; faculty supervised experience in approved professional public and mental health employment settings; application for September assignments must be approved the previous October. May be repeated up to 9 hours. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Completion of required coursework except CPSY 684 and CPSY 691 ; approval of instructor
title: Professional Internship

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Directed individual study of selected problems
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

description: This seminar models the processes of developing and defending research proposals
prerequisites: EPSY 640 and EPSY 641
title: Research Proposal Development

prerequisites: Graduate classification

May be repeated for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Theory of Counseling Psychology Research

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Research for thesis or dissertation. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Approval of instructor

description: Introduction to the concepts and design methodologies of database systems for non-computer science majors; emphasis on E. F. Codd's relational model with hands-on design application. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: CSCE 310 or CSCE 603
prerequisites: CSCE 601; graduate classification
title: Database Systems and Applications

description: Advanced topics in compiler writing; parser generators and compiler-compilers; dynamic storage and scope resolution; data flow analysis and code optimization
prerequisites: CSCE 434
title: Compiler Design

description: Development of advanced concepts in software engineering; software development environments as a mechanism for enhancing productivity and software quality; the classification, evaluation and selection of methodologies for environments; rapid prototyping and reusability concepts; artificial intelligence techniques applied to software engineering
prerequisites: CSCE 431 or approval of instructor
title: Software Engineering

description: Database modeling techniques; expressiveness in query languages including knowledge representation; manipulation languages data models; physical data organization; relational database design theory; query processing; transaction management and recovery; distributed data management
prerequisites: CSCE 310 or approval of Instructor
title: Database Systems

description: Review of computer architecture hardware/software evolution leading to contemporary operating systems; basic operating systems concepts; methods of operating systems design and construction; algorithms for CPU scheduling memory and general resource allocation; process coordination and management; case studies of several operating systems; quality-of-services of operating systems and their impact on applications. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: CSCE 410 or CSCE 611
prerequisites: CSCE 313 ; graduate classification
title: Operating Systems

description: Fundamentals, including network design and protocol analysis, in the context of computer communications; mixes fundamentals with both programming and pragmatic views of engineering issues; it includes network architecture as well as principles of network engineering; focus is on applying principles of layered architecture to analyzing real networks; lab exercises focus on protocol understanding and programming; knowledge of UNIX and C programming helpful, but not required. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: CSCE 463 or CSCE 612
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Applied Networks and Distributed Processing

description: Reviews of von Neumann architecture and its limitations; parallel computer structures and concurrent computation; pipeline computers and vectorization methods; array processors, multiprocessor architectures and programming; dataflow computers
prerequisites: CSCE 350/ECEN 350 , ECEN 350/CSCE 350 , or CSCE 312 ; background in undergraduate computer engineering or computer science
title: Computer Architecture

description: Introduction to hardware functional verification; case studies on verification in integrated circuit design; introduction to industry best practices; introduction to logic functional verification
prerequisites: CSCE 312 or CSCE 350/ECEN 350 , or equivalent in computer architecture; familiarity with C/C++/Verilog/VHDL programming
title: Introduction to Hardware Design Verification

description: Design and analysis of algorithms for solving geometrical problems; includes convex hull problems, Voronoi diagrams, range searching and proximity problems
prerequisites: CSCE 311 or approval of instructor
title: Computational Geometry

description: Analysis, implementation, and comparison of sketch recognition algorithms, including feature-based, vision-based, geometrical, timing-based, and path-based recognition algorithms; methods for combining these recognition methods for greater accuracy, using known AI techniques
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Sketch Recognition

description: Fundamental concepts and modern methods of artificial intelligence; search (uninformed, informed, iterative improvement, constraint satisfaction, space/time complexity); game playing: minmax, alpha-beta pruning; knowledge representation and reasoning; propositional logic, first-order logic and automated theorem proving, etc.; planning; uncertainty and probabilistic reasoning; machine learning and deep learning basics; selected topics include cognitive models, distributed AI, intelligent agents, perception, robotics, natural language, etc.; philosophical issues, including ethics
prerequisites: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor; graduate classification
title: Artificial Intelligence

description: Design of algorithms for use on highly parallel machines; area-time complexity of problems and general lower bound theory; application (of these concepts) to artificial intelligence, computer vision and VLSI design automation
prerequisites: CSCE 221
title: Parallel Algorithm Design and Analysis

description: Formal models of computation such as pushdown automata; Turing machines and recursive functions; unsolvability results; complexity of solvable results
prerequisites: CSCE 433
title: Theory of Computability

description: Introduction to computational biology; formulations of biology problems as computational problems; computational approaches to solve problems in genomics and proteomics
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Computational Biology

description: Concrete algorithm design and analysis; abstract models to analyze the complexity of problems; NP-Completeness; approximation and probabilistic algorithms
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Analysis of Algorithms

description: Speech production and perception (speech apparatus, articulatory/auditory phonetics); mathematical foundations (sampling, filtering, probability, pattern recognition); speech analysis and coding (short-time Fourier analysis, linear prediction, cesptrum); speech recognition (dynamic time warping, hidden Markov models, language models); speech synthesis (front-end, back-end); speech modification (overlap-add, enhancement, voice conversion)
prerequisites: ECEN 314 or equivalent or approval of instructor; basic knowledge of signals and systems, linear algebra, probability and statistics; programming experience in a high-level language is required
title: Speech Processing

description: On the design and implementation of Intelligent Agents and coordination mechanisms among multiple agents, ranging from theoretical principles to practical methods for implementation
prerequisites: CSCE 420 or CSCE 625
title: Intelligent Agents

description: Exploration of traditionally disenfranchised user populations due to disability including discrimination and population characteristics; review of ethical and legal motivations for creating accessible technology; universal design and its role in the development, evaluation, design, and implementation of equitable and inclusive software and computer-based solutions; application of accessibility standards; compilation of a literature review on a current topic in accessible computing
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Accessible Computing

description: Machine learning is the study of self-modifying computer systems that can acquire new knowledge and improve their own performance; survey machine learning techniques, which include induction from examples, conceptual clustering, explanation-based learning, exemplar learning and analogy, discovery and genetic algorithms
prerequisites: CSCE 420 or CSCE 625
title: Machine Learning

description: Intersection of artificial intelligence and computer-human interaction; emphasis on designing and evaluating systems that learn about and adapt to their users, tasks, and environments
prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of instructor
title: Intelligent User Interfaces

description: Introduction and survey of artificial intelligence methods for mobile robots (ground, aerial, or marine) for science and engineering majors; theory and practice of unmanned systems, focusing on biological and cognitive principles which differ from control theory formulations
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: AI Robotics

description: Basic concepts in neural computing; functional equivalence and convergence properties of neural network models; associative memory models; associative, competitive and adaptive resonance models of adaptation and learning; selective applications of neural networks to vision, speech, motor control and planning; neural network modeling environments
prerequisites: MATH 251 and MATH 304 or approval of instructor
title: Deep Learning

description: Deterministic, non-deterministic, alternating and probabilistic computations; reducibilities; P, NP and other complexity classes; abstract complexity; time, space and parallel complexity; and relativized computation
prerequisites: CSCE 627 or approval of instructor
title: Complexity Theory

description: Focus on teaching Natural Language Processing (NLP) fundamentals including language models, automatic syntactic processing and semantic understanding; introduction to major NLP applications including information extraction, machine translation, text summarization, dialogue systems and sentiment analysis
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Natural Language Processing - Foundations and Techniques

description: Introduction to the design and analysis of quantum algorithms; basic principles of the quantum circuit model; gives a gentle introduction to basic quantum algorithms; reviews recent results in quantum information processing
prerequisites: CSCE 629 or approval of instructor
title: Quantum Algorithms

description: Representation of 3-dimensional objects, including polyhedral objects, curved surfaces, volumetric representations and CSG models; techniques for hidden surface/edge removal and volume rendering; illumination and shading; antialiasing; ray tracing; radiosity; animation; practical experience with state-of-the-art graphics hardware and software
prerequisites: CSCE 441 or approval of instructor
title: Computer Graphics

description: Fundamentals of formalizing reinforce learning (RL) problems such as Markov Decision Process as well as various techniques and approaches for optimizing the agent's behavior given such problems; exploration of basic concepts and approaches in deep neural networks; overview of state-of-the-art algorithms that integrate deep learning with reinforcement learning; basics of reinforcement learning as well as deep reinforcement learning
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Deep Reinforcement Learning

description: Problems, methods and recent developments in intelligent systems and robotics. May be taken at multiple times for credit as content varies
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Seminar in Intelligent Systems and Robotics

description: Geometric and solid modeling concepts, Freeform curves and surfaces (splines and Bezier) with their relational, intersectional and global mathematic properties; parametric representation of solids, topology of closed curved surfaces, boundary concepts and Boolean/Euler operators; construction and display of curves and surfaces, and solid models
prerequisites: CSCE 441 and CSCE 442 or equivalent
title: Geometric Modeling

description: Tools and techniques for generation, handling and analysis of two dimensional digital images; image representation and storage; display, media conversion, painting and drawing; warping; color space operations, enhancement, filtering and manipulation
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Digital Image

description: Principles of image synthesis from 3-D scene descriptions; topics may include local and global illumination, shading, shadow determination, hidden surface elimination, texturing, raster graphics algorithms, transformations and projections
prerequisites: Graduate classification in Visualization; VIZA 652 , or approval of instructor
title: Image Synthesis

description: Mathematical and artistic principles of 3-D modeling and sculpting; includes proportions, skeletal foundation, expression and posture, line of action; curves, surfaces and volumes, interpolation and approximation, parametric and rational parametric polynomials, constructive solid geometry, and implicit representations
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Computer Aided Sculpting

description: Physical simulation as used in choreography, geometric modeling, and the creation of special effects in computer graphics; a variety of problems and techniques are explored which may include particle-methods, modeling and simulation of flexible materials, kinematics and constraint systems
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Physically-Based Modeling

description: Theory and practice of virtual reality (VR); interactive 3D virtual environments, immersive technology, perceptual realism, and embodied interaction experience; overview of VR with topics including input devices, output devices, 3D interaction techniques, augmented reality, the role of realism in VR, navigation techniques, design guidelines, and evaluation methods; hands-on experience designing VR experiences emphasizing application, demonstration, or research purposes
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Virtual Reality

description: Introduction to the compilation mechanism to generate executable files and raw binary codes from sources codes; the executable file formats for an operation system to run the binary code; disassembly algorithms and control graph analysis; static and dynamic analyses; case studies on code obfuscation, codebreaking and malware analysis
prerequisites: CSCE 313 or approval of instructor
title: Software Reverse Engineering

description: Classical and modern techniques for the computational solution of problems of the type that traditionally arise in the natural sciences and engineering; introductions to number representation and errors, locating roots of equations, interpolation, numerical integration, linear algebraic systems, spline approximations, initial-value problems for ordinary differential equations and finite-difference methods for partial differential equations
prerequisites: CSCE 442 or MATH 417 ; graduate classification
title: Computer Methods in Applied Sciences

description: Principles of high-performance scientific computing systems, vectorization, programming on supercomputers, numerical methods for supercomputers, performance measuring of supercomputers, multitasking
prerequisites: CSCE 614
title: Supercomputing

description: A foundation course in human centered systems and information; understanding and conceptualizing interaction; design and prototyping methodologies; evaluation frameworks; visual design using color, space, layering, and media; information structuring and visualization; animation and games; individual and team programming projects
prerequisites: Graduate classification or CSCE 436 or 444 or approval of instructor
title: Human-Centered Computing

description: This class investigates the potential and realized impact of computers in the design of new media, explores the variety of relationships between authors and readers of interactive materials, and explores the influence of media design and content expressed
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Computers and New Media

description: Introduction to randomized algorithms; selected tools and techniques from probability theory and game theory are reviewed, with a view towards algorithmic applications; the main focus is a thorough discussion of the main paradigms, techniques, and tools in the design and analysis of randomized algorithms; a detailed analysis of numerous algorithms illustrates the abstract concepts and techniques
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Randomized Algorithms

description: Principles and practices of distributed processing; protocols, remote procedure calls; file sharing; reliable system design; load balancing; distributed database systems; protection and security; implementation
prerequisites: CSCE 313 and CSCE 463 or CSCE 612
title: Distributed Processing Systems

description: Wireless and mobile systems; wireless communication fundamentals; wireless medium access control design; transmission scheduling; network and transport protocols over wireless design, simulation and evaluation; wireless capacity; telecommunication systems; vehicular, adhoc, and sensor network systems; wireless security; mobile applications
prerequisites: CSCE 463 or CSCE 464 or approval of instructor
title: Wireless and Mobile Systems

description: Security aspects of various network protocols including investigation and tool development using "live" machines and networks
prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of instructor
title: Advanced Networking and Security

description: Introduction to methods for the analysis, classification and clustering of high dimensional data in Computer Science applications; includes density and parameter estimation, linear feature extraction, feature subset selection, clustering, Bayesian and geometric classifiers, non-linear dimensionality reduction methods from statistical learning theory and spectral graph theory, Hidden Markov models, and ensemble learning
prerequisites: MATH 222, MATH 411 or equivalent, and graduate classification
title: Pattern Analysis

description: Introduction to fundamental algorithmic results in distributed computing systems; leader election, mutual exclusion, consensus, logical time and causality, distributed snapshots, algorithmic fault tolerance, shared memory, clock synchronization
prerequisites: CSCE 411 or equivalent or approval of instructor
title: Distributed Algorithms and Systems

description: Combinatorial theory of polytopes as a tool for the solution of combinatorial optimization problems; applications to max flow, matching and matroids; geometric interpretation of the results indicating the profound role that polyhedral combinatorics play in the design and complexity of approximation algorithms
prerequisites: CSCE 629
title: Computational Optimization

description: Representation, storage, and access to very large multimedia document collections; fundamental data structures and algorithms of information storage and retrieval systems; techniques to design and evaluate complete retrieval systems, including cover of algorithms for indexing, compressing, and querying very large collections
prerequisites: CSCE 310 or CSCE 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification
title: Information Storage and Retrieval

description: Comprehensive coverage of Computer-human Interaction (CHI) including history, importance, design theories and future direction; modeling computer users and interfaces, empirical techniques for task analysis and interface design, and styles of interaction
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Computer-Human Interaction

description: Covers design, implementation and use of technical systems that support people working cooperatively; draws from the research area of Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW) and includes current theoretical, practical, technical and social issues in CSCW and future directions of the field
prerequisites: CSCE 671 or CSCE 610 or approval of instructor
title: Computer Supported Collaborative Work

description: Broad overview of data mining, integrating related concepts from machine learning and statistics; exploratory data analysis, pattern mining, clustering and classification; applications to scientific and online data
title: Data Mining and Analysis

description: Fundamental concepts of distributed systems with a focus on the emerging application of cloud computing; design, analyze, and optimize distributed systems; includes MapReduce, synchronization, peer-to-peer systems, election, distributed agreement, replication, job assignment
title: Distributed Systems and Cloud Computing

description: Visual representation and design of data and information; 3D visualization, infographics, data narratives, principles of visual data encoding, and interaction techniques
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Data Visualization

description: The theory and techniques of testing VLSI-based circuits and systems, and design for testability

description: Research leading to thesis or dissertation in respective fields of dairy production and dairy manufacturing
