description: Research for thesis or dissertation
title: Research

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: School of Performance, Visualization & Fine Art Study Abroad. For Graduate students in approved study abroad programs participation in reciprocal educational exchange programs. This course acts a designated placeholder course for TAMU Graduate students studying away
prerequisites: Admission to approved program
title: School of Performance, Visualization & Fine Art Study Abroad

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Investigation of how to write and publish scholarly articles, reviews, and essays in the arts; investigation of the requirements of journals in specialization areas of the arts; overview of how to write effectively in the arts; navigation of the publishing process with understanding of the different aspects of successful publications
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Writing for Publication in the Arts

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Discussion of the theories and principles of teaching and learning in higher education as it relates to arts education; exploration of the unique challenges and opportunities of teaching arts courses in higher education, including issues of funding, faculty workload and research in the arts, accessibility and inclusion, ethics, student engagement, and technology as it relates to arts in higher education
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: The Arts in Higher Education

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Exploration of aesthetic, sociocultural, political, and ecological issues in creating art that engages community and affects positive change; study of exemplary artworks and creation of proposals for new ones; emphasis on creative thinking, community involvement, collaborative enterprise, research, and the creation of art works honoring aesthetic and cultural values
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Understanding Communities in the Arts

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Examination of the research processes and practices and initiates students' preparation for executing scholarly research and writing; critical examination of quantitative and qualitative research; overview of how to formulate research questions, research design, data collection, and analysis
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Research Methods in the Arts

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Overview of skills and knowledge to critically analyze and evaluate research in the arts; introduction to key concepts, methods, and ethical considerations involved in analyzing arts research; examination of the role of research in the creative process and how it contributes to production and innovation; research literacy in the context of the arts
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Analyzing Research in the Arts

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Faculty-supervised, project-based, collaborative art making experience with artist(s) in residence. May be taken four times for credit
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Interdisciplinary Arts Practicum

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Individual problems involving application of theory and practice in performance, visualization and fine arts in an international setting
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Selected topics in an identified area of performance, visualization and fine arts
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Methods and materials of reading instruction in the elementary grades; past, present and emerging programs; organization and administration of programs and classroom management; teaching reading to special groups; issues in reading
title: Teaching Reading in the Elementary Grades

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Examination of pedagogies that use literacy to help students learn across disciplines and content areas; exploration of aspects of literacy practices including reading, writing, discussion, interpretive and critical activities for the comprehension and evaluation of new content; strategies for teaching new literacies skills associated with ICT, media and visual reading; examination of theoretically grounded and empirically supported instructional methods
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Using Advanced Literacy to Teach and Learn Across Disciplines

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Appraisal and diagnosis of reading problems; practicum in administration and interpretation of individual reading inventories
prerequisites: RDNG 602 or concurrent enrollment
title: Reading Diagnosis

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Practicum in recognition, diagnosis, remediation and corrective procedures of reading-study problems; demonstration and laboratory analysis of physiological and psychological factors related to reading disabilities
prerequisites: RDNG 604
title: Practicum in Literacy Intervention

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Psychological, linguistic and physical factors related to reading performance; implications for content and teaching methods; appraisal of current research and related reading for teachers, supervisors and reading specialists
title: Foundations of Reading Instruction

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Children's Literature and Literacy. Critical selection and evaluation of various children's literature genres; comparative studies of children's literature; development, implementation and evaluation of research in children's literature and literacy; integration of reading and response theory into the study of literature
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Children’s Literature and Literacy

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Analysis and evaluation of a wide range of children's and adolescent literature; development, implementation, and evaluation of research in literature and literacy for meeting the needs of all students; analysis of issues influencing literature and literacy in a pluralistic society
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Children's Literacy and Literature for all Children

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Procedures, skills and dispositions associated with the development, implementation and leadership of literacy programs at a school and district level; roles of reading specialists, professional development, program evaluation, change processes
prerequisites: Doctoral classification; approval of instructor
title: Organization and Supervision of Reading Programs

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Orthography of different languages and its relation to literacy acquisition and failure to acquire basic literacy skills. This is a seminar course in reading, language arts, bilingual education, psychology, linguistics, and related fields
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Literacy and Language

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Examines the nature of writing development and how to assess both formally and informally; includes successful instructional techniques based on empirical evidence
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Writing: Development, Assessment and Instruction

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Exploration of recent research in reading; identification of trends and patterns in research designs and findings; and generation of new hypotheses and guidelines for improving current practice
prerequisites: Doctoral classification or approval of instructor
title: Reading Research and Trends

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Seminar in the study and critique of major theories of the reading process that have been influential in the fields of reading, language arts, educational psychology and related fields
prerequisites: Doctoral classification or approval of instructor
title: Theories of the Reading Process

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Selected topics in an identified area of reading
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Analysis of current research; instruments and analytic techniques used in the selection and formulation of research problems
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Analytic Techniques in Recreation, Parks and Tourism

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Principles and practices of youth development supports, opportunities, programs and services; emphasis on the role of out-of-school time settings in youth development; programming considerations related to gender, disability and culture; introduction to evaluation and financing of youth development programs
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Youth Development Programs and Services

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Development of skills and competencies needed to successfully manage paid and volunteer staff, design youth programs, address safety and risk management issues; build community support of public, non-profit, and for profit or commercial youth programs and agencies; history and scope of youth serving organizations; programming and staffing strategies; managing, mentoring and training staff; diverse approaches to program curriculum and design; behavior management and recognition of youth participants; youth protection; relevant laws and legal mandates; safety, health and wellness; youth advocacy and engagement; working with parents and community partners; and issues and innovations in youth development
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Practice and Development of Effective Skills for Youth Development

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Development of knowledge and skills to successfully write grant proposals and design program evaluation plans for youth development organizations, including clarifying organization mission and program needs, locating funding opportunities, following grant guidelines and using different methods to evaluation programs
prerequisites: ALEC 670/RPTS 670 or approval of instructor
title: Grant Writing and Program Evaluation for Youth Development Organizations

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Organizational behavior, administration and management of public, non-profit and for-profit youth programs and agencies; foundations of management and organizational behavior in the context of youth organizations; organizational culture; strategic planning; capacity building; evaluation; marketing and communication; human resource management; financial resource development; budgeting and fiscal management; contemporary issues facing the youth development field
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Administration, Management and Leadership in Youth Programs

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Application of recreation and youth development knowledge to a specific project or program of a cooperating youth development organization
prerequisites: Graduate classification; enrollment in the MRYD program
title: Youth Development Capstone Experience

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Elements of watershed management and principles and practices of wildland management for protection, maintenance and improvement of water resources values; current literature and research advances
title: Wildland Watershed Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Designed for ecologists, naturalists, and other parties who wish to have a deeper understanding of the behavior of terrestrial animals in terms of the habitats they frequent, what and where they feed, den and bedding locations, and other activities; designed for wildlife professionals who work in the field conducting animal surveys, observations, and capturing/handling wildlife or who are otherwise involved in teaching field skills
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Wildlife Tracks and Signs

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Understand ways communities manage natural resources; understand the roles of collaboration, participation, agency, power, and resilience in solving local resource management problems
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Community Organization and Natural Resources Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Designed to acquaint with major land use practices on lands that produce wildlife, how these influences wildlife production and alterations or manipulations of habitat used to achieve specific wildlife management goals
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Wildlife Habitat Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Techniques available to directly and indirectly manipulate wild animal populations to achieve balance between socioeconomic and aesthetic values
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Techniques of Wildlife Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: This class provides an overview of diseases that affect wild mammals, birds, amphibians and reptiles. Emphasis is placed on diseases with population-level impacts to wildlife and those that are transmissible to humans or domestic animals and those found in Texas. For exams students should know common names of diseases, synonyms and the etiologic agent. They should be able to describe the agent and its basic history, its hosts and geographic distribution. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. They should be able to describe the signs of the disease, how it is transmitted, gross lesions, diagnostic criteria and prevention/control measures
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Wildlife Diseases

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: This course introduces the principles and practices of grazing management with a focus on developing adaptive, ecologically sound and economically viable grazing systems. Students will explore how timing, intensity, frequency and duration of grazing affect plant, soil and animal responses across different forage types and production contexts
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Grazing Management Principles and Planning

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Principles of rangeland brush and weed control with mechanical, chemical, burning and biological methods; interrelationships of brush management with grazing, wildlife and watershed management; planning and economic analysis of range improvement practices
title: Rangeland Vegetation Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Examination of the causes, consequences, and management of biological invasions by exotic plant and animal species in North America and globally; critical evaluation and synthetization of primary literature; emphasis on original research in basic or applied invasion ecology
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Invasive Species Ecology and Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Study of the fundamentals of the restoration of animal populations and the resources they require; factors that control the distribution and abundances of animals in relation to restoration; and how restoration plans for wildlife are developed
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Wildlife Restoration

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Study and compare human and natural ecosystems using diversity, interrelations, cycles, and energy as the conceptional organization; central themes of the course are sustainability, stewardship and science
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Ecology and Society

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Principles of effectively communicating natural resource science to a diverse stakeholder group; development of critical skills for obtaining and retaining employment in the Rangeland, Wildlife, and Fisheries Management fields; experience in audience identification, mixed-media presentations and interpersonal communications skills unique to the culture of diverse natural resources stakeholders
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Communicating Natural Resources

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Management of various herbivorous large mammals, both game and non-game; development of knowledge on how to implement habitat and population management techniques to achieve management goals; history of modern wildlife management as it relates to the restoration and harvest of various species as game that once were imperiled; utilization of natural history information in the selection of the most beneficial management techniques and a survey of the techniques currently used in large mammal population management
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Large Mammal Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Integrated framework for watershed planning that addresses the related biophysical, social and economic issues; comprehensive in scope and approach; tools and techniques for developing sound watershed management policy and practice; water issues, problems and regulations for Texas
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Contemporary Issues in Water Resource Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Approaches used to identify, evaluate and manage ecological risks of chemicals on aquatic and terrestrial environments; emphasis on methods useful to assess effects of contaminants on ecosystems; testing techniques, site assessment and monitoring procedures, regulatory requirements and field and laboratory techniques
title: Ecological Risk Assessment

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Wetlands as ecological systems that are prime habitats for wildlife and fish; geomorphology, hydrology, limnology, plant and animal communities, and humans use and management; wetlands as ultimate reservoirs of environmental pollutants; distribution, fate and effects of environmental pollutants on aquatic and terrestrial wildlife
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Wetland Ecology and Pollution

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Importance of private lands and how collaboration between landowners and natural resource professionals is essential for their conservation; introduction to general concepts and principles of private land stewardship (PLS); acquaintance with the origins of land stewardship and private lands, trends and status of private lands at the national and regional levels, and common approaches and tools for PLS, legal, regulatory and economic challenges and opportunities; introduction on how to foster land stewardship from multiple perspectives (agency, professional manager and landowner), the spiritual responsibility of stewardship and the development of a land ethic
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Private Land Stewardship

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Integration of past conservation actions and icons with modern day polices; exploration of conservation funding mechanisms; instruction in hands-on learning related to firearm safety, components; hunter education certification; field exercises on departmental facilities and field trip to state conservation agency
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Conservation Principles and the Role of Hunting

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Principle of fish production for stock enhancement and human food. Species of fish used for production, cross-breeding and selection; feeds and feeding of fish and nutritional and environmental requirements for optimum productivity; effects of fish production on land and water uses as related to conservation
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Aquaculture

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Application of the 1987 Wetland Delineation Manual in use by the Army Corps of Engineers; field indicators of hydrophytic vegetation, hydric soils, wetland hydrology, methods for making jurisdictional determination in non-disturbed and disturbed areas, recognition of problem wetlands and technical guidelines for wetlands
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Wetland Delineation

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Overview of the Department of Defense (DOD) lands within a temporal, geographic, and environmental context and perspective; major policies/laws impacting military land use and areas critical to mission sustainment; management strategies important to sustaining installations and ranges
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Sustainable Military Land Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Review of land management practices and challenges on military and adjacent private lands through field visits of select military installations. Field trips required. Previous or concurrent
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Field Military Land Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Review formation and implementation of major natural resource laws and policies that impact land uses; overview of natural resource laws/policies followed by presentations of a selected case study; current natural resource management (including forestry, air, water, wildlife, climate change and energy) programs and institutions analyzed and related to current natural resource policy challenges
title: Wildlife and Natural Resource Policy

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Health disorders and diseases of finfish and shellfish including water quality issues and management, environmental endocrine disruptors, biosecurity and practical techniques used to isolate, identify and manage or mitigate diseases
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Fish Health and Diseases

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Connects the life history of wild and domestic animals with the quality of their habitat by examining the transfer of energy and nutrients from foods to body tissues and activities for survival, growth and reproduction; exploration of the use of nutrition for management and conservation of animal populations and their habitats
prerequisites: Graduate classification; ECCB 205 or BIOL 357 ; ANSC 107 or BIOL 107 ; or approval of instructor
title: Nutrition of Range and Wild Animals

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Geographic Information System (GIS) approach to the integration of spatial and attribute data to study the capture, analysis, manipulation and portrayal of natural resource data; examination of data types/formats, as well as the integration of GIS with remote sensing and Global Positioning System; laboratory includes extensive use of GIS applications to conduct analyses of topics in natural resources
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Geographic Information System for Resource Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Theories and methods of psychology applied to conservation behavior for the improvement of relationships between people and natural systems; understand challenges and generate solutions related to the human psyche and wilderness, children and nature, role of culture
title: Conservation Psychology

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Ecological, cultural, and historical dimensions of human-wildlife interactions; root causes of conflict; multidisciplinary frameworks of analysis; lessons learned from practitioners; examples of coexistence; case studies across taxa and continents
prerequisites: Graduate classification
title: Human-Wildlife Conflict and Coexistence

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Theoretical and applied literature on the interaction between individuals, communities and parks and protected areas; study of socio-ecological systems, individual and societal values of parks and protected areas, visitor experiences, human impacts, environmental policy and sustainability
prerequisites: Graduate Classification or permission from the instructor
title: Human Dimensions of Parks and Protected Areas

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Development and application of leadership theories and models within natural resource settings; introduction to and examination of historical, philosophical and theoretical aspects of leadership; exploration and evaluation of the ethical and influential dimensions of leadership within a natural resource context; critical examination of the contemporary research characteristics of effective leadership in relation to natural resources; engagement with natural resources leaders and exploration of case studies within the profession
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Leadership in Natural Resource Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Overview of seminal readings in rangelands, wildlife and fisheries; examination of foundational theories and concepts in rangelands, wildlife and fisheries
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Foundations in Rangeland, Wildlife, and Fisheries Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Basic quantitative principles and methods applied to ecological systems
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Quantitative Methods in Natural Resources

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Analysis of the legal theories used to allocate and protect environmental resources; common law, federal and state statutes, and international treaties dealing with the environment; policies and laws for controlling air, water, solid waste, toxic waste and water pollution; species protection and natural resource use
title: Environmental Law and Policy

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Evolution of natural resources regulatory policies and how this influences current procedures for environmental and natural resources assessment and management; demonstration of the environmental impact assessment procedures and policy issues associated with environmental impacts
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Environmental Impact Assessment

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Practices and principles with a focus on the variations in regional management techniques in North America, from north to south; history of fisheries and pond management, the pond environment, stocking strategies for recreational small impoundments, fisheries management in small bodies of water, water quality management, problem troubleshooting in small impoundments and management opportunities
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Fisheries and Small Impoundment Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Identification and management of common and problematic aquatic vegetation species; aquatic plant ecology and management of aquatic vegetation as aquatic animal habitat; management methods include physical, chemical and biological methods as well as propagation and introduction and restoration
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Aquatic Vegetation Identification and Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Introduction to structural equation modeling (SEM); background on conceptual issues, application of the method, and insight on SEM software; measurement theory, missing data analysis, non-normal data, confirmatory factor analysis, path analysis, multi-group models
prerequisites: STAT 636 , STAT 652 , EPSY 641 , EPSY 643 , EPSY 650 or approval of instructor
title: Latent Variable Model Applications

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Important current developments in wildlife or fisheries fields with special reference to literature. Students may register up to but no more than two sections of this course in the same semester
title: Seminar

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: On-the-job training in fields of wildlife and fisheries sciences
prerequisites: Graduate classification in Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences
title: Professional Internship

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Individual study and research on selected problem approved by instructor and graduate advisor. Credit adjusted in accordance with requirements of each individual case
prerequisites: Approval of the department head or associate department head
title: Directed Studies

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Special topics in wildlife ecology, fisheries ecology, vertebrate systematics, evolutionary biology of vertebrates and conservation education
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Original research on selected wildlife and/or fisheries problem to be used in thesis or dissertation
title: Research

description: Evaluation of the historical evolution of supply chain and operations management; analysis of current research and controversial issues in the field. May be taken four times for credit
prerequisites: Doctoral classification and approval of department head
title: Doctoral Seminar in Operations and Supply Chain Management

description: Utilization of quantitative tools such as forecasting, optimization and Monte Carlo simulation in order to deal with uncertainties in business and to assist in making better business decisions. May be repeated up to 3 hours credit. Classification 6 students may not enroll in this course
prerequisites: Enrollment is limited to MBA students
title: Business Analytics

description: Collection, tabulation and presentation of numerical data; sampling, estimation of averages and variation, probability and error, hypothesis testing, linear and logistic regression; practical applications to functional problems in accounting, finance, marketing and management
title: Statistical Foundation of Data Analytics

description: Theory and applications of designing, analyzing and controlling productive systems in the allocation and use of resources to produce goods and services. May be repeated for up to 3 hours credit. Classification 6 students may not enroll in this course
prerequisites: SCMT 610 or equivalent; enrollment is limited to MBA students
title: Operations Management

description: Focus on the integrated management of the total product delivery system; purchasing, inventory management and distribution functions with emphasis on physical and information flows
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Supply Chain Management

description: Processes to identify and manage suppliers for goods and services to support operations; including sourcing, contracting, negotiations, buying procedures, cost and price analysis, vendor relations, auditing and inspection, supplier relations and applications to information technology systems
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Sourcing and Procurement Management

description: Application of quantitative decision-making techniques to management decision problems; focus on model development, solution and implementation of results with particular emphasis on linear and mixed-integer programming
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Supply Chain Modeling and Optimization

description: Study of the global environment of business; development of a conceptual framework and analytical skills for managing supply chains spanning multiple countries and regions; logistics and risk management of firms operating in the global market
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Global Supply Chain and Logistics

description: Introduction to business process design and analysis; tools and techniques to document, analyze and improve business processes; Six Sigma process design and improvement; process metrics; computer simulation of processes; aligning business process with organizational goals and objectives; and case study of real world business problems
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor; SCMT 614 , SCMT 660 or approval of instructor
title: Business Process Design

description: Study of how to build and evaluate the “operating system” of the firm to maximize value; study of how to tailor the firm’s operational competencies, assets and processes to a specific business strategy with focus on product companies
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Operations Strategy

description: Development of analytical techniques used by large, multiple site service businesses; study of analytical tools to augment or replace the more qualitative management decision making historically prevalent in service sector firms
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Service Operations Models

description: Security of global supply chains; selection of appropriate technologies utilized in securing global supply chains; exploration of planning responses to disaster events in relation to the delivery and receipt of goods and services; design of draft security policies for an organization’s supply chain
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Supply Chain Security

description: Provision of key tools for operational transformation using practical lean principles; exploration of how time pressures and turnaround needs in organizations can benefit from lean implementations; exploration of lean strategies such as root cause analysis, batch to pull processes, value stream mapping, level loading, line balancing
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Practical Lean Business Systems

description: Evaluation of the historical evolution, current research, and significant issues in management information systems, production/operations management, or management science

Topics include revenue generation, franchise valuation, media rights, sponsorship, labor issues, and emerging trends such as esports. Through case studies and guest speakers, students will develop a foundational understanding of sports business operations
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor

description: Focuses on the practical application of data analytics in the sport business industry, emphasizing data-driven decision-making across general business operations, including marketing, finance, operations, strategy, and performance management. The course is designed to provide students with an introduction to sport data analytics utilizing linear regression-based modeling approaches to analyze real-world sport datasets, applying a variety of statistical techniques to predict and optimize performance, financial outcomes, and operational efficiency. The course prioritizes hands-on data applications to produce actionable insights for sport organizations, and students will learn the iterative process of model building through trial and error and by working with other students on hands-on problems and an additional team-based project. At the conclusion of this course, students will be able to collect and analyze sport-related data using data analytics, whether the dependent variable is continuous (i.e., attendance or revenue), binary (i.e., a win or a loss) in nature, or whether group membership is being predicted. Several processes that students will gain experience in include the decision of which type of model is appropriate given the data to be analyzed or research question to be answered, the selection of appropriate independent variables based on knowledge of the sport business industry, the proper interpretation of coefficients and measures of model fit, and the ability to communicate advanced statistical information to a lay audience
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor

description: A rigorous and data-driven course, equipping students with advanced analytical skills to optimize athlete performance, prevent injuries, and inform team strategies. Students will analyze athlete performance metrics (e.g., biomechanical, physiological, statistical data) using Python, R, and Tableau, applying sophisticated statistical modeling, machine learning, and visualization techniques. Emphasis on practical applications, with projects involving datasets from professional and collegiate sports (e.g., NFL, NBA, NCAA, EPL)

description: This course provides students with the analytical, technical and strategic tools to understand and shape the future of fan engagement in the sports industry. Through applications of artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, natural language processing (NLP) and predictive modeling, students will learn how to analyze fan behavior and design data-driven engagement strategies across digital and physical platforms. Emphasis is placed on both the technical implementation of AI tools and their ethical, cultural and strategic implications in sport business decision-making

description: Intensive, project-based course where student teams serve as consultants for professional sports teams, college athletic programs or sports-related businesses (e.g., sports tech startups, agencies). Course is entirely project-based, with all work focused on scoping, analyzing and presenting actionable recommendations to real clients

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course introduces students to the essential creative, technical and analytical foundations of digital filmmaking. Emphasizing the integration of production craft and cinematic literacy, students engage in hands-on exercises in camera operation, lighting, sound recording and non-linear editing while critically analyzing how these techniques shape meaning, emotion and rhythm. Through the study of film form, aesthetics and visual storytelling, students develop the ability to translate abstract narrative ideas into concrete audiovisual expressions. The course positions filmmaking as both a practical craft and an interpretive art, an iterative process of seeing, composing, recording and refining, linking the expressive choices made on set and in post-production to the analytical understanding of cinematic form. By the end of the term, students will have completed a short digital project demonstrating technical fluency, aesthetic awareness and reflective critical insight
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Foundations of Digital Filmmaking

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course introduces students to the creative, analytical and technical techniques required to translate rich narrative ideas into innovative digital experiences across multiple media forms. Building from script analysis and visual storytelling fundamentals, students will explore how story structure, character and thematic intent transform when reimagined for screen, immersive and interactive contexts. The course spans linear and nonlinear modes of narrative, from short-form cinematic sequences and documentary hybrids to site-specific installations, augmented reality environments and online participatory works. Through both individual and collaborative exercises, students learn to adapt written and conceptual materials into digital storytelling prototypes that integrate visual, spatial and experiential design. Students will also examine the cultural and industrial frameworks surrounding intermedia and transmedia production, including intellectual property development, adaptation ethics and cross-platform authorship. By semester’s end, participants will have created a portfolio-ready project demonstrating their ability to translate complex textual or thematic material into a compelling, media-specific form of digital storytelling
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Digital Storytelling - Narrative Design Across Media

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the art, theory and technical practice of film editing and the post-production pipeline. Anchored in a non-linear editing system the fundamental principles taught are applicable across all professional, leading, editing platforms. Students explore the history and theory of film montage, continuity editing and stylistic techniques across fiction and non-fiction cinema. Technical training covers the complete editorial workflow, from media management, assembly, rough and fine cuts, to post-processing stages that include sound design fundamentals, professional color correction and grading, and final delivery for multiple distribution formats. The primary goal is to teach students to think like editors, understanding post-production as both a technical discipline and a vital phase of cinematic storytelling where rhythm, structure and affect are refined into expressive coherence
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Cinema Editing and Post-Production

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course explores the principles and practices of cinematography and lighting in the context of contemporary virtual production. Students engage with both the practical craft of image, making and the critical analysis of cinematic form, investigating how light, lens and movement operate as expressive, technical and interpretive tools. Through film analysis, design exercises and virtual simulation with a 3D real-time game and simulation development system, the course bridges the traditions of studio cinematography with emerging digital workflows. Students learn how to construct, evaluate and refine cinematic imagery, translating aesthetic and narrative intention into visual and spatial composition. The course emphasizes cinematography as a language of thought and emotion, uniting analytical insight with creative experimentation in both physical and virtual environments
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: Virtual Cinematography and Lighting

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course serves as the culminating experience for the virtual production focus area, integrating prior coursework in digital storytelling, virtual cinematography, lighting and post-production. Structured as a simulated professional production environment, students work in small teams to conceive, pitch, plan and execute a short narrative film utilizing the university’s LED volume stage (or equivalent virtual production technology). The course emphasizes advanced project management, iterative content development (ICVFX/Unreal Engine asset creation), collaborative pre-visualization and the rigorous schedule of a physical virtual production shoot. The semester functions as a single, continuous production cycle culminating in post-production finishing and professional delivery, resulting in a portfolio-ready short film that demonstrates technical fluency, creative leadership and team-based collaboration
prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor
title: On Set Virtual Production

description: CONTENT. Blacks in the United States from the colonial period to 1877. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how Black freedom has been expressed across art, speech, political action, media, visual cultures and writings designed to challenge injustice, build solidarity and imagine alternative futures. Considers both well-known and lesser-known figures, recognizing that activism operates through leaders, communities and collective voices. Course content may include material involving racial conflict, oppression and struggle in the United States and/or around the globe. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds recognition of communication as a tool for social response, institutional critique and public engagement. Provides perspective for professional fields that require cultural awareness, ethical judgment and responsiveness to diverse audiences, such as education, media, public service, community leadership, law and advocacy-related work. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media, history, social movements or communication. Contributes to civic understanding by tracing how ideas become actions through communication practices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how articulations of Black freedom have long served as catalysts for action, social change and public debate in the United States and across the globe. Positions their strategies, not only as expressions of a specific community, but as case studies in persuasion, resistance, leadership and/or collective voice that have shaped constitutional interpretation, civic participation and public opinion more broadly. Considers how struggles for justice by one group reveal broader questions shared across groups, such as rights, authority, belonging and national identity. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of abolitionist writings, protest speeches, spirituals and freedom songs; rhetorical strategies of civil rights, Black Power and/or contemporary justice movements; analysis of communication through sermons, manifestos, poetry, performance and/or media; exploration of visual and digital media as tools of resistance and community-building; consideration of leadership, collective action and messaging in local and/or global liberation struggles. Course material may reference conflict, repression or political controversy as relevant to understanding communication within movements for freedom and justice. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 105

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 313 or approval of instructor

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 307

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 306

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 311 ; junior or senior classification
title: Advanced Research in Agriculture and Life Sciences Communications

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 105 ; junior or senior classification
title: Emerging Media in Agriculture and Life Sciences

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGCJ 301
title: Digital Storytelling in Agriculture and Life Sciences II

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

Characteristics of our economic system and basic economic concepts; survey of the farm and ranch firm and its organization and management; structure and operation of the marketing system; functional and institutional aspects of agricultural finance; government farm programs

title: Fundamentals of the AgriFood Sales Industry

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

title: Building Customer Relationships in AgriFood Selling

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

For AGEC majors, this class will provide a foundation for advanced AGEC courses, while non-AGEC majors will acquire a broad foundational understanding of agribusiness management skills to complement their technical major
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AGEC 105 ; junior or senior classification; knowledge of Microsoft Excel
title: Decision-Making for the Agribusiness Professional

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: AGEC 105 or 3 hours of economics; ACCT 209 or ACCT 229 ; and junior or senior classification
title: Financial Management in Agriculture

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Survey of management practices using case studies to evaluate management issues in agribusiness firms in the context of the four functions of management such as planning, organizing, leading and controlling; emphasis on best practices throughout the food marketing chain; examination of how businesses and business executives succeed; application of previously learned knowledge in making business decisions similar to those encountered in professional careers
prerequisites: AGEC 105 or 3 hours of economics; and junior or senior classification
title: Agribusiness Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification

prerequisites: AGEC 105 or 3 hours of economics; junior or senior classification or approval of department head

prerequisites: AGEC 105 , ECON 202 , or equivalent

prerequisites: AGEC 317 ; MKTG 321 ; and junior or senior agribusiness majors only
title: Agribusiness and Food Market Analysis

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: AGEC 105 or ECON 202 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor

description: (ANTH 2346, HUMA 2323) Introduction to Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates anthropology as the holistic and relativistic study of humankind, exploring human life across diverse cultures, time periods and geographical locations. Examines the discipline through its four major subfields: archaeology (the study of material culture and the past), biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), sociocultural anthropology (the study of cultural systems and social organization) and linguistic anthropology (the study of language construction and symbolism). Applies fundamental concepts, including the scientific method and evolutionary theory, to complex human experiences. Develops abilities in critical thinking, analysis of empirical data and effective communication, engaging with culturally diverse and sometimes controversial subjects. Analyzes the discipline’s relationship with society and its impact on global communities over time. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores human evolutionary history, including primate behavior and hominin development; analyzes the history of human biological variation and the lack of a scientific basis for "race"; examines material culture, ancient civilizations and archaeological methods; studies language construction, symbolism and communication patterns; investigates social organization, including kinship, family, marriage and gender; explores economic systems, political structures, religion and belief systems; and applies anthropological thinking to contemporary issues such as, but not limited to, health, medicine, forensics, violence and global challenges. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world; also taught at Qatar campus
title: Introduction to Anthropology

description: Introduction to Archaeology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the basic principles of studying past human cultures through material remains. Surveys the fundamentals of archaeological practice and frameworks, applying interdisciplinary methods to reconstruct and interpret the archaeological record. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces careers in anthropology and archaeology and the skills needed for them. TOPICS AND THEMES. Interdisciplinary nature of archaeological research. Site formation, survival and identification. Field and laboratory methods including survey, excavation, recording, curation and various types of analysis including dating methods. Relationships between humans and environments. Human evolution and behavior including past movement, subsistence strategies, foraging strategies, trade, tool production and development, sedentism, symbolic and ritual behaviors, domestication, city and state formation and reconstruction of past social and individual identities. Archaeological ethics, the role of archaeology in contemporary society and heritage management. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Introduction to Archaeology

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the development of human societies and world prehistory from the earliest humans to the emergence of complex civilizations. Applies archaeological and historical methods and theories used to reconstruct past lifeways including culture, identity, migration and social development. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological and historical data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces ideas of personal and social responsibility and the skills needed for careers in anthropology and archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Human evolution and migration. Human relationships with the environment including climate change, subsistence strategies, extinction events, domestication and agriculture. Production, evolution and spread of material culture. Symbolic and ritual behavior. Development of sedentism, complex societies, urbanism, collective labor, written language, monument building, early states and empires. Discussion of individual and social identity, individual agency, archaeological ethics and the role of archaeology in contemporary society. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology
title: The Human Past

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys human cultures around the world using case studies of customs and cultural organization. Explores how anthropology is a holistic discipline focused on all of humanity, which integrates knowledge from diverse fields like history, economics, psychology, sociology and traditional sciences. Explores global interconnectedness alongside cultural diversity, addressing questions of "us and them". Develops a greater understanding of the breadth of variation in the human condition and the power of culture to shape individual experience. Recognizes the trade-offs between cultural relativist and universalist perspectives. Gains cultural awareness to inform future evaluations of domestic and global issues. Practices communicating opinions in a culturally respectful manner. Relates outcomes of cultural study to one’s understanding of one’s own culture. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes key anthropological concepts, including fieldwork, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, holism and ethnography. Considers human universals and cultural uniqueness. Studies cultural expressions related to basic perceptions (color, space, distance) and the body (beauty standards, adornment, modification). Explores systems of social organization, including gender, sports, games, communication, gestures and greetings. Investigates cultural practices concerning food, eating, reciprocity, trade, etiquette, folklore and magic. Examines cultural approaches to death, dying, medicine, illness and health
title: Peoples and Cultures of the World

description: Social and Cultural Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides overview of the field of social and cultural anthropology, exploring the diverse ways that human cultures shape experience across the globe, and the anthropological theory and research that attempt to understand this process. Through an exploration of different cultures, examines the major dimensions of cultural variation, including subsistence, family structure, political systems, language, religion and more. Fosters critical evaluation of cultural theories and different perspectives while promoting respectful discussion of complex and provocative topics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Key themes include culture, ethnographic methodology and the tension between relativist and universalist perspectives. Additional topics include kinship, family structure, gender, religion, language, subsistence, political systems, race, colonialism and applied anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Social and Cultural Anthropology

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of museum studies, exploring how museums collect, preserve, interpret and exhibit material culture to convey cultural, historical and scientific knowledge. Emphasizes museums as dynamic institutions shaped by ethical, educational and civic responsibilities and fosters critical inquiry into questions such as: Who do museums serve? How do objects acquire meaning? What responsibilities do museums have to communities and history? Provides a foundation for further study in museum work while developing skills in civic engagement, applied learning, collaboration, inclusion and leadership. Engages museums as spaces for dialogue and lifelong learning, encouraging reflection on how they shape public understanding and express broader social values. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in museum studies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include: history and development of museums; collecting practices from antiquity to the present; analysis of museum organization, leadership structures and varying types of institutions; consideration of professional standards, collections stewardship; evaluation of interpretation, educational programming and strategies for access and inclusion; ethical, educational and civic responsibilities of museums
title: Foundations of Museum Studies

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops skills vital for effective engagement in an increasingly diverse and interconnected world. Fosters personal awareness of biases, attitudes, values, beliefs and ways of knowing (epistemology). Explores the profound impact of culture on the ability to think critically and communicate effectively. Trains students to critically appraise how their worldview and life experiences shape the decisions they make. Synthesizes core concepts like culture, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, stereotypes, worldview and holism, applying them to the student's chosen discipline or subject of interest. Promotes enhanced self-knowledge and cross-cultural awareness through active, reflexive inquiry. Encourages challenging one's own thinking, especially when subject matter elicits an emotional reaction, to ensure critical engagement with evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes fundamental concepts in anthropology, including culture, diversity, race and ethnicity. Consideration of holism and reductionism in understanding systems and thought processes. Explores personal learning styles, personality strengths and systems of knowledge (epistemology). Examines communication dynamics, ethnocentrism, stereotypes, myths, fallacies and assumptions. Discusses ethical frameworks, including critical cultural relativism. Studies critical thinking skills applicable across varied professional, cultural and scientific contexts
title: Cross Cultural Competency

description: (ANTH 2301, 2401*) Introduction to Biological Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates human biology and evolution by exploring the origins of humanity through evolutionary processes and the Primate fossil record. Analyzes the mechanisms of evolutionary change, such as human genetics and heredity, that shape human populations and non-human primate diversity. Trains students to ask how shared evolutionary history influences modern human adaptation and variation, gaining a deeper awareness of how humans fit into the natural world. Discussion addresses the genetic and environmental basis of human biological variation, our relationship to other primates and the fossil record associated with our extinct hominin relatives/ancestors. Writing-intensive assignments are designed to develop students' critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers evolutionary processes acting on modern and ancient human populations; analyzes human genetics, heredity and molecular biology; studies non-human Primate anatomy, fossil record, classification, behavior and ecology; methods used to study the fossil record including comparative anatomy, taphonomy, basic fieldwork protocols and age estimation techniques; examines the human fossil record, including our earliest possible relatives, the Australopithecines, and species in the genus Homo; explores contemporary human biological variation, anatomy, adaptation, health and forensic anthropology; develops skills in critical thinking, inquiry and analysis of relevant sources. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world
prerequisites: Concurrent registration in ANTH 226 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology

description: (ANTH 2101, 2401*) Introduction to Biological Anthropology Laboratory. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fundamental evolutionary principles and the concepts of population genetics. Applies the scientific method to investigate evolutionary trends relevant to humans through hands-on exposure to fossils of non-human primates, human relatives and ancestors, and modern human evolution. Evaluates and synthesizes information regarding human ancestry and contemporary variation. Analyzes key trends related to human evolution, such as encephalization and bipedalism, by measuring and comparing real and modeled skeletal specimens. Lab exercises are designed to complement and reinforce topics covered in the lecture course ANTH 225 . TOPICS AND THEMES. Discussions of basic genetic principles, evolutionary mechanisms and population genetics. Analyzes human and non-human primate anatomy, focusing on skeletal morphology. Applies qualitative and quantitative methods for bone identification, skeletal growth, dental variation and locomotor function. Studies extant and extinct primate specimens, including their taxonomy, behavior and fossil record. Examinations of the hominin fossil record including casts of specimens from the following taxa: Australopithecus, Paranthropus and the genus Homo, including H. habilis, H. erectus, Middle Pleistocene Homo, Neanderthals and H. sapiens
prerequisites: Concurrent registration in ANTH 225 is recommended; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology Laboratory

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examine the foundational role of forensic anthropology within the broader forensic sciences which involves analyzing human skeletal remains for medico-legal applications, covering the history of the field and its development. Build theoretical knowledge of the discipline including the history of how the discipline developed and its role in the broader forensic sciences and international, federal and state levels. Apply proper anatomical terminology, taphonomy and comparative morphological methods to discuss and describe skeletal trauma, pathologies and anomalies. Apply and practice methods used to create a "biological profile" for an individual by estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry. Explore scene recovery methods and how skeletal analysis is applied in a variety of contexts, including routine casework, large-scale natural disasters, war casualties and human rights investigations. Critically discuss and analyze forensic methods by addressing the practical and ethical issues facing practicing forensic anthropologists today. TOPICS AND THEMES. Consider the history and foundations of forensic anthropology; study the broader medicolegal system, professional ethics and error assessment; apply osteological methods and anatomical terminology to describing human skeletal material; describe scene recovery methods such as location, recovery and taphonomic processes; apply and critically examine methods for estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry; identify and classify infectious disease, congenital conditions and nutritional deficiencies on the skeleton and teeth; explore individual identification techniques such as facial reconstruction and genetic genealogy; critically assess how forensic anthropology is portrayed in popular culture and the media. Discuss current topics considered relevant to the field by the American Academy of Forensic Science including, but not limited to, research ethics, reassessment of biological profile estimation methods and demographic underrepresentation in comparative collections
title: Introduction to Forensic Anthropology
