description: This course introduces the fundamental principles and applications of bioremediation as a sustainable approach to managing contaminated environments. Students will investigate common and emerging environmental contaminants, the critical factors influencing microbial activity, and conduct an in-depth analysis of the microbial metabolic pathways involved in contaminant degradation. Both in-situ and ex-situ bioremediation technologies are explored, alongside complementary physicochemical remediation processes. Through real-world case studies and applied projects, students evaluate recent advances in bioremediation pathways and innovative technologies. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the necessary knowledge and analytical skills to evaluate effective strategies for environmental restoration
prerequisites: CHEM 222 or CHEM 227
title: Microbial Processes in Bioremediation

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: This course integrates the principles and practices of environmental sampling and monitoring, focusing equally on theory and hands-on application. Students will examine the fundamentals of environmental monitoring and data analysis, pollutant chemistry, regulatory frameworks and Phase I Environmental Site Assessments. Building on this foundation, the course delves into sampling approaches and methodologies for environmental analysis using both in-situ and ex-situ analytical techniques. A dedicated laboratory component provides essential hands-on experience through projects that reinforce concepts, good laboratory practices, quality control and data interpretation. The course culminates with comprehensive capstone experiences, enabling students to apply their knowledge to real-world environmental challenges
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Sampling and Environmental Monitoring

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Management processes for managing projects in academic, government or industry settings; exploration of projects that are hypothesis driven, exploratory and product-driven; critical communication planning, meeting stakeholders and sponsors expectations and ensuring regulatory compliance; emphasis on project management life cycle, managing change, communication planning and the work environment
prerequisites: BESC 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Bioenvironmental Project Planning and Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Data management, analysis and interpretation specifically for bioenvironmental research purposes; development of skills required to draw conclusions from data, specifically the types of data relevant to studying the interface of biological and environmental processes; exposure to and development of presentation skills in communicating results and conclusions that rely on interpretation and assumptions
prerequisites: BESC 201 ; STAT 201 , STAT 302 or STAT 303
title: Bioenvironmental Data Analysis

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Capstone course for topics in bioenvironmental sciences; critical analysis of environmental issues through written themes and presentations. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: BESC 201 and senior classification in BESC major
title: Seminar

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: An on-the-job supervised experience program conducted in the area of the student's specialization
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head
title: Field Experience

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Special problems for advanced undergraduates to permit study of subject matter not available in existing courses
prerequisites: BESC 201 or approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Selected topics in an identified area of bioenvironmental sciences
prerequisites: BESC 201 or approval of instructor
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in bioenvironmental sciences. May be repeated 3 times for credit
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor
title: Research

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Foundational concepts for biochemistry and genetics research methods; topics include principles of the scientific method, experimental design, analytical tools, and logical thinking, with a special focus on the use of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) in biochemical and genetics research
prerequisites: Freshman classification in biochemistry or genetics
title: Introduction to Biochemical and Genetics Research Methods

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Introduction to biochemistry and genetics essential techniques; concepts learned from BICH/ GENE 101/BICH 101 utilized in practical laboratory situations to understand the relevance and use of these techniques in real-world research settings
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BICH 101/GENE 101 or GENE 101/BICH 101 ; freshman classification in biochemistry or genetics
title: Introduction to Biochemical and Genetic Techniques

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Introduction to essential skills and knowledge for effective learning, information retrieval, evaluation, and utilization of AI tools in the fields of biochemistry and genetics; developing critical thinking abilities, learning to navigate scientific literature, evaluating the credibility of information sources, and leveraging AI tools to enhance their research and problem-solving capabilities
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BICH 102/GENE 102 or GENE 102/BICH 102 ; sophomore classification in biochemistry or genetics
title: Introduction to Information Literacy and Artificial Intelligence Tools for Biochemistry and Genetics

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Exploration of the link between fundamental genetic and biochemical processes and disease states, using case studies of several human diseases; deeper comprehension and critical thinking about molecular causes of diseases and treatment strategies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BICH 201/GENE 201 or GENE 201/BICH 201 ; sophomore classification in biochemistry or genetics
title: Biochemical and Genetic Concepts in Medicine - Case Studies

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Introduction to laboratory research
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification in biochemistry or approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in Biochemistry. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor
title: Research

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Survey of the biochemical sciences designed for the non-biochemistry major; overview of the chemistry and metabolism of biologically important molecules, the biochemical basis of life processes, cellular metabolism and regulation. Students requiring biochemistry in greater depth should register for BICH 410 and BICH 411
prerequisites: CHEM 222 , CHEM 227 or CHEM 257 ; not open to biochemistry majors
title: Elements of Biological Chemistry

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Current topics in cellular biophysics and systems biology; quantitative and predictive perspectives of cellular life; basic tools of biophysics such as fluorescence imaging and data analysis
prerequisites: BIOL 112 and MATH 152 ; BICH 440 or concurrent enrollment
title: Cellular Biophysics

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Quantitative and computational approaches to biochemical problems
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BICH 440 or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification
title: Biochemical Calculations

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Current topics in biomolecules, natural product antibiotics and application in infectious diseases, modern and historical approaches to antibiotic discovery, biomedical glycobiology, glycosylation in diseases and pathobiology
prerequisites: BICH 441
title: Molecular Mechanisms of Cell Interactions

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: A rigorous, survey of topics in biochemistry; topics include structure and function of molecules within living cells, major metabolic pathways and their regulation and role in disease; provides preparation for advanced study in the health sciences
prerequisites: CHEM 228 or CHEM 258
title: Principles of Biochemistry

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Structure, function and chemistry of proteins and carbohydrates; kinetics, mechanisms and regulation of enzymes; metabolism of carbohydrates. Not open to biochemistry or genetics majors
prerequisites: CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; junior or senior classification
title: Comprehensive Biochemistry I

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: A continuation of BICH 410 ; structure, function, chemistry and metabolism of lipids and nucleic acids; cellular metabolism viewed from the standpoint of energetics and control mechanisms; interrelationships of metabolic pathways
prerequisites: BICH 410 ; not open to biochemistry or genetics majors
title: Comprehensive Biochemistry II

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Selected methods used to identify, isolate, purify and characterize biomolecules. Not open to biochemistry or genetics majors
prerequisites: BICH 410 or registration therein
title: Biochemistry Laboratory I

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Analysis of the effects of charge on protein function and stability; techniques include site-directed mutagenesis, protein purification, affinity chromatography, SDS-PAGE, enzyme kinetics, MALDI-TOF, molecular modeling, and protein folding
prerequisites: BICH 440 , BICH 409 , or BICH 410 ; major in biochemistry, genetics, microbiology, and molecular and cell biology
title: Biochemical Techniques I

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Mitotic cell cycle; progression of biochemical and morphological phases and events; duplication of cellular constituents and segregation into daughter cells
prerequisites: BICH 409 , BICH 410 , or BICH 440 ; junior or senior classification in biochemistry or genetics
title: Mechanisms of Cell Division

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Computational techniques for studying evolution; algorithms for construction and analysis of evolutionary relationships
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Computational Techniques for Evolutionary Analysis

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: The application of ethical theory to the use of modern genetics and biochemistry stressing the social implications of genetic engineering, agricultural manipulation and biotechnology
prerequisites: GENE 302 or GENE 303 ; BICH 409 , BICH 410 , or BICH 440
title: Bioethics

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Molecular basis for inheritance; gene structure and function, chromosomal organization, replication and repair of DNA, transcription and translation, the genetic code, regulation of gene expression, genetic differentiation and genetic manipulations
prerequisites: BICH 409 , BICH 410 , or BICH 440 ; GENE 301 , GENE 302 , GENE 303 , GENE 320/BIMS 320 or BIMS 320/GENE 320
title: Molecular Genetics

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Laboratory for molecular genetics providing technical experience with tools of molecular biology
prerequisites: GENE 301 , GENE 302 , GENE 303 , BIMS 320/GENE 320 or GENE 320/BIMS 320 ; BICH 431/GENE 431 or GENE 431/BICH 431
title: Laboratory in Molecular Genetics

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Rigorous treatment of the structure, function and chemistry of proteins and carbohydrates; kinetics, mechanisms and regulation of enzymes; metabolism of carbohydrates; designed for biochemistry and genetics majors
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; grade of C or better in BICH 404 or concurrent enrollment
title: Biochemistry I

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Continuation of BICH 440 ; structure, function, chemistry and metabolism of lipids and nucleic acids, cellular metabolism viewed from the standpoint of energetics and control mechanisms; interrelationships of metabolic pathways. Course designed for biochemistry and genetics majors and honors students only
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BICH 440
title: Biochemistry II

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Emphasis on novel roles and mechanisms of newly discovered Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) species including non-coding RNA's; RNA silencing, circular RNA's, RNA guided epigenetic regulation, clustered regulary interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-Cas immunity, genome editing, telomerase biogenesis, riboswitches, exosome, editosome and RNA remodeling
prerequisites: GENE 301 , GENE 302 , or GENE 303 ; BICH 410 , BICH 440 , BIOL 351 , or BIOL 413
title: Ribonucleic Acid World

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Critical reading and annotation of the biological literature; annotation using ontologies as structured controlled vocabularies for the organization of biological data; area of focus may vary at instructors discretion. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: BIOL 111 and BIOL 112 , or equivalent; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Creating Annotations through Critical Analysis of Original Research

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Examination of the latest technologies in genomic analysis by sequencing and annotating the genomes of novel bacterial viruses (phage); generates real data which will be submitted to the NIH/NCBI public database; includes phage biology and potential uses
prerequisites: GENE 302 or GENE 303 ; BIOL 351 or concurrent enrollment
title: Bacteriophage Genomics

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Directed study in biochemistry not included in established courses
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor and department head
title: Directed Studies

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Selected topics in an identified area of biochemistry, biophysics or nutrition
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification in life or physical sciences
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Laboratory research supervised by faculty in biochemistry or biophysics
prerequisites: Biochemistry major
title: Research

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Integration into the BIMS program through content and assignments; understanding of problem solving, personal, and social responsibility; development of self-efficacy, self-awareness, and sense of purpose; becoming actively engaged inside and outside the classroom; becoming socially integrated within the university community
prerequisites: BIMS major
title: Introduction to Biomedical Sciences

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: To explore the concept of One Health; the health of humans, animals and ecosystems are interconnected and interdependent; the conceptual framework that encompasses human and veterinary medical sciences, agricultural sciences, food safety, public health and epidemiology, environmental health and toxicology, wildlife ecology and conservation and many related fields of study or research
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification or approval of instructor
title: One Health in Action

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Introduction to integration of humans and animals in society, focusing on animal, human and environmental health of common species as well as special roles of animals
prerequisites: Freshman classification
title: Animals in Society

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: This interdisciplinary course explores the most significant medical advances that fundamentally changed the course of health and biomedical treatment. The curriculum is structured around major body systems, with each module delivered by a content expert. Students will analyze breakthroughs from the past to the current era, focusing on the scientific, ethical and societal impact of key discoveries — such as the development of vaccines, the first successful organ transplant, the introduction of antibiotics and advances in neuroimaging. The goal is to provide a comprehensive, system-by-system understanding of how medical innovation, discovery and research has shaped modern medicine
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BIOL 111
title: Biomedical Breakthroughs - Significant Developments in Biomedical Sciences

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Skills and ethical procedures to assist in professional practice of Biomedical Sciences; exploration of business and professional concepts; topics include development of the individual, ethical integrity, interpersonal dynamics, effective communication skills
prerequisites: Sophomore classification in Biomedical Sciences
title: Professionalism, Skill Development, Career Exploration, and Ethical Conduct in BIMS

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Selected topics in an identified area of biomedical science
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in biomedical sciences
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor
title: Research

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: For students in approved programs abroad. May be repeated for credit. Maximum 3 hours free elective credit in the BIMS degree plan. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
title: Biomedical Sciences Study Abroad

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Exploration of various research methodologies and experimental designs; includes lab-based, field based, quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods approach; emphasis on best practices in research; analysis and interpretation of data to draw conclusions; development of critical thinking skills; focus on appropriate methodologies for various experimental designs
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 257 ; junior classification
title: Research Methodologies and Experimental Design in Biomedical Sciences

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Study of modern genetics with an emphasis on biomedical and health-related applications of the mammalian genome. Topics include classical Mendelian inheritance, pedigree and genetic risk analysis, population genetics, quantitative genetics and the molecular basis of gene structure and function, including DNA replication, transcription, mutation and gene regulation. The course examines how genetic variation and chromosomal abnormalities contribute to disease and phenotypic diversity, and introduces advanced concepts in cytogenetics, epigenetics, cancer genetics and genomics. Contemporary applications such as genome sequencing, gene therapy, personalized medicine and associated ethical considerations are also addressed. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: GENE 301 , GENE 302 , GENE 315, GENE-320 or BIMS-320
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202 ; junior or senior classification
title: Biomedical Genetics

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Course explores equine assisted services (EAS) best practices, including: principles of EAS, horse welfare, safety factors, effective techniques to promote healing of participants, and career options. Upon completion of this course, students will have demonstrated the ability to define what constitutes a safe and effective EAS program and outline a business model for such a program
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Equine-Assisted Activities and Therapies - Best Practices

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Clinical and functional anatomy focused on pre-professional training; includes anatomy of all major body systems
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BIOL 112 and CHEM 258 ; junior or senior classification; minimum GPA 2.75; or approval on instructor
title: Anatomy

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Emphasis on current research and technology application in comparative mammalian genetics and genomics including advanced reproduction technologies and cloning, animal models of disease, biodiversity and functional genetics, cancer genetics, conservation, coat color genetics, cytogenetics, development and stem cells, domestication, epigenetics and gene regulation, forensics applications, genomic medicine, genomics and computational analysis, sex determination and sex chromosomes
prerequisites: GENE 302 , BIMS 320/GENE 320 or GENE 320/BIMS 320 ; junior or senior classification in biomedical sciences, genetics, biochemistry and biology
title: Mammalian Genetics

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: A rigorous, analytical approach to genetic analysis of humans including diagnosis and management of genetic disease in humans; transmission of genes in human populations; human cytogenetics; the structure of human genes; human gene mapping; molecular analysis of genetic disease; genetics screening and counseling
prerequisites: GENE 302 ; BICH 410 or BICH 440
title: Advanced Human Genetics

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Application of peer teaching techniques in an undergraduate lab course; discussion of current pedagogical theories and practices; focus on using effective communication in the classroom; development of personal teaching philosophy, assessments and learner-centered engagement strategies
prerequisites: Grade of B or better in VIBS 402/BIMS 402 , BIMS 402/VIBS 402 , VIBS 446 , or VIBS 243 and approval of instructor
title: Learning and Applying Peer Teaching Principles in Biomedical Sciences

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Exploration of published scientific research via guided discussions; familiarization with the necessary skills to conduct an appropriate literature search of the scientific record; extensive practice in effectively communicating biomedical science through oral presentation. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; BIMS major; BIOL 401 , BIOL 402 , BIOL 403 , VIBS 310 , or VIBS 311
title: Seminar

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Supervised internship in the biomedical sciences workforce for practical application of biomedical sciences knowledge. May be taken for credit up to six hours. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Internship

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Directed individual study of problems in the biomedical sciences with emphasis in the allied health professions, hospital administration, and the health-related industry approved by the instructor
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor; BIMS major with a minimum overall 2.5 TAMU GPA
title: Directed Studies

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Selected topics in an identified area of biomedical science
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; BIMS major with a minimum overall 2.5 TAMU GPA
title: Special Topics in

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in biomedical sciences
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; grade of C or better in PHYS 202 ; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor
title: Research

college: College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences
description: Integration of foundational biomedical science knowledge, competencies, and coursework through an individual capstone project based on research and presentation of an approved topic; formal presentation of both translational and integrative application of information as well as the expected impacts of the selected topic
prerequisites: Senior classification and approval of instructor, or concurrent participation in the Biomedical Research Certificate
title: Biomedical Sciences Capstone Experience

description: Introduction to the study of biology at Texas A&M University; gain knowledge of departmental and campus resources to assist and enhance the pursuit of a degree in biology, microbiology, molecular and cellular biology or zoology
prerequisites: First-year and first-time-in-college freshman majoring in BIOL, MBIO, BMCB and ZOOL
title: Horizons in Biology

description: Structure, physiology and development of plants with an emphasis on seed plants. (Not open to students who have taken BIOL 111 and BIOL 112 or BIOL 113 .); includes laboratory that reinforces and provides supplemental information related to the lecture topics
title: Botany

description: This team-taught, interdisciplinary course builds scientific literacy by examining contemporary issues — current questions, discoveries and challenges at the intersection of science and society. Topics may include the Big Bang, evolution, genetics, human reproduction and health, vaccines, drugs, artificial intelligence, cryptography and cybersecurity. Students will learn to evaluate scientific claims and critically analyze how science is presented in the news, on television and on social media
title: Contemporary Issues in Science - Cosmos, Earth and Humanity

description: (BIOL 1313 and 1113, 1413) Zoology. Survey of animal life with respect to cell organization, genetics, evolution, diversity of invertebrates/vertebrates, anatomy/physiology, and interaction of animals with their environment; includes laboratory that reinforces and provides supplemental information related to lecture topics. (Not open to students who have taken BIOL 111 and BIOL 112 or BIOL 113 )
title: Zoology

description: (BIOL 1306 and 1106, 1406) Introductory Biology I. First half of an introdutory two-semester survey of contemporary biology that covers the chemical basis of life, structure and biology of the cell, molecular biology and genetics; includes laboratory that reinforces and provides supplemental information related to the lecture topics; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Introductory Biology I

description: (BIOL 1307 and 1107, 1407) Introductory Biology II. The second half of an introductory two-semester survey of contemporary biology that covers evolution, history of life, diversity and form and function of organisms; includes laboratory that reinforces and provides supplemental information related to the lecture topics
prerequisites: BIOL 111 ; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Introductory Biology II

description: (BIOL 1308, BIOL 1408) Essentials in Biology. One-semester biology for non-majors; overview of essential biological concepts and their application to real world and contemporary issues; topics include evolution, biodiversity, cellular, molecular and forensic biology, genetics and heredity to scientific literacy, human impact on the environment, genetically modified organisms and emerging diseases
title: Essentials in Biology

description: (BIOL 2320 and 2120, BIOL 2321 and 2121, BIOL 2420, BIOL 2421) Introductory Microbiology. Basic microbiology of prokaryotes and eukaryotes; main topics include morphology, physiology, genetics, taxonomy, ecology, medically important species and immunology; mandatory laboratory designed to give hands-on experience and to reinforce basic principles
prerequisites: BIOL 101 , BIOL 107 , BIOL 111 , or BIOL 113 ; CHEM 119
title: Introductory Microbiology

description: This course covers how cells are built, powered and regulated. Topics include macromolecules; membranes and transport; energy production and conversion; genome organization and evolution; DNA structure and replication; gene expression and regulation; intracellular trafficking; cytoskeleton; cell communication and electrical signaling; cell division and cancer. Additional topics may be presented based on time and instructor expertise. The course emphasizes evidence-based reasoning, quantitative skills and core experimental methods
prerequisites: BIOL 112 and CHEM 120
title: Molecular Cell Biology

description: A genetically-based introduction to the study of ecology and evolution; emphasis on the interactions of organisms with each other and with their environment
prerequisites: BIOL 112
title: Genes, Ecology and Evolution

description: Problems in various phases of plant, animal and microbial science
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; approval of ranking professor in field chosen and Undergraduate Advising Office
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified area of biology
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Special Topics in

description: Active research of basic nature under the supervision of a Department of Biology faculty member
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of faculty member
title: Research

description: Development of job search skills; utilization of career resources; self-assessment of career interests and career objectives; strategies for professional correspondence and networking; business etiquette and interviewing techniques; insight into life science career opportunities
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; department of biology majors only; or approval of instructor
title: Careers in Biology

description: Classification, phylogeny, comparative anatomy, and biology of chordates; diversity, protochordates, vertebrate skeletons, shark and cat anatomy studied in laboratory
prerequisites: BIOL 214 or approval of instructor
title: Chordate Anatomy

description: Integrated approach to cellular, neural, skeletal, muscular anatomy and physiology; includes some histology, histopathology, radiology and clinical correlations
prerequisites: BIOL 111 and BIOL 112 , or BIOL 107
title: Integrated Human Anatomy and Physiology I

description: Continuation of BIOL 319 . Integrated approach to endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive and developmental anatomy and physiology; includes some histology, histopathology, radiology and clinical correlations
prerequisites: BIOL 319 or approval of instructor
title: Integrated Human Anatomy and Physiology II

description: Morphology, taxonomy, natual history and phylogeny of invertebrate animals, with emphasis on biodiversity; class includes both lecture and lab. Labs include study of preserved material and demonstration of living animals in aquaria and terraria
prerequisites: BIOL 214 or approval of instructor
title: Invertebrate Zoology

description: Comprehensive analysis of bioinformatics tools applicable to eukaryotic organisms; theoretical background of computational algorithms, with an emphasis on application of computational tools related to modern molecular biological research
prerequisites: BIOL 213 ; GENE 301 , GENE 302 , GENE 303 , BIMS 320/GENE 320 , or GENE 320/BIMS 320 recommended; or approval of instructor
title: Bioinformatics

description: Hands-on approach to obtaining, organizing and analyzing genome-related data; emphasis on asking and answering biologically relevant questions by designing and performing experiments using computers; understanding biology from a computational perspective
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification in life sciences, engineering, mathematics, chemistry
title: Computational Genomics

description: Introduction to modern microbiology with emphasis on prokaryotes; includes microbial cell structure, function, and physiology; genetics, evolution, and taxonomy; bacteriophage and viruses; pathogenesis and immunity; and ecology and biotechnology; includes laboratory experience with microbial growth and identification
prerequisites: BIOL 112 ; CHEM 257 , or CHEM 227 and CHEM 237 , or CHEM 231 ; or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Fundamentals of Microbiology

description: Survey the genetics, ecology and evolution of microbes, review their role in defining the environment of the earth and their impact on all forms of life on earth
prerequisites: BIOL 351
title: Ecology and Evolution of Microbes

description: Analysis of ecosystems at organismal, population, interspecific and community levels
prerequisites: BIOL 214 or approval of instructor
title: Ecology

description: Introduction to how animals function, including basics of neurophysiology, endocrinology, muscular, cardiovascular, respiratory, ormoregulatory, and metabolic physiology; broadly comparative in scope and encompassing adaptation of physiological systems to diverse environments; the laboratory stresses techniques used for monitoring and investigating physiological mechanisms and responses to environmental changes
prerequisites: BIOL 214 , CHEM 228 , or CHEM 258 , or approval of instructor
title: Principles of Animal Physiology

description: Reading scientific papers and writing short synopses of papers with a focus on learning how to think and write like a scientist; fills the current Writing Intensive "W" course requirement for biology
prerequisites: BIOL 213 or CHEM 228 ; junior or senior classification
title: Critical Writing in Biology

description: Interpretation of scientific papers; analysis of how research findings are communicated to lay audiences; creation of synopses of research findings for the general public
prerequisites: BIOL 213 or CHEM 228 ; junior or senior classification
title: Communicating Biological Research to the Public

description: Focus on reading and analyzing brief nonfiction stories about medicine; exploration of different perspectives and experiences with illness and medicine
prerequisites: BIOL 213 or CHEM 228 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Medical Narratives

description: Basic principles of endocrinology including structure and functions of hormones in vertebrates; hormonal control of growth, metabolism, osmoregulation, and reproduction; endocrine techniques and mechanism of hormone action
prerequisites: BIOL 214 ; CHEM 227 or CHEM 257
title: Comparative Endocrinology

description: A problem oriented course surveying the manipulation and mechanisms of genetic systems in bacteria; recombination, gene structure and regulation of bacterial genes, plasmids and phages
prerequisites: GENE 302 ; BIOL 351
title: Bacterial Genetics

description: Examination of the basic mechanisms of biological timing; in depth study of clocks in model organisms and the relationship between clocks and human health and disease
prerequisites: BICH 431/GENE 431 , BIOL 213 or GENE 431/BICH 431
title: Biological Clocks

description: Underlying technical basis for synthetic biology; tools used to generate recombinant molecules; genetic circuitry and modules applied to bacteria; design and fabrication of genes, biological components and entire organisms; survey actual and theoretical applications
prerequisites: BIOL 351 or BICH 431/GENE 431
title: Synthetic Biology of Microbes

description: Structure, function, and biogenesis of cells and their components; interpretation of dynamic processes of cells, including protein trafficking, motility, signaling and proliferation
prerequisites: BIOL 213 , GENE 302 , or GENE 303 ; BICH 410 or BICH 440
title: Cell Biology

description: Concepts of development in systems ranging from bacteriophage to the mammalian embryo; use of recombinant DNA technology and embryo engineering to unravel the relationships between growth and differentiation, morphogenesis and commitment, aging and cancer
prerequisites: BIOL 213 or GENE 302 ; BICH 410 or BICH 440
title: Developmental Biology

description: Modern methods of study of cell structure and cell function
prerequisites: BICH 410 and BIOL 413 , or concurrent enrollment or approval of instructor
title: Cell Biology Laboratory

description: This course will explore the molecular aspects of plant growth, development, reproduction and evolution, with an emphasis on gene manipulation and the practical applications of plant molecular biology
prerequisites: GENE 302 or equivalent, or approval of instructor
title: Plant Molecular Biology

description: Cell biology, molecular biology and biophysics of neurons as it pertains to their fundamental role in the physiological basis of behavior; study of how neurons create, maintain and exploit electrical signals for information coding and transmission; principles of electrical and chemical signaling between neurons, and the role of intracellular signaling for signal modulation and synaptic plasticity; exploration of a broad range of state-of-the-art molecular tools currently used to study the nervous system, and the cellular basis for many of the most common neurological disorders affecting humans as well as the strategies and therapies for their treatment
prerequisites: BIOL 213 and PSYC 235, or approval of instructor
title: Cellular Neuroscience

description: Still and video photography and photomicrography, computerbased digital image analysis and processing of biological images; theory and principles of light and electron microscopy including transmission and scanning electron microscopy; optical contrast methods for light microscopy including phase contrast, DIC, polarizing light and confocal laser scanning microscopy
prerequisites: Junior classification or approval of instructor
title: Biological Imaging

description: Cell biology and biophysics of neurons; functional organization of the vertebrate nervous system; physiological basis of behavior
prerequisites: BIOL 213 ; BIOL 319 , BIOL 320 , BIOL 388 , BIOL 413 , or PBSI 235 , or approval of instructor
title: Regulatory and Behavioral Neuroscience

description: Study of modern methods and tools used to investigate nervous system structure and function
prerequisites: BIOL 213 ; BIOL 319 , BIOL 320 , BIOL 388 , BIOL 413 , BIOL 428 , BIOL 434/NRSC 434 , NRSC 235, NRSC 335, NRSC 428/BIOL 428 , NRSC 434/BIOL 434 , or PBSI 235 , or approval of instructor
title: Laboratory for Regulatory and Behavioral Neuroscience

description: Structure and function of prokaryotic cells, with emphasis on evolutionary adaptations to different environmental, developmental, and pathogenic selections pressures; formation of teamsa and preparation of presentations on specific topics in microbiology
prerequisites: BIOL 351 ; BIOL 406/GENE 406 or concurrent enrollment; BICH 410 , BICH 431/GENE 431 and GENE 302 strongly recommended
title: Bacterial Physiology

description: Introduction to biology of common organisms inhabiting bays, beaches and near-shore oceanic waters with special reference to Gulf of Mexico biota; emphasis on classification, distribution, history, ecology, physiology, mutualism, predation, major community types and economic aspects of marine organisms
prerequisites: BIOL 214 or approval of instructor
title: Marine Biology

description: Analysis of the earliest stages of animal evolution by integrating various scientific fields such as genomics, paleontology, metabolism, morphology, environment, development and behavior; includes hands-on exploration of fossils and modern animals to understand how evolution shaped our world
prerequisites: BIOL 214 ; junior or senior classification
title: Early Stages of Animal Evolution

description: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of nervous system development including neural induction and the basis of complex behaviors; use of a wide range of model organisms with a specific emphasis on vertebrate nervous system development

description: This course offers an innovative exploration of fundamental concepts in biology through their portrayal in film, highlighting the intersection of scientific discovery, medicine and society. Students will engage with primary scientific literature to develop a firsthand understanding of the discovery process underlying topics such as neurodegenerative disease, genetic engineering, addiction and disease transmission. Class discussions will connect these foundational insights to critical analyses of how such themes are represented in film, encouraging students to evaluate both the processes of scientific discovery and their societal implications. Through this dual approach, the course fosters scientific literacy, ethical reasoning and a deeper appreciation for the relationship between science and society
prerequisites: BIOL 111 , BIOL 112 and BIOL 213 ; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor

description: An introduction to the study of chemistry at Texas A&M University and departmental and campus resources helpful to success in the degree; information about research and internship opportunities; information about careers with and without a graduate-level degree
prerequisites: Major in chemistry or approval of instructor
title: Horizons in Chemistry

description: This team-taught, interdisciplinary course is designed to build scientific literacy by examining contemporary issues in science - current questions, discoveries and challenges that shape our understanding of the environment. Topics may include climate change, energy systems, plastics and pollution, agriculture, water and food safety, biodiversity, environmental health and chemicals and drugs (including vaccines). Students will learn to evaluate scientific claims and critically analyze how science is presented in the news, on television and on social media
title: Contemporary Issues in Science - The Environment

description: (CHEM 1305, 1405*) Molecular Science for Citizens. Molecules that control daily life explored via a conceptual approach to molecular science; properties, synthesis, transformations and utility of important molecules and fuels, fibers, metals, pharmaceuticals, foods, biomolecules and structural materials; pollution, consumerism, energy production, disease, biotechnology and risk-benefit analysis considered; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Molecular Science for Citizens

description: (CHEM 1309, 1409*) General Chemistry for Engineering Students. Introduction to important concepts and principles of chemistry; emphasis on areas considered most relevant in an engineering context; practical applications of chemical principles in engineering and technology. Students completing CHEM 107 and changing majors to curricula requiring CHEM 101 and CHEM 102 may substitute CHEM 107 for CHEM 101. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: CHEM 107 or CHEM 101
prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in CHEM 117 ; grade of C or better in MATH 150 , or equivalent, or acceptable score on Texas A&M University math placement exam; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: General Chemistry for Engineering Students

description: (CHEM 1109, 1409*) General Chemistry for Engineering Students Laboratory. Introduction to important concepts and principles of chemistry in the laboratory; emphasis on areas considered most relevant in an engineering context; practical applications of chemical principles in engineering and technology. Students completing CHEM 117 and changing majors to curricula requiring CHEM 111 and CHEM 112 may substitute CHEM 117 for CHEM 111. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: CHEM 117 or CHEM 111
prerequisites: CHEM 107 or registration therein; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: General Chemistry for Engineering Students Laboratory

description: (CHEM 1311 and 1111, 1411) Fundamentals of Chemistry I. Introduction to modern theories of atomic structure and chemical bonding; chemical reactions; stoichiometry; states of matter; solutions; equilibrium; acids and bases; coordination chemistry; methods and techniques of chemical experimentation; qualitative and semiquantitative procedures applied to investigative situations; also taught at Galveston campus
prerequisites: Completion of at least 90% of the ALEKS chemistry preparatory module; or grade of C or better in MATH 140 , MATH 150 , or equivalent; or acceptable score on Texas A&M University math placement exam
title: Fundamentals of Chemistry I

description: (CHEM 1312 and 1112, 1412) Fundamentals of Chemistry II. Theory and applications of oxidation-reductions systems; thermodynamics and kinetics; complex equilibria and solubility product; nuclear chemistry; descriptive inorganic and organic chemistry; introduction to analytical and synthetic methods and to quantitative techniques to both inorganic and organic compounds with emphasis on an investigative approach
prerequisites: CHEM 119 , or CHEM 107 and CHEM 117 ; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Fundamentals of Chemistry II

description: Introduction and integration of current learning theory, evidence-based learning, and educational psychology into the daily operations and practice of the Chemistry Learning Laboratory; must be a peer-tutor for the Chemistry Learning Laboratory
prerequisites: Grade of B or better in CHEM 107 , or CHEM 119 and CHEM 120 ; or grade of B or better in CHEM 257 and CHEM 258 ; approval of instructor
title: Peer-Assisted Learning Pedagogy for Chemistry

description: Organic chemistry and its applications to biological and agricultural chemistry, including chemistry of functional groups, acid-base and redox chemistry, stereochemistry and chemistry of important biological compounds. Not to be used as the basis for further study in organic chemistry or biochemistry
prerequisites: CHEM 101, CHEM 119 , or CHEM 107
title: Elements of Organic and Biological Chemistry

description: (CHEM 2323, 2423*) Organic Chemistry I. Introduction to chemistry of compounds of carbon; general principles and their application to various industrial and biological processes
prerequisites: CHEM 102 or CHEM 120 ; concurrent enrollment in CHEM 237 is suggested; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Organic Chemistry I

description: (CHEM 2325, 2425*) Organic Chemistry II. Continuation of CHEM 227

title: Organic Chemistry II

description: Techniques of organic chemistry; preparation, properties of typical organic compounds; separation, purification, analysis, and characterization of organic compounds
prerequisites: CHEM 112 or CHEM 120 ; concurrent enrollment in CHEM 227
title: Techniques of Organic Chemistry

description: The synthesis of significant types of organic compounds and study of their properties; laboratory separations of mixtures of organic substances, identification of compounds by functional group tests and preparation of derivatives; instrumental methods of separation, identification and analysis
prerequisites: CHEM 228 or concurrent enrollment; CHEM 231 , CHEM 237 or CHEM 257
title: Organic Synthesis and Analysis

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification

description: CONTENT. History of Christianity from its inception until the beginnings of European colonial expansion in the first half of the 16th century. Themes include the teachings of Jesus and his disciples; the growth of Christianity as it spread throughout the Mediterranean basin into Mesopotamia, Africa, Northern Europe and central Asia; variations in doctrinal development and religious practice in diverse social, political and geographical situations. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce
title: History of Christianity I - Origins to the Reformation

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Greece from the Stone Age through the Hellenistic Period, concluding with the rise of Rome. Explores the material culture, art, architecture and social history of the Greek world across its major cultural phases, from the Bronze Age civilizations of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece to the flourishing of Classical Athens and the cosmopolitan Hellenistic kingdoms. Emphasizes the integration of archaeological evidence, ancient texts and artistic traditions to illuminate Greek religion, civic life, domestic space and cultural interactions across the Mediterranean. By examining key sites, monuments, artifacts and artistic achievements, students gain a comprehensive understanding of Greek society and its enduring legacy in Western civilization. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age and Neolithic Greece; Bronze Age civilizations; Minoan Crete; Mycenaean palaces and the Trojan War; the Greek Dark Ages; Geometric period art and society; Archaic architecture, sculpture and vase painting; Classical Athens and the Acropolis; sanctuaries such as Delphi; fourth-century Greece and the rise of Macedon; Hellenistic art, architecture and urbanism; Greek houses and domestic mosaics; shipwreck archaeology; coinage and economic history; Greek religion and votive practices; interactions with Magna Graecia and the wider Mediterranean; Greek artistic and cultural legacy in Rome and later neoclassicism
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Archaeology of Ancient Greece

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Italy from the Stone Age through the collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Students examine the material culture, art and architecture of the Etruscans and Romans, as well as the prehistoric and early Italic foundations that shaped them. Explores how Italy’s peoples expressed identity, religion and power through sculpture, painting, mosaics, inscriptions, temples, homes and civic monuments. Special emphasis is placed on the development of Rome from a small city-state into a vast imperial capital, the role of urbanism and daily life, and the ways in which material remains reveal both continuity and transformation across centuries of Italian history. TOPICS AND THEMES. Prehistoric Italy and the Stone Age; Villanovans and the emergence of the Etruscans; Etruscan cities and art; early Rome and urban foundations; Romanization and the Republic; Augustan classicism; imperial art and architecture under the Julio-Claudians, Flavians and Antonines; wall painting, mosaics and domestic life; Pompeii and Herculaneum; the lure of the games and public spectacles; baths, theaters and civic monuments; coinage and inscriptions as evidence of social and political life; Ostia and imperial urbanism; ships and shipwrecks of Roman Italy; Severan and Late Roman art; Constantine and the transformation of Roman identity; collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Archaeology of Ancient Italy

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys topics such as Greek and Roman warships, naval warfare, naval strategy and tactics, drawing upon archaeological evidence, literary documentation and iconographic material. Covers the development of Mediterranean naval power from the Bronze Age (including Ancient Egypt and the mythical Trojan War) to the Imperial Roman Navy. Examines Greek naval dominance during the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars, the evolution of warships such as triremes, Roman naval organization and imperial fleets, and the technological, strategic and political dimensions of naval warfare. Students analyze ship construction, rigging, armament and naval technology within their historical and cultural context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Bronze Age Mediterranean warships; Egyptian naval warfare; Bronze Age naval battles; Athenian Navy; trireme; Greco-Persian Wars (499-449 B.C.); Peloponnesian Wars (431-404 B.C.); naval campaigns of Alexander the Great; Age of Titans; Greek war machines and weapons; Greek naval monuments; Phoenician Navy; Punic Navy; Roman naval organization; Roman Imperial Navy; Roman warships and tactics; Mare Nostrum; Punic Wars (264-146 B.C.); Roman Navy in the Eastern Mediterranean; naval campaigns of Julius Caesar; naval campaigns of Octavian; Roman fluvial warships; Roman naval shipwrecks; Roman war machines and tactics; ship construction; rigging; armament; naval technology; maritime strategy; naval logistics; naval archaeology; iconography; material culture; maritime military history; technological arms race at sea
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor
title: Naval Warfare and Warships in Ancient Greece and Rome

description: Introduction to Communication. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces the field of communication as a broad and interdisciplinary area of study. Surveys major topics, research traditions and contexts of communicative practice across interpersonal, organizational, public and/or mediated settings. Examines verbal and nonverbal communication, media and technology, intercultural and health communication, strategic and religious communication, and leadership and conflict management. Considers how communication is studied from both humanities and social science perspectives, with attention to culture, ethics and methods of inquiry. Provides a foundation for understanding communication as both theory and practice in everyday life, civic engagement and/or professional contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how communication functions across personal, academic, professional and/or civic settings. Develops foundational skills in analyzing, adapting and applying communication strategies to wide-ranging contexts. Enhances the ability to critically interpret messages in a world shaped by media convergence, cultural difference and/or global interconnectedness. Prepares for advanced coursework in communication and media fields, while also strengthening transferable skills valued across professions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about communication differ from scholarly perspectives developed in the field. Expands understanding of communication as both a practical skill and an area of research shaped by theory, culture and/or ethics. Examines ways of knowing that include humanistic, social scientific and/or critical approaches. Highlights how communication influences relationships, organizations and/or society, deepening appreciation for the complexity of interaction and meaning making. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include verbal and nonverbal communication; media and technology; intercultural communication; health communication; strategic communication; religious communication; leadership and conflict management; and/or academic research and methods of inquiry. Attention to contemporary issues and applications of communication theory may introduce perspectives that are unfamiliar and/or challenging, reflecting the broad relevance of communication to personal, professional and civic life
title: Introduction to Communication

description: Public Speaking. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and criticism of public speaking. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills, including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Attention to ethical communication and sensitivity to diverse audiences across professional, political, religious, cultural and ideological contexts. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking, developing verbal and nonverbal communication strategies. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with skills essential for professional, academic and civic life. Builds competence in organizing ideas, supporting arguments, adapting them to varied audiences. Develops confidence in extemporaneous speaking, critical listening and communication across diverse contexts. Prepares students for leadership roles, workplace communication and active participation in public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about public speaking, such as viewing it only as performance or memorization, differ from research-based and practical perspectives. Develops understanding of speaking as a process involving invention, organization, style, delivery and audience adaptation, enhancing skills in extemporaneous speaking. Emphasizes that effective speaking requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as confidence in delivery. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why public speaking matters in contemporary society; study of ethical principles in communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of audiences and rhetorical situations; research and organization of supporting materials; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of language and presentation aids; practice in informative, persuasive and ceremonial speaking; application of digital rhetoric and multimedia tools. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Public Speaking

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles, practice and criticism of public speaking adapted for online audiences and platforms. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills, including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Attention to ethical communication and sensitivity to diverse audiences across professional, political, religious, cultural and/or ideological contexts. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and ceremonial speaking, developing competence in composition, digital presentation and multimedia editing. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with skills essential for professional, academic and civic life. Builds competence in organizing ideas, supporting arguments, adapting them to varied online audiences. Develops confidence in digital delivery, critical listening and communication across diverse platforms. Prepares students for leadership roles, workplace communication and/or active participation in public dialogue through online media. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about public speaking, such as viewing it only as performance or memorization, differ from research-based and practical perspectives. Develops understanding of speaking as a process involving invention, organization, style, delivery and audience adaptation across both in-person and digital contexts. Emphasizes that effective speaking requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences, as well as confidence in both live and recorded delivery. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why public speaking matters in digital society; study of ethical principles in communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of digital audiences and rhetorical situations; research and organization of supporting materials; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of language and presentation aids; practice in informative, persuasive and/or ceremonial speaking; training in composition, delivery, recording and editing of speeches for digital distribution; application of digital rhetoric and multimedia tools across video conferencing, online platforms and social media. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor
title: Public Speaking for Digital Platforms

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles, practice and criticism of public speaking adapted for technical fields. Focus on rhetorical invention and delivery for engineers, scientists and other technical professionals who must present complex information to general audiences, policymakers and interdisciplinary teams. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Special attention to clarity, analogy and visualization as tools for translating technical knowledge. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking while integrating visual and graphic materials into their presentations. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with communication skills essential for technical professions. Builds competence in simplifying complex information, supporting arguments with evidence and adapting content for non-experts. Develops confidence in delivering technical presentations in professional, academic and civic settings. Prepares students for roles requiring leadership, interdisciplinary collaboration and the ability to explain technical processes to decision-makers and the public. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ways of describing technical work may not be effective outside specialized fields. Develops understanding of ways technical communication techniques—such as analogy, narrative and visualization—shape audience comprehension and trust. Emphasizes that effective technical communication requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as subject matter expertise. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why communication matters in technical professions; study of ethical principles in technical communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of general and specialized audiences; research and organization of technical content; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of analogies, language and presentation aids to explain complex information; practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking; integration of visual and graphic materials into technical presentations. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Communication for Technical Professions

description: Group Communication and Discussion. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and research on small group communication. Focuses on definition, structure and functions of groups, including roles, norms, power and/or communication climate. Examines processes such as problem-solving, role-playing, decision-making, leadership, organization and/or conflict management. Attention to verbal and nonverbal codes, listening, relationships and/or cooperation as foundations for interaction and group productivity. Considers professional, political, religious, community and/or cultural contexts in which group communication occurs. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops both understanding and practical ability for effective participation and leadership in group settings with diverse participants across professional, academic and/or civic contexts. Builds competence in problem solving, decision-making and conflict management within teams. Strengthens ability to manage power dynamics, foster positive communication climates and/or adapt to cultural differences in group interaction. Enhances capacity for collaboration, organizational effectiveness and leadership in contexts where teamwork and collective decision-making are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about group work differ from research-based perspectives. Develops understanding of the ways roles, norms, leadership and/or power can shape group interaction. Emphasizes that effective group communication requires cooperation, critical thinking and constructive conflict management to improve decision-making and outcomes. Explores how divergent or unfamiliar perspectives and backgrounds shape group interaction, offering insight into effective collaboration in diverse teams. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of group definition, structure and functions; study of roles, norms and power in group dynamics; analysis of communication climate and culture; approaches to problem solving and decision-making; strategies for leadership, organization and conflict management; examination of verbal and nonverbal codes and listening skills; techniques for fostering cooperation and productivity in groups. Course discussions may also engage with diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting the variety of professional, political, religious, community and/or cultural contexts in which group communication occurs
title: Group Communication and Discussion

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of interviewing as a purposeful form of interpersonal communication. Focus on questioning strategies, listening and interaction between the interviewer and interviewee. Examines informative, persuasive, survey and/or employment interview contexts. Develops skills as both the interviewer and the interviewee. Emphasizes how structure, audience, goals and setting shape communication choices. Addresses the logical and psychological bases of interviewing. Class applications may involve exposure to perspectives and experiences across social, cultural and professional backgrounds. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds transferable skills essential to journalism, media, public communication and organizational practice. Involves questioning, listening, adaptation to audience and purpose and interaction across varied goals. Applies to situations that require navigating unfamiliar or sensitive territory with professionalism. Develops skill in effectively navigating differences in belief, identity, experience and disagreement within interview contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how interviews function as purposeful conversations, showing how credibility, preparation and strategy shape outcomes. Encourages awareness of the interview as a structured exchange rather than spontaneous talk. Broadens understanding of how perspective and authority influence communication across roles and settings for both interviewer and interviewee. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of questioning techniques, listening practices, rapport-building, credibility assessment and ethical responsibility; examination of informative, persuasive, survey, research and/or employment interviews; consideration of how audience, purpose and context govern interview structure and performance. Course work may involve engagement with people from varied backgrounds and experiences. Interview practice may include topics connected to identity, culture, ethics, work and/or participants’ personal lives. Exposure to differing viewpoints and/or lived realities reflects the range of issues encountered in professional and public communication. May include resume writing skills in preparation for career interviews
title: Interviewing - Principles and Practice

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines principles and practices of communication technology in the digital domain. Surveys the history and standards of television, radio, video gaming, streaming media, e-publishing and/or social networking industries and markets. Focuses on production skills such as composing, recording and editing digital content, as well as media literacy across platforms, including the ability to evaluate social, cultural and/or ethical implications of communication technologies. Emphasizes media-centric strategic foresight to postulate regarding the future of the communication and technological landscape. Class applications may also draw on popular culture and/or current events, connecting course concepts to contemporary media environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds technical competence and media literacy skills applicable across professional, academic and civic contexts. Develops the skills necessary to create digital media content, adapt communication strategies to emerging technologies, tell stories across multiple media platforms and evaluate the impact of communication technologies on audiences and industries. Strengthens preparation for careers in journalism, media production, marketing, communication design, public relations and related fields where technological fluency and critical analysis are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how communication technologies shape interaction, identity and/or culture beyond their technical functions. Highlights how tools such as streaming platforms, social media and/or virtual environments influence professional practice, everyday communication and public dialogue. Clarifies both opportunities and challenges presented by digital media, including questions of access, ethics and/or social impact. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of the development and application of communication technologies across industries; exploration of audio, video, web and interactive media tools; analysis of digital platforms and markets; consideration of issues such as media convergence, intellectual property, ethics and sociocultural impact. Course work may incorporate case studies from popular culture and/or current events to connect course concepts with real-world practices. The course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of discourses relating to digital technologies and practices
prerequisites: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor
title: Communication Technology Skills

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles and practices for analyzing speeches and other forms of public discourse. Deploys rhetorical analysis to explain how symbols, images, language, performances and/or narratives shape meaning. Considers how communicative acts function in cultural, political, religious, institutional and/or historical contexts. Includes exposure to discourses and theories across a wide spectrum of political, cultural and/or ideological differences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Demonstrates how public discourse shapes civic life. Provides tools for interpreting speeches, media and other forms of public discourse across various contexts. Builds skills in analysis, research and writing that transfer to fields including law, politics, media, public relations and education. Shows how studying rhetorical strategies can uncover arguments and explain how communication impacts civic decision-making, public controversy and cultural understanding. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Expands the understanding of rhetoric to be beyond speechmaking to include other forms of public discourse such as popular media, advertisements and digital content. Introduces frameworks scholars use to study how communication may be shaped by context, culture, ideology and/or power. Emphasizes understanding and evaluating these perspectives, building awareness of the range of approaches scholars bring to the study of public discourse. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include scholarly traditions of rhetorical analysis, including feminist, narrative, ideological, dramatistic and/or classical criticism. Material may draw from political speeches, media messages, entertainment media and social movements. Because rhetorical criticism examines communication across many areas of public life, the course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ideas present in society
title: Rhetorical Criticism

description: Argumentation and Debate. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles of argumentation and skills of debate, with emphasis on reasoning, evidence, refutation and briefing. Examines how arguments are constructed, supported, challenged, revised and delivered. Considers the standards of sound reasoning, common fallacies and tests of evidence and credibility. Attention to ethical and cultural considerations in arguments, including analysis of audiences and contexts. Explores the role of debate in decision-making. Includes exposure to debate topics across political, religious, ideological and/or cultural spectrums, reflecting the diversity of arguments found in society. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops skills in critical thinking, research and communication essential for professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds competence in evaluating arguments, analyzing evidence and presenting claims effectively to diverse audiences. Strengthens oral and written study of advocacy, responsive listening and adaptability in structured debate and informal discussion. Skills gained are directly relevant to law, politics, business, media, public policy and other areas where persuasive communication and sound reasoning are central. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday argument practices differ from structured approaches developed in debate and communication studies. Expands understanding of argument as more than personal opinion, showing how reasoning, evidence and ethical standards shape persuasion. Explores frameworks for evaluating arguments across different contexts, including individual decision-making, group deliberation, political campaigns and/or public debates. Highlights how cultural values and ideological perspectives influence the ways arguments are constructed and received. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include foundations of argument and debate; analysis of debate propositions; evaluation of evidence and proof; construction of affirmative and negative cases; cross-examination and refutation; ethical and cultural considerations in argument; listening and evaluation; debate as a form of public speaking; formats in academic, political and public debates. Course materials and debate topics may address diverse and sometimes controversial issues, reflecting the range of perspectives present in public discourse
title: Argumentation and Debate

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the practice of difficult dialogues and the communication skills needed to engage productively across differences. Focus on active listening, perspective-taking, deliberation, collaborative decision making, teamwork and/or additional processes of collective problem solving. Examines how dialogic processes can be designed and organized to minimize destructive consequences of bias, prejudice, discrimination, power disparities and/or unexamined privilege across dimensions of difference, such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and/or religion. Considers the role of facilitation techniques in creating conditions for constructive conversations on complex and often polarizing issues. Includes exposure to perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops skills for navigating conversations on sensitive and complex issues in professional, academic, civic and personal contexts. Builds competence in listening across differences, managing conflict and fostering collaborative and intentional decision making. Strengthens the ability to engage constructively in contexts marked by diversity, disagreement or polarization. Skills gained apply to leadership, teamwork, organizational communication, relationships and community engagement across families, workplaces and/or public settings. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how different models of interaction, such as debate, dialogue, negotiation and/or everyday conversation, frame the goals and norms of communication, allowing for comparison, application or critique. Expands understanding of how communication shapes perceptions of power, privilege and/or difference in personal, organizational and/or civic contexts. Introduces frameworks for recognizing how bias, equity and/or cultural perspectives can influence interaction. Emphasizes awareness of diverse viewpoints, the productive value of disagreement and the role of constructive exchange in building community. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of dialogue as a communication practice distinct from debate or analysis of persuasion; exploration of active listening, perspective-taking and deliberation; skills in conflict management, collaborative decision making and team problem solving; consideration of communication in the context of bias, prejudice, discrimination, power, equity and/or privilege. Attention to how dialogue functions across interpersonal, organizational and civic settings. Course materials and discussions may address sensitive or controversial issues, reflecting a wide range of political, cultural and/or religious perspectives present in society
title: Difficult Dialogues on Power, Privilege and Difference

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores basic audio storytelling techniques required for podcast production within journalism and digital content creation, including principles of podcast development, scripting, interviewing, voice performance, audio recording and editing. May include instructions in microphone selection, sound environments and use of editing software. Covers branding elements such as titles, descriptions, cover art, music and metadata. Introduces strategies for publishing, promotion and audience growth across distribution platforms. Course content may include legal and ethical considerations related to privacy, attribution, licensing or defamation.
