description: Introduction to statistical methods and data analysis in economics; covers descriptive statistics, probability theory and the principles of statistical inference as foundations for empirical research; introduces data management and analysis techniques using spreadsheet and statistical software; emphasizes hypothesis testing and the fundamentals of regression analysis; develops skills for summarizing, visualizing and interpreting economic data to draw evidence-based conclusions about real-world economic relationships
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 142 , MATH 151 , or MATH 171 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor
title: Economic Data Analysis

description: Application of mathematics and statistics to interpret economic phenomena; elementary econometric models and estimation techniques useful for estimating economic relationships and theories
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 ; grade of C or better in ECMT 461 , STAT 211 or STAT 303
title: Introduction to Econometrics

description: Application of econometric methods to analyze economic data with a focus on modern data analytics; focuses on the application of statistical software for model specification, estimation, and evaluation of complex economic relationships; designed for data-driven analysis in academic and professional settings
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 ; grade of C or better in ECMT 461 , STAT 211 , or STAT 303 ; grade of C or better in CSCE 110 , CSCE 111 , or CSCE 121
title: Applied Econometrics

description: Application of econometric techniques to the prediction of economic and financial variables; develops tools for modeling and forecasting with time-series data; covers model specification, estimation and evaluation using methods such as ARMA models, trend analysis and tests for structural change; examines issues of overfitting, model selection and forecast combination; explores the assessment of forecast accuracy; integrates theoretical and empirical approaches using statistical software to generate and evaluate forecasts in real-world settings
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECMT 463 ; junior or senior classification
title: Economic Forecasting

description: Principles of Economics. Examination of how individuals, firms and governments make choices under scarcity and how their interactions shape markets and economic outcomes; emphasizes opportunity cost, marginal reasoning and the determinants of demand and supply; explores how prices, competition and policy affect efficiency; highlights the value of economic reasoning for understanding real-world behavior and guiding sound policy and decision-making; applications may include causes of market and government failures, labor-market outcomes and strategic behavior in business decision-making; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Principles of Economics

description: Principles of Economics. Study of the overall performance of the economy and the forces that drive growth, inflation and unemployment; measuring and interpreting key indicators such as GDP, prices and labor-market outcomes; examines fiscal and monetary policy tools and their influence on output, employment and prices; applications may include the effects of taxation, government debt and international trade on macroeconomic stability and long-term prosperity; emphasizes how macroeconomic reasoning informs business and policy decisions
prerequisites: ECON 202 or approval of undergraduate advisor; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Principles of Economics

description: Directed studies in specific problem areas of economics
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified area of economics
prerequisites: Approval of undergraduate advisor
title: Special Topics in

description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in economics. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification
title: Research

description: Study of money, financial institutions and monetary policy in the U.S. and global economy; examines the structure and functions of financial markets and intermediaries; examines the nature, role and measurement of money; explores the organization and policy tools of the Federal Reserve System and the transmission of monetary policy; links between interest rates, credit conditions and macroeconomic performance; develops understanding of how financial systems support stability, growth and effective policy-making
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 203 ; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Money and Banking

description: Analysis of the causes and consequences of poverty and inequality and the role of public policy in shaping economic outcomes; examines the measurement of income, wealth and mobility; explores theoretical and empirical perspectives on market forces, discrimination and opportunity; evaluates the design and impact of social insurance and welfare programs on poverty reduction, incentives and economic performance; emphasizes evidence-based approaches to understanding how policy choices affect efficiency and distributional outcomes in modern economies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Poverty, Inequality and Social Policy

description: Application of microeconomic theory to the business and practice of sports; analyzes market structure, pricing and competition in sports industries; concepts of market power, antitrust policy and valuation of long-term assets; explores strategic behavior using game theory and the effects of imperfect information on decision-making; examines public finance aspects such as stadium subsidies and distributional impacts; emphasizes how sports contexts illustrate broader economic principles and empirical testing of models of behavior
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 202
title: Sports Economics

description: Analysis of how work, family and public policy interact to shape labor market outcomes and inequality; theories and evidence on labor supply, human capital formation and earnings differences; effects of family structure, workplace flexibility and government policies on employment and wages; explanations and empirical measurement of discrimination; emphasizes the use of quantitative methods to evaluate costs and benefits of policies addressing inequality in the United States and abroad
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 or approval of instructor
title: Work, Family and Public Policy

description: Analysis of how consumers and firms make decisions under scarcity and how their interactions determine prices and resource allocation; develops the theoretical foundations of demand, supply and market equilibrium; examines consumer choice and utility maximization, firm production and cost minimization, and profit-maximizing behavior under competition; explores outcomes when markets depart from perfect competition, including monopoly and oligopoly; emphasizes the efficiency and distributional consequences of market structures
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 202 ; grade of C or better in MATH 142 , MATH 151 or MATH 171 ; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Microeconomic Theory

description: Application of economic principles to the study of education systems and policy; examines theoretical foundations for private and public investment in education; analyzes returns to education, human capital formation and the role of non-cognitive skills; explores how resources, financing, accountability and choice affect educational outcomes in K-12 and higher education; focuses on empirical approaches to evaluating education policy and the measurement of effectiveness
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 202 ; grade of C or better in ECMT 461 , STAT 211 or STAT 303
title: Economics of Education

description: Analysis of the causes and consequences of economic development and underdevelopment across countries; topics may include historical and contemporary theories of growth, structural transformation and inequality; measures of income, poverty and well-being and their use in comparing nations; the challenges of agricultural and industrial transition, institutional change and policy design; emphasizes empirical approaches to evaluate development strategies and innovations
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 202 and ECON 203
title: Economic Development

description: Student participation in an approved high-impact learning practice; reflection on professional outcomes; documentation and self-assessment of the learning experience at mid-curriculum point
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: High Impact Experience

description: Analysis of the determinants of national income, employment and prices in modern macroeconomic theory; models of long-run growth, short-run fluctuations and policy responses; examines aggregate demand and supply frameworks and the role of expectations in shaping economic outcomes; explores how monetary and fiscal policy influence inflation, output and stability across business cycles; emphasizes the use of theoretical and empirical tools to interpret macroeconomic data and evaluate policy
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 203
title: Macroeconomic Theory

description: Examination of the economic role of government in market economies; analyzes the rationale for public intervention through the provision of public goods, correction of externalities and design of social insurance and transfer programs; evaluates the effects of taxation and government spending on resource allocation, income distribution and incentives; explores the concepts of market and government failure and the tradeoffs inherent in policy design; emphasizes the use of theoretical and empirical tools to evaluate policy
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Public Finance

description: Analysis of the organization, financing and delivery of health care in the U.S. and global context; examines the demand for health and health care, the behavior of providers and insurers and the impact of public and private insurance on costs, access and quality; explores market imperfections arising from information asymmetries, moral hazard and adverse selection; evaluates the role of competition and regulation among hospitals, insurers, physicians and pharmaceutical firms; considers how policy design and innovation affect the health care sector
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Health Economics

description: Analysis of recent research in the economics of microfinance; fundamental issues with microfinance and wealth creation; study of both theory and empirical work of recent research on microfinance; use of academic research to see how relevant it is to the practical aspects of microfinance
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Economics of Microfinance

description: Analysis of how labor markets determine wages, employment and the allocation of labor across sectors; develops theoretical and empirical models of labor supply and labor demand to explain patterns of work and compensation; examines the role of human capital, discrimination, unions and labor-market institutions; topics may include minimum wages, taxation, social insurance and immigration
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Economics of Labor

description: Exploration of the economics of the workplace using the insights of economic models and behavioral economics; focus on incentives and information, motivation of workers through incentive pay, promotion tournaments and threats, design of the hiring process to recruit a talented workforce, attraction and retention of employees, downsizing
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Personnel Economics

description: Application of economic reasoning to legal rules, institutions and outcomes; examines how property, contract and tort law shape incentives and resource allocation; analyzes the efficiency and distributional consequences of legal decisions and regulatory frameworks; develops testable hypotheses on how laws influence behavior and market outcomes; uses economic models and empirical evidence to interpret court rulings, evaluate legal reforms and understand the reciprocal relationship between law and the economy
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Law and Economics

description: Application of economic theory and empirical methods to the study of crime and criminal justice policy; examines how incentives, deterrence and opportunity costs influence criminal behavior; analyzes the effects of policing, punishment, incarceration and rehabilitation on crime rates and social welfare; explores issues of rationality, discrimination and inequality within the justice system; considers evidence on crime-reduction policies; integrates data analysis to assess the effectiveness of crime-control strategies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Economics of Crime

description: Analysis of how market structure and firm behavior determine industry performance and economic welfare; develops theoretical and empirical tools to study competition, market power and strategic interaction among firms; examines pricing, product differentiation, entry, innovation and advertising as determinants of market outcomes; explores the role of antitrust policy and regulation in promoting efficiency and preventing collusion; demonstrates how industrial organization principles explain firm strategy and market design in the modern economy
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: The Organization of Industry

description: Analysis of competition, regulation and antitrust policy through the lens of modern industrial organization; examines how strategic interactions among firms affect efficiency, innovation and consumer welfare; studies the economic rationale behind antitrust laws and their application to practices such as price discrimination, collusion, mergers and vertical restraints; evaluates landmark judicial decisions and regulatory actions shaping competition policy and market outcomes
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Economics of Antitrust and Regulation

description: Analysis of the operation and regulation of energy markets and the design of efficient energy policy; applies microeconomic theory and empirical methods to sectors including oil, gasoline, electricity, natural gas, renewables and nuclear power; examines market structure, pricing and investment under evolving technologies and environmental constraints; studies the interaction between energy and environmental policies such as fuel economy standards, carbon pricing and cap-and-trade programs; considers domestic and international experiences to evaluate how regulation and innovation shape energy efficiency, sustainability and market performance
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Energy Markets and Policy

description: Application of economic theory to the analysis of global environmental challenges and policy design; examines how market failures and externalities give rise to pollution and resource depletion; evaluates alternative approaches to environmental management including regulation, taxation and market-based instruments such as tradable permits; introduces methods for cost-benefit analysis and non-market valuation of environmental goods
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Environmental Economics

description: Study of how experiments and behavioral insights advance understanding of economic decision-making; examines deviations from standard models of rationality and self-interest in choices under risk, time and social interaction; introduces experimental methods for testing economic theories and evaluating policy-relevant behavior in laboratory, field and online settings; explores issues of experimental design, data reliability and statistical analysis; emphasizes the development and interpretation of experiments to study individual and group behavior in economics and related fields
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Experimental Economics

description: Experimental approaches to evaluating economic policies and programs in real-world settings; introduces field experimental methods used to identify causal effects of interventions implemented by firms, governments and NGOs; examines how individuals and organizations respond to changes in incentives across contexts such as education, labor, health, political economy and development; explores the design, implementation and interpretation of randomized evaluations; demonstrates how experimental evidence informs effective and evidence-based policy making in both developed and developing economies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 202 and ECMT 461
title: Economics of Policy Evaluation

description: Introduction to the economic principles underlying financial markets and asset pricing; examines the structure and operation of equity, bond, foreign exchange and derivative markets in domestic and international contexts; topics may include portfolio choice, risk management, intertemporal decision-making, models of market efficiency, arbitrage and the relationship between financial markets and the broader economy; integrates theoretical and empirical perspectives to understand how financial systems allocate resources and influence economic performance
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 and ECMT 461 ; or approval of instructor
title: Financial Economics

description: Analysis of individual and strategic decision-making; develops formal models of choice under risk, uncertainty and interdependence; explores how preferences, information and incentives shape behavior and outcomes in competitive and cooperative settings; applies these concepts to the design and evaluation of mechanisms and institutions that govern exchange and allocation; topics may include auctions, matching, contract design, signaling, bargaining and repeated interaction
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Economics of Decision-Making Strategy

description: Analysis of the causes and consequences of international trade and trade policy; develops theoretical foundations based on comparative advantage and factor endowments to explain patterns of trade and the distribution of gains across individuals and countries; examines the determination of product and factor prices and the effects of trade on income inequality and economic welfare; evaluates the rationale and impact of trade policies such as tariffs, quotas and subsidies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 ; also taught at Galveston campus
title: International Trade Theory and Policy

description: Interaction of people, firms and governments across countries in the global macroeconomy; examines international flows of goods, capital and currencies and their implications for output, employment and prices; models of exchange rate determination, balance of payments and cross-border borrowing and lending; explores the effects of fiscal and monetary policy in open economies; causes and consequences of currency, debt and financial crises
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 410 , or approval of instructor
title: Global Macroeconomics

description: Examines strategic interaction and decision-making using game theory; develops the concepts of strategy, equilibrium and rational behavior in simultaneous, sequential and repeated games; examines topics such as uncertainty, information, coordination and collective action; explores equilibrium refinements and evolutionary stability; applies theoretical tools to real-world settings including auctions, bargaining, oligopoly, voting and cooperation; emphasizes how strategic reasoning and experimental evidence inform understanding of competition and cooperation among individuals and organizations
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323
title: Games and Economic Behavior

description: Introduction to the mathematical methods used in modern economic analysis; develops tools for solving systems of linear equations, conducting comparative statics and optimizing economic models; covers topics in linear algebra, calculus and constrained optimization with applications to consumer and producer theory; emphasizes mathematical reasoning as a tool to formalize economic relationships, derive testable implications and build a foundation for advanced study in economics and related fields
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 and ECON 410
title: Foundations of Mathematical Economics

description: Applies microeconomic and macroeconomic principles to the analysis of current policy and market challenges; topics vary by instructor but may include evaluating issues such as fiscal and monetary policy, globalization and trade, labor markets, technological change, health care, innovation and long-run growth; emphasizes critical interpretation of data, policy evaluation and evidence-based reasoning; encourages application of economic tools to real-world topics. May be taken two times for credit as content varies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 and ECON 410
title: Contemporary Economic Issues

description: Application of economic and quantitative methods to the analysis of decisions made by individuals, firms and policymakers; focuses on causal inference and the identification strategies that distinguish correlation from causation; includes coding fundamentals and data management techniques to clean, summarize and analyze data using statistical software; develops skills in implementing and interpreting empirical models, presenting results through data visualization and written analysis and evaluating the effectiveness of policies and programs; topics and applications vary across instructors. May be taken two times for credit as content varies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECMT 463 or ECMT 464 , or approval of instructor
title: Data Science for Economic and Social Issues

description: Introduction to modern data science methods and their application to real-world economic and business decision-making; integrates economic reasoning with computational tools for analyzing and interpreting data; introduces coding and statistical modeling, including resampling, cross-validation and machine learning techniques such as random forests and neural networks; emphasizes how data-driven insights complement economic intuition in organizational and policy contexts; designed for students seeking to apply economic analysis and data skills in professional, multidisciplinary environments; topics and applications vary across instructors. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECMT 463
title: Applied Data Science in Economics

description: Directed internship in an organization to provide on-the-job training and applied research experience with professionals in settings appropriate to economics and student professional interest. Maximum 6 hours can count toward major. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Major in economics; 12 completed hours of economics including ECON 323 with a grade of C or better; 2.5 cumulative GPA; 3.0 GPA in economic courses; pre-approval of the director of economics internship programs
title: Internship

prerequisites: Major or minor in economics; approval of undergraduate advisor

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 315 ; junior or senior classification
title: Human Capital Acquisition, Management, and Development

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor
title: Applied Learning Principles

college: College of Education and Human Development

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 203 and EHRD 210 ; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Learning and Development in HRD

college: College of Education and Human Development

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 203 and EHRD 210 ; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Organizational Development

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Measurement and evaluation techniques in the field of Human Resource Development and Technology Management; emphasis on understanding, calculation and application of basic testing, assessment and interpretation methods
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; EHRD 203 with a grade of C or better; MATH 140 and MATH 142
title: Measurement and Evaluation in Human Resource Development and Technology Management

description: This course introduces the design, development and evaluation of technology-enhanced learning experiences in organizational and educational contexts. Emphasis is placed on the application of instructional design models, adult learning principles and emerging tools to create effective and engaging instructional materials. Students will examine the role of instructional technology within the design process, evaluate learning platforms and authoring tools and produce digital learning content using accessible software. The course also explores current trends shaping instructional technology practice in the field of human resource development
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 371 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Instructional Technology and Design

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Theories and concepts associated with learning in individuals and organizations; overview of leadership theories and learning theories within a context of developing leadership programs
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor
title: Principles and Practices of Leadership in Human Resource Development and Technology Management

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Assist learners in the identification and understanding of globalization and engagement issues in learning, work and community; exploration of current issues, theories, trends and policy issues
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor
title: Workplace Dynamics in a Globalized World

college: College of Education and Human Development
description: Conflict management principles and practices in the workplace; engagement in meaningful conflict from a training and development perspective
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 203 and EHRD 210 ; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Conflict Management and Dialogue

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EHRD 203 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor
title: Seminar

prerequisites: Senior classification and approval of instructor, admitted to professional phase, EHRD 481 , EHRD 490

description: Design Process. Fundamental design processes, issues and theories relevant to design resolution and the creation of new ideas; creative thought processes from the formation of ideas through incubation to final product and future impact on the physical environment and society
title: Design Process

description: Introduction to Rhetoric and Composition. Intensive study of and practice in writing processes, from invention and researching to drafting, revising and editing, both individually and corroboratively; emphasis on effective rhetorical choices including audience, purpose, arrangement and style; focus on writing the academic essay as a vehicle for learning, communicating and critical analysis
title: Introduction to Rhetoric and Composition

description: Composition and Rhetoric. Focus on written communication through the development of analytical reading ability, critical thinking and information literacy; emphasis on effective rhetorical choices such as audience, purpose, arrangement and style. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Composition and Rhetoric

description: How does one tell the story of the natural world and human interactions within it? This course explores that question through environmental literature, investigating creative efforts that imagine, celebrate, exploit and advocate for the more-than-human world. Students will engage with a variety of texts, practice interpretive methods from literary studies and ask critical questions about how narrative and other forms of representation shape our understanding of the environment and our personal or social responsibilities to the natural world of which humans are a part. This course is reading intensive. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus
title: Environmental Literature

description: Focus on writing about literature through practice in skills such as literary analysis, close reading and interpretation; practice in writing, discussion and other forms of communication about texts; may include works drawn from a wide range of definitions of literature, such as novels, films, songs, poetry, drama and/or other kinds of texts. Text selection organized thematically and/or by genre. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Writing About Literature

description: Introduction to literature by African Americans emphasizing major themes and traditions. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. ENGL-204 also taught at Galveston campus
title: Introduction to African-American Literature

description: This course covers a variety of cultural texts (individual works, literary movements, genres and so forth) by authors of African descent in Africa, Europe and the Americas. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Introduction to Africana Literature

description: Introduction to some of the major literary and cultural forms of the twenty-first century. Course topics might include texts from a variety of national and cultural origins, different approaches to a relevant topic or representations of contemporary historical events. Students will explore how contemporary aesthetic and intellectual texts develop and express ideas about the human condition across cultures. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus
title: 21st-Century Literature and Culture

description: Introduction to digital culture(s); exposure to some methodologies for the interpretation and critique of digital media from the humanities. These may include but are not limited to approaches from critical data studies, media studies, digital humanities, and the history of science and technology. Students can expect to gain experience analyzing digital media and expect to develop critical thinking and intercultural competence while engaging in respectful discourse on complex topics related to digital cultures. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Human Thinking and Digital Culture

description: Nature of human language and of linguistics; includes an introduction to phonology, syntax, semantics and morphology and the role of spoken and written discourse in sustaining societal arrangements
title: Introduction to Linguistics

description: Technical and Professional Writing. Focus on writing for technical and professional rhetorical situations with an emphasis on document design, audience awareness, clarity of communication and collaborative teamwork. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Technical and Professional Writing

description: Introduction to history, influence and major ideas of Cultural Studies; use of culture as a means to critique social problems and understand social forces; analysis of culture in its relationship to power; participation in project investigating contemporary U.S. youth subcultures
title: Foundations in Cultural Studies

description: Exploration of selected works of Shakespeare in text, performance and/or adaptation, with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing Shakespeare’s texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Shakespeare

description: Exploration of the interrelationships of literature and other arts, including the exchange or adaptation of aesthetic principles, techniques and content among textual, visual and multimedia art forms, such as painting, sculpture, film, music, architecture, graphic and decorative arts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus
title: Literature and the Other Arts

description: An exploration of the graphic novel as a medium, with a focus on the form’s varieties, use of both textual and visual elements and impacts on our understanding of storytelling and artistic expression; analysis of texts in relation to social and cultural contexts, various theoretical lenses and/or scholarly engagements with graphic novels. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Graphic Novel

description: World Literature I. Survey of world literature from the ancient world through the sixteenth century in relation to its historical and cultural contexts; texts selected from a broad group of authors, traditions and genres. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. ENGL-221 also taught at Qatar campus
title: World Literature I

description: World Literature II. Survey of world literature from the seventeenth century to the present in relation to its historical and cultural contexts; texts selected from a broad group of authors, traditions and genres. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. ENGL-222 also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: World Literature II

description: American Literature - The Beginnings to Civil War. This course is a survey introduction to American literature from the beginnings of the Americas to the Civil War examining writers, genres and movements of the period. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: American Literature - The Beginnings to Civil War

description: American Literature - Civil War to Present. This course is a survey introduction to American literature from the Civil War to the present examining writers, genres and movements of the period. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: American Literature - Civil War to Present

description: Introduction to the historical scope of Asian American literature and culture, primarily though not limited to writing and cultural artifacts from the late 19th century to the present. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Asian American Literature and Culture

description: Survey of English Literature I. Literature of England from the early medieval period through the 18th century, with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Survey of English Literature I

description: Survey of English Literature II. Literature of Great Britain and its colonies from the late 18th century to the 21st century, with attention to various historical, cultural, political and/or critical contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus
title: Survey of English Literature II

description: Introduction to the speculative and marvelous genres of literature; survey of genres such as science fiction, fantasy, horror, fairy tales and/or related media such as film with their respective genre concepts, narrative frameworks and significant authors and directors; examination of different methodological approaches and historical contexts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Introduction to Speculative and Marvelous Literatures

description: Elements of Creative Writing. Initiation into the craft of creative writing in prose and poetry; extensive reading in the genres; peer workshops. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Elements of Creative Writing

description: Focus on and practice in the writing of advanced academic and/or professional prose. May consider topics such as scholarly genres of writing and/or questions related to writing process, research, style, audience awareness, digital writing or ethics in scholarly discourse. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Also taught at Galveston campus
title: Advanced Composition

description: Fundamental aspects of film analysis and criticism; ENGL-251 also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Introduction to Film Analysis

description: Introduction to Cultural Studies and Popular Cultural. An introduction to the history, theories and methods of contemporary cultural studies. The course will explore key concepts in cultural theory to examine specific aspects of popular culture as well as cultural sites and practices so as to expand upon the analytical and critical thinking skills learned in ENGL 104 and 203
prerequisites: ENGL 104 ; Galveston campus
title: Introduction to Cultural Studies and Popular Culture

description: Introduction to Latinx literature and cultural production; emphasis on methods and approaches, historical breadth and context and the diverse literary traditions of people of Hispanic and Latinx descent throughout the United States and the Americas. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Introduction to Latinx Literary Studies

description: Readings selected for specific need of major or minor in English
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified area of English
title: Special Topics in

description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in English
prerequisites: 3 hours of 200-level literature; freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor
title: Research

description: Introduction to methodology, scope and practice of literature and medicine studies; analysis of literature and/or other texts dealing with health and illness; engagement with different disciplinary perspectives as a tool for critical thinking. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Introduction to Literature and Medicine

description: A writing intensive introduction to the central methods of the discipline and the operations of the major at Texas A&M. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: ENGL 104 or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Approaches to English Studies

description: Examination of a particular digital theme, genre or technology from a humanities perspective, such as introduction to making and/or interpreting digital materials; study of digital culture and/or digital archives. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Topics in Digital Research

description: Examination of Texas literature, culture and multi-media; exploration of the development of Texas identities and responses to the rich cultural expressions within the state; topics vary with each section. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Texas Literature

description: Examination of texts written in English that de-center the nation-state as the central way to organize cultural comparison; includes colonialism, economics, empire, globalization, migration, race and refugees. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Qatar campus
title: Transnational Literature and Culture

description: History of critical thought about art and culture from antiquity to the present; topics and readings span a variety of eras, approaches and artistic genres. Key themes and ideas in criticism may be presented in the context of historical figures or entire critical movements such as new criticism, structuralism and poststructuralism, historical materialism, feminism, race and ethnic studies and cultural studies, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent historic and current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: History of Literary Criticism

description: Exploration of the concept of cultural politics across several academic disciplines in the humanities and social sciences; broad interrogation of relationships that mediate culture and power in national and international contexts; focus on how culture shapes and is shaped by society, political perspectives and actions
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of the instructor
title: Cultural Politics

description: Phonological, grammatical and lexical history of the English language; brief discussion of some other Indo-European languages; principles of linguistic change, as reflected in English in relation to its historical and cultural contexts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: History of the English Language

description: Introductory study of Old and Middle English literature, exclusive of Chaucer, surveying major genres and topics. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: Medieval English Literature

description: Period course in the poetry, prose and drama of the intellectual and artistic movement known as the Renaissance, which flourished in England throughout the 16th and early 17th centuries. Additional attention will be given to historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: The English Renaissance

description: Period course in English poetry, prose and drama of the 17th century with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: 17th-Century Literature

description: Period course studying literature written in English created during the “long” 18th century (1660-1820) with attention given to its cultural contexts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: 18th-Century Literature and Culture

description: Period course in early British, non-Shakespearean drama to 1642 with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing early drama and its study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at the 200-level or above
title: Early British Drama

description: Exploration of historical and contemporary utopian literature through a variety of writers and texts. Topics may include but are not limited to: the relationship between utopia and dystopia; various critical theories related to utopia, dystopia and/or planning for the “good life”; myriad developments of the genre in relationship to developments of politics, history, culture and/or literary study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: Utopian Literature in the English Tradition

description: Focus on the practice of principles and methods of technical and professional editing across print and digital media, including copyediting, comprehensive editing and editorial project management with attention to standards, style and design. Topics may include understanding rhetorical situations of editing projects; editing for organization, clarity, accuracy, grammar and usability; and collaboration with writers and editors. Students can expect to strengthen skills in critical thinking, written communication and professional collaboration while developing an understanding of the role of editors in contemporary workplaces. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: ENGL 210
title: Technical and Professional Editing

description: Representative texts in English generated throughout the British empire in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, with attention to the cultural and historical contexts that produced them. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: 19th-Century Literature - Romantic

description: Exploration of some representative works of literature by writers resident in Great Britain and its colonies during the Victorian period. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: 19th-Century Literature - Victorian

description: Period course in American literature and culture from the 1820s to the 1860s, covering writers who may include, but not limited to, Emerson, Hawthorne, Thoreau, Walker, Douglass, Melville, Poe, Whitman, Dickinson, Jacobs and others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: The American Renaissance

description: History and trajectory of science fiction cinema into the 21st century by significant filmmakers, attending to film theory and genre studies; historical, aesthetic and technical developments; and the cultural and philosophical issues of the films. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: Science Fiction and Film

description: This course includes writers, genres and movements in the African American literary tradition from the beginnings through the Harlem Renaissance studied within cultural and historical context. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: African-American Literature Pre-1930

description: Legend of King Arthur in the original language or translation from its Medieval origins to the present. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that are represented in current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Arthurian Literature

description: An exploration of the development of the fantasy genre which may include a survey of foundational texts (medieval romance, myth, fairy tales, etc.) and such topics as significant authors, movements, sub-genres and media. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Fantasy Literature

description: LGBTQ texts studied in their cross-cultural, historical, political contexts. Topics may include but are not limited to studies in camp, authorship, (mis)representations in popular culture, the closet and queer coding, queer visual and performance cultures; race, sex, empire. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Literatures

description: Origins and development of the science fiction genre. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Science Fiction Present and Past

description: Significance of the sea in fictional and factual accounts, such as novels, short stories, poems and narratives of sailors and seafaring life
prerequisites: Three credits of literature at 200 level or above; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; Galveston campus; also taught at College Station campus
title: Literature of the Sea

description: The Southwestern region of the United States is a complicated place of competing values and cultures and peoples. In this class we will read novels and view films and artwork by Southwestern writers and artists, and we will discuss the ways these works do — or do not — reflect the complex ways in which we define the Southwest and America. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Life and Literature of the Southwest

description: Study of writing, culture and genres of the American South based on reading and analysis of key texts by representative authors and scholars of Southern studies. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Life and Literature of the American South

description: Multi-ethnic study of American literature, including writings of Black Americans, American Indians, Jewish Americans, Latino/as and other ethnic groups. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus
title: American Ethnic Literature

description: Works of the African-American literary tradition from the 1930s to the present studied in their cultural and historical context. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: African-American Literature Post-1930

description: Representative plays and performances from the late nineteenth century to the present
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: Modern and Contemporary Drama

description: Study of field of rhetoric of health and medicine with specific attention to the study of gender, including issues in reproduction, expertise and illness; range of methods and methodological approaches within the field
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: The Rhetoric of Gender and Health

description: An exploration of the history, development, theory and practice of fairy tales, including traditional tales from writers such as Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm and modern fairy tale retellings in text, which may include long form genres, film and/or other media. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: Fairy Tales in the English Tradition

description: A different topic for prose writers or poets each term; may include — among other approaches — historical development of genres; connection between biography and artistic production; aesthetic theories and craft techniques. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: ENGL 235 ; junior or senior classification
title: Writers’ Studies - Prose or Poetry

description: Production of advanced, complete stories; peer workshops; extensive reading. Students may encounter major authors and varied prose styles in established literary fiction writing, and the course may cover creative nonfiction and fiction. Close reading, critical thinking and written communication will be prioritized. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: ENGL 235 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Writers' Workshop - Prose

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: ENGL 235 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Writers' Workshop - Poetry

description: This course explores some of the major cultural texts from the late nineteenth to mid-twentieth century. Students can expect to encounter materials that grapple with the vast historical and social changes occurring during the time and to consider how texts represent diverse viewpoints. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: 20th-Century Literature to World War II

description: Exploration of variable film topics each semester; possible topics include major directors, historical periods, fiction into film, film genres, theoretical discourses in cinema studies and film movements. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent critical scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: ENGL 251/FILM 251 , FILM 251/ENGL 251 , FILM 301 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification
title: Advanced Film

description: Literature in English from 1945 to the present with attention to form and representation, thematic concerns and cultural implications. Students will develop their skills in close reading and literary scholarship. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Literature, World War II to Present

description: Exploration of a selection of major approaches to the theory and practice of oral and written rhetoric and discourse up to the end of the 19th century. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus
title: History of Rhetoric

description: Study of 20th and 21st century rhetorical theories and theorists; focus on relationships among rhetoric and culture, such as philosophy of language, theories of the public, public discourse, theories of media and/or rhetoric’s relationship to embodiment, identity and/or community. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Modern Rhetorical Theory

description: Focus on analysis of textual styles from a rhetorical perspective; impact of culture and contexts on style; practice in analysis and/or imitation of thematically chosen texts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: The Rhetoric of Style

description: Study of literature and film as narrative mediums and representative authors and directors. Topics may include adaptation, authorship, literary and visual storytelling, film as literature, genre studies, intended audiences. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent critical scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Literature and Film

description: Examination of Native American literature from the 19th century to the present, with a focus on the formal and narrative techniques used by Native authors to translate Indigenous survival, governance, storytelling traditions and kinship networks into the novel form. Class material may also cover the way native literature responds to the mythologization of “The Indian” in American popular media. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Native American Rhetorics and Literatures

description: Analysis of screenplay structure and content coupled with writing assignments applying principles of form. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Screenwriting

description: Advanced study of major forms of prose or poetry, analysis of structure coupled with writing assignments illustrating principles of form in narrative and/or lyric modes. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: ENGL 235 ; junior or senior classification
title: Forms of Creative Writing

description: Survey of historical and contemporary literature for children, including such forms as fairy tales, picture books, poetry, novels, film and/or other media. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Literature for Children

description: Survey of literature for adolescents, including works intended for young adults from a variety of sub-genres, which might include fantasy, dystopia, domestic fiction and the problem novel. Students identify common characteristics of literature published for young adults, construct literary arguments using select texts and appreciate young adult literature for its particular qualities. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Young Adult Literature

description: Examination of focused topics in literature and cultural production by U.S.-based Latina/o authors writing mostly in English; examination of historical and social contexts of cultural production; may include novels, poetry, short stories, plays, films and other media to gain understanding of aesthetic expression of diverse Latina/o authors, including but not limited to Mexican Americans, Puerto Ricans, Cuban Americans and Dominican Americans. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Although not required, may be taken in sequence with ENGL 262/HISP 262 or HISP 262/ENGL 262
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Latino/a Literature

description: Narrative, structural and thematic study of the Hebrew and Christian Scriptures in English translation. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: The Bible as Literature

description: History, theory and criticism, and major genre developments in horror studies. Semester topics may include Gothic literature into modern horror cinema, horror by the decades, subgenre formation, the aesthetics of horror and horror’s national and transnational influences. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent critical scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Horror Studies

description: Exploration of LGBTQ+ authorship through film and literary criticism and theories of performing the self in the act of authoring
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Authorship

description: Exploration of the development of American poetic traditions, with an emphasis on the major poetry of 19th and 20th centuries
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: American Poetry

description: Exploration of American literature and culture from the Civil War to World War I, covering writers who may include Twain, James, Freeman, Jewett, Chesnutt, Crane, Dreiser, Wharton and others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: American Realism and Naturalism

description: Writings by women in English, with emphasis on issues pertaining to women’s experiences and on their literary contributions in a variety of genres. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; ENGL-374 also taught at Galveston campus
title: Women Writers

description: An exploration of the development of the American novel; study of representative novels, topics and relevant histories from the early national period through the antebellum era until the end of the century. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: 19th-Century American Novel

description: Selected novels by 20th and 21st century American writers; emphasis on varied literary movements and on thematic and formal innovations as reflections of/responses to transformations in American society and culture since 1900. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: The American Novel Since 1900

description: Exploration of some representative works illustrating the development of the novel, by writers resident in Great Britain and its colonies, from its beginnings to the late nineteenth century. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above
title: The British Novel to 1870

description: Exploration of some representative works illustrating the development of the novel by writers resident in Great Britain and its colonies (present or former) from the late nineteenth century forward. Students may encounter major authors and varied prose styles in the British literary tradition, including literature and criticism. Close reading, critical thinking and written communication will be prioritized. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: The British Novel, 1870 to Present

description: Exploration of key terms, themes and debates within global literature written by colonized, occupied and diasporic peoples
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at the 200-level or above
title: Postcolonial Literatures

description: Advanced study and practice of creative nonfiction forms and principles of craft. Extensive reading, workshop and peer review. Students may encounter texts in literary nonfiction, memoir, lyric essay and other related nonfiction forms. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current creative publication and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: ENGL 235 ; junior or senior classification
title: Creative Nonfiction

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification
title: Studies in British Literature

description: Theories of folklore and vernacular culture; exploration of the relationship between oral literature and the forms of vernacular culture, including recorded texts, film, festival and dance. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Folklore, Literature and World Cultures

description: Exploration of literature treating significant religious topics in the context of cultural setting. Features topics such as writing as a spiritual practice, religious autobiography and memoir, poetry and rhetoric as a mode of religious inquiry. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification
title: Studies in Literature, Religion and Culture

description: Literary movements, genres, groups of authors, topics or issues in the literature and culture of people of African descent. Instructors teaching this class will choose topics, texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

description: Focus on a single genre (e.g., detective fiction, historical novel, Western fiction), including analysis of its history and development; exploration of the chosen genre's typical stylistic and/or thematic components. Students can expect to gain an understanding of the dynamics of genre as a shaping force on cultural texts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent historic and current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification
title: Studies in Genre

description: Examination of a particular period, theme or genre within literature and medicine studies; analysis of literature and/or other texts dealing with health and illness; engagement with different disciplinary perspectives as a tool for critical thinking; topics will vary. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at the 200-level or above; junior or senior classification

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives

title: Studies in Shakespeare

description: Study of selected poetry, drama and prose works of John Milton, with attention to historical, political, cultural and critical contexts. May also consider significant literary and/or philosophical texts that influenced Milton’s writing, as well as texts Milton’s writing in turn influenced. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at the 300-level; junior or senior classification

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives

Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the structures, economics and regulation of media industries across sectors such as film, television, music, publishing, video games, streaming and/or digital platforms. Examines how content is produced, financed, distributed and governed within commercial, public and hybrid systems. Considers trends in media ownership, labor practices, media convergence, globalization, audience markets and/or media policy. Attention to the roles of technology, culture and/or law in shaping how media industries operate. Course material may engage with real-world issues involving politics, regulation, representation and/or controversy, as relevant to understanding industry practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media production, media law and policy, journalism, strategic communication, entertainment management, marketing, publishing and digital platforms. Informs understanding of how media businesses make decisions, respond to regulatory pressures and adapt to changing technologies and audiences. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, business, law and policy. Useful for those navigating or analyzing industries shaped by ownership structures, market forces and cultural influence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media industries function beyond consumption and cultural familiarity. Highlights the interplay of economic interests, creative labor, technology and public policy. Encourages recognition of the power dynamics and institutional processes that shape media access, visibility and innovation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of media ownership and consolidation; production, distribution and exhibition systems; financing models and supply-chain relations; regulation and public policy; labor and creative work; technology and convergence; niche and mass markets; globalization and cultural circulation; media ethics and advocacy. Examples may draw on current and historical cases across major and emerging sectors
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Media Industries

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Exploration of variable film topics each semester; possible topics include major directors, historical periods, fiction into film, film genres, theoretical discourses in cinema studies and film movements. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent critical scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: ENGL 251/FILM 251 , FILM 251/ENGL 251 , FILM 301 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor
title: Hispanic Literature and Film

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Study of literature and film as narrative mediums and representative authors and directors. Topics may include adaptation, authorship, literary and visual storytelling, film as literature, genre studies, intended audiences. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent critical scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

description: History, theory and criticism, and major genre developments in horror studies. Semester topics may include Gothic literature into modern horror cinema, horror by the decades, subgenre formation, the aesthetics of horror and horror’s national and transnational influences. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent critical scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Horror Studies

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students examine the concept of evil through the medium of film, exploring how cinema reflects, interprets and interrogates philosophical understandings of morality, suffering and human nature. Students engage with major philosophical approaches to evil, such as classical theodicies and free will defenses and modern accounts of cruelty, moral psychology and systemic violence, while analyzing cinematic depictions that illuminate these themes. Students investigate how film both represents and questions moral experience. Lectures, discussions, screenings and writing projects combine to cultivate philosophical insight through visual storytelling in cinema. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware discourse on contentious issues and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they are able to competently navigate a variety of cultural environments
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Philosophy, Film and Evil

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts

Depending on the semester, specific foci or methodologies may be applied in an extended way to a given genre or samplings of genres, such as: science fiction films and reception studies, the western and historical consciousness, the musical and cinematic authorship, the horror film and theories of gender and sexuality, or action films and materialist analyses of culture.
