description: Philosophy challenge students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate key questions, concepts and debates in social and political thought, including those that were particularly influential on the founding generation of the United States. Sources include canonical primary texts but may also encompass more contemporary or critical responses to the canon. Emphasis is on fundamental problems in political life and may include: the source of political authority, the just distribution of the burdens and benefits of social life, the limits of state authority, the essence of political community, citizenship or responsibilities of civic life
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Social and Political Philosophy

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students survey debates regarding foundational philosophical issues about the law. While the specific issues covered may vary from semester to semester, paradigmatic topics include: what makes a law a law, the relation of law to morality, the appropriate aim of criminal punishment, the basis of criminal responsibility, methods for interpreting the U.S. Constitution, the scope or limits of a specific constitutional right, the obligation to obey the law and civil disobedience, critiques of liberalism and the aim of tort law. Students examine major jurisprudential theories — such as natural law, positivism, realism and critical and phenomenological approaches — to understand how legal systems define justice, obligation and authority. Readings include both historical and contemporary jurisprudence as well as case law
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Philosophy of Law

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students pursue focused and in-depth study of a specific topic in philosophy of law. The topic changes semester to semester. Recent versions focused on: the meaning and scope of First Amendment rights, the legal protection of privacy, the history of differing conceptions of the rule of law, modern theories of legal positivism and realism and the study of legal ontology, which investigates the ways in which laws and legal institutions exist relative to other social objects. Readings are drawn from historical and/or contemporary jurisprudence as well as case law. Students design and execute independent research projects connected to the theme of the seminar. Contact the department for information about the theme for an upcoming semester. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Advanced Topics in Philosophy of Law

description: Students explore the metatheory (formal languages, model theory and proof theory) of several basic systems of mathematical logic, including at least classical propositional logic and first-order logic with the theory of identity
prerequisites: PHIL 240 or approval of instructor
title: Symbolic Logic I

description: Students explore advanced topics in logical theory. Instructors choose from topics such as: modal logic, higher-order logic, set theory, the theory of computability, Gödel's incompleteness theorems and non-classical logic
prerequisites: PHIL 240 , PHIL 341 or approval of instructor
title: Symbolic Logic II

description: Major topics in epistemology such as the problem of induction, perception theory, memory and the problem of other minds
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Theory of Knowledge

description: Students understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view and may consider perspectives from a range of cultures. Students examine the philosophical contributions born of and germane to the experience of the African diaspora, which includes but is not limited to those who identify as African, Afro-Caribbean or African-American. Emphasis, themes and readings vary depending on the instructor; possible themes may include various conceptions of modern notions of freedom, equality, humanity and reason, taken up in the historical context of institutional slavery and the colonization of the Global South
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Africana Philosophy

description: Topics concerning the fundamental nature of reality such as what exists, the mental and the physical, universals and individuals, space and time, God
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Metaphysics

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students analyze multifaceted relationships between philosophy and literature. Class may include philosophical analysis of major recurrent themes in world literature as well as examination of what is philosophical about literature itself. Students may read works by philosophers in addition to novelists and essayists
title: Philosophy of Literature

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students examine the concept of evil through the medium of film, exploring how cinema reflects, interprets and interrogates philosophical understandings of morality, suffering and human nature. Students engage with major philosophical approaches to evil, such as classical theodicies and free will defenses and modern accounts of cruelty, moral psychology and systemic violence, while analyzing cinematic depictions that illuminate these themes. Students investigate how film both represents and questions moral experience. Lectures, discussions, screenings and writing projects combine to cultivate philosophical insight through visual storytelling in cinema. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware discourse on contentious issues and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they are able to competently navigate a variety of cultural environments
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Philosophy, Film and Evil

description: Values and conduct such as moral relativism, self-interest, utilitarianism, rules, nature of valuation, ethical language and argumentation
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Ethical Theory

description: Ethical, social, and epistemic aspects of the development of artificial intelligence (AI); foundational normative principles and their application; consequences of AI; responsible use and regulation
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor
title: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

description: Philosophical investigation of the creation and use of technology; the relations between technology, science and engineering; and how technology influences human existence, ethics and society
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Philosophy and Technology

description: Advanced philosophical investigation into the tradition of Latin American philosophy and its key approaches, ideas, cultural production and politics; major figures from the colonial period to the present; philosophical themes related to areas such as legacies of colonialism, identity, ethics, culture, politics, knowledge and meta-philosophy
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Latin American Philosophy

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students pursue advanced philosophical investigation into key approaches and themes of feminist thought. Students engage in philosophical and critical evaluation of the role of gender and sex in the formation of intellectual and cultural history, social norms and identity. May be taken two times for credit as content varies
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Philosophy of Gender

description: Major philosophers from 600 BCE to the end of the third century CE such as the Pre-Socratics, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Hellenistic, and Roman philosophy
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Classical Philosophy

description: Major philosophers from the fourth century through the 14th century, emphasizing writers such as Augustine, Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Hildegard of Bingen, and William of Ockham
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Medieval Philosophy

description: Significant seventeenth-century texts in metaphysics, epistemology, moral psychology, and political philosophy; authors such as Cavendish, Descartes, Hobbes, Spinoza, Leibniz, and Locke
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Seventeenth-Century Philosophy

description: Significant eighteenth-century texts from philosophers such as Berkeley, Cockburn, Hume, Kant, and Rousseau
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Eighteenth-Century Philosophy

description: Significant nineteenth-century texts from philosophers such as Bettina, Bradley, Dubois, Hegel, Husserl, Kierkegaard, Marx, Mill, and Nietzsche
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Nineteenth-Century Philosophy

description: The thought of philosophers such as Peirce, James, Royce, Santayana, Mead, Dewey and Whitehead
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: American Philosophy

description: Major philosophers in contemporary Anglo-American thought such as Moore, Russell, Wittgenstein, Ayer, Quine, Austin, Ryle, and Barcan Marcus
prerequisites: PHIL 240
title: History of Early Analytic Philosophy

description: Phenomenology from its nineteenth-century origins to the present; authors such as Brentano, Husserl, Scheler, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Levinas, Henry, Marion, and Irigaray
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Phenomenology

description: Existentialism from its nineteenth-century origins to the present; philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Buber, Rosenzweig, Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Camus
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Existentialism

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students focus on major philosophers and philosophical approaches from the 20th and 21st century in reference to primary texts associated with areas such as: phenomenology; hermeneutics; critical theory; structuralism, deconstruction and poststructuralism; feminist theory; postmodernism; and related areas. Students explore themes such as understanding and interpretation, language and meaning, ideology critique, power and issues of social justice
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Current Continental Philosophy

description: Use of comparative methods, ranging from comparison and contrast of methods, problem framing, and argumentation, to cross-cultural problem-solving employing resources drawn from different traditions, to examine philosophical topics such as reality, knowledge, and morality
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Comparative Philosophy

description: The nature of language; the various uses of language and their philosophical import; the nature of meaning, truth, reference and issues surrounding formal representations of natural languages
prerequisites: PHIL 240 and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Philosophy of Language

description: Philosophy of probability, including such topics as competing interpretations of probability, confirmation theory and the relation between probability and degrees of belief; decision theory, including such topics as utility and expected utility, causal decision theory vs. evidential decision theory and game theory
prerequisites: 3 hours of core MATH and 3 hours of PHIL
title: Probability and Decision

description: An exploration of social choice theory and different approaches to decision-making in groups, including applications to voting and democratic theory. Possible topics include interpersonal utility comparison, Arrow's impossibility theorem, Condorcet’s jury theorem, strategic voting, gerrymandering and political polarization
prerequisites: 3 hours of core MATH and 3 hours of PHIL
title: Social Choice

description: Key conceptions of animal welfare; approaches to animal ethics; analysis of important ideas in animal law; consideration of animal contexts such as agricultural, experimental, wild, companion and zoo animals
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor
title: Animal Welfare, Ethics and Law

description: Critical analysis of major ethical issues in medicine including truthtelling, confidentiality, paternalism, genetics, abortion, infanticide, euthanasia and social justice in health care
title: Medical Ethics

description: Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students explore ethical and social theories, principles and engineering codes of ethics and their application to ethical challenges faced by engineers. Students engage with issues, such as satisfying responsibilities to an employer, client, fellow employees, one’s profession and the public; managing project pressures, risks, liability, regulations and environmental concerns. Students practice resolving challenges that arise from varying norms found in international and cross-cultural initiatives, especially on gifts, bribes and extortion. Students critically consider the ways engineers and engineering change the human experience, cultures and the environment. Students practice respectful and thoughtful dialogue on contemporary issues, become aware of their own perspectives and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they can competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. Coursework focuses on independent ethical analysis of real and hypothetical cases and on the techniques that can be used to evaluate them
prerequisites: Junior classification
title: Ethics and Engineering

description: Practical experience in an institutional or organizational setting appropriate to analysis and understanding of issues in some area of applied philosophy. May be taken five times for credit
prerequisites: Approval of instructor and department head
title: Professional Internship

description: Directed studies in specific problem areas of philosophy
prerequisites: Approval of department head
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified area of philosophy; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Special Topics in

description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in the department of philosophy and humanities. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of dean of college
title: Research

description: Directed independent studies in specific philosophical problems
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification either as Honors students or with overall GPR of 3.25; letter of approval from head of student's major department
title: Independent Honors Studies

description: The purpose of this course is to create a welcoming and affirming environment for new public health students. Through the course, students will develop self-efficacy, self-awareness and a sense of purpose while learning strategies for success both inside and outside the classroom. Topics include academic success skills and campus resources, wellness, Aggie traditions and core values, active engagement in and beyond the classroom, and social integration within the School of Public Health community. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: First-year and first-time-in-college public health student
title: Public Health First Year Experience I

description: The purpose of this course is to build on the foundation established in PHLT 101 by deepening students’ understanding of personal, academic and professional growth within public health. Students will continue developing self-efficacy, self-awareness and a sense of purpose while exploring topics such as leadership, communication, professionalism, career readiness and community engagement. Emphasis will be placed on applying academic success strategies, strengthening connections within the School of Public Health and preparing for continued success in upper-level coursework and future public health experiences. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: PHLT 101
title: Public Health First Year Experience II

description: Healthy Lifestyles. Health issues relevant to students; included are mental health, use and abuse of drugs, human sexuality, communicable diseases, environmental and consumer health
title: Healthy Lifestyles

description: First year experience; coverage of a range of topics for success inside and outside of the college classroom such as, self-efficacy, self-awareness, sense of purpose, active engagement in and out the classroom and social integration
prerequisites: Approval of instructor; freshman classification; PHLT majors
title: First Generation Scholars I

description: First year experience; coverage of a range of topics for success inside and outside of the college classroom such as, self-efficacy, self-awareness, sense of purpose, active engagement in and out the classroom and social integration
prerequisites: Approval of instructor; freshman classification; PHLT majors only
title: First Generation Scholars II

description: Introduction to the program, development of critical thinking skills and international perspectives; introductory for the Public Health Studies Broad Street Honors Learning Community
prerequisites: Admission to Broad Street Society Honors Learning Community; public health major
title: Broad Street Learning Community I

description: Selected topics in an identified area of public health. May be taken three times for credit
prerequisites: PHLT major or approval of instructor
title: Special Topics In

description: Familiarization with public health including aspects such as different disciplines within the profession; local, national and international agencies that have interest in public health and public health code of ethics
title: Public Health Concepts

description: History, philosophy, development and careers of public health; core values, ethics, concepts, functions and essential services of public health; population health and health improvement
prerequisites: Public health major or minor, junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor
title: Foundations of Public Health

description: Exploration of social determinants of population health and the socio-cultural roots of health improvement; socio-economic, behavioral and other factors that impact human health and contribute to health improvement and health disparities
prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification
title: Social Context of Population Health

description: Biological Basis of Public Health Diseases & Disorders. Overview of the underlying science of human health and disease, considering biological mechanisms in the individual and in populations; topics include a broad set of categories of adverse health events: infectious and chronic diseases, exposure to pathogens and toxins, nutritional deficiencies, child and maternal health, biological bases of mental and behavioral health and addiction; examination of the interactions between biologic and sociocultural factors and the biology of epidemics; foundational understanding of opportunities to promote and protect health across the life course; application of disease knowledge in community and allied health professions
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification
title: Biological Basis of Public Health Diseases & Disorders

description: Principles of epidemiology, a systematic approach to collecting and evaluating information on distributions of health outcomes in populations; history of epidemiology, descriptive epidemiology, epidemiologic methods, association and causation, evidence-based public health and applications
prerequisites: Public Health major or minor; junior or senior classification
title: Epidemiology in Public Health

description: Frameworks for understanding public health on a global scale; description of current and emerging global health priorities, such as emerging infectious diseases and chronic diseases; health systems reforms; cultural competence, human rights and ethics in global health; science and technological innovation for global health; global institutions and partnerships
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Public Health in the Global Context

description: Exploration of the application of social determinants of health to population health promotion; identification of socio-economic, behavioral, cultural, societal and political factors that influence population health promotion; utilization of a socio-ecological approach in health promotion to address major health-related needs and concerns of populations; use public health planning models, theories and methods for effective health promotion
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Population Health Promotion

description: Strategies to become more familiar with types of writing required as public health students or public health professionals; strengthens and increases general writing skills; establishes a foundation for continued development in writing. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor
title: Public Health Writing

description: Familiarization with the writing style required for public health; instruction in writing styles and narrative techniques to increase and strengthen writing abilities in public health disciplines such as environmental and occupational health, health promotion and community health sciences, health policy and management, epidemiology and biostatistics. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Narrative Approach to Public Health

description: Two distinct systems – health care system: an individual and medical services model and the public health system: population level disease prevention and health education
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Health Care and Public Health System

description: Familiarization with using the CDC software Epi-Info for managing, analyzing and assessing population health data; focus on using Epi-Info to produce descriptive data reports including tables and graphs
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Public Health Data Management and Assessment I

description: Continuation of PHLT 314 ; familiarization with using the CDC software Epi-Info for managing, analyzing and assessing population health data; focus on using Epi-Info to generate inferential statistics such as confidence intervals and p-values
prerequisites: Public health major; grade of C or better in PHLT 314
title: Public Health Data Management and Assessment II

description: Familiarization with descriptive and analytical statistics and biostatistical methods with using Microsoft Excel for managing, analyzing and assessing population health data; focus on using Microsoft Excel as a biostatistical tool to produce descriptive and analytical data reports including tables, graphs and biostatistical analysis results; to analyze and assess public health data for decision making
prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification
title: Public Health Data Management and Assessment

description: Preparation as peer health educators and campus community leaders; experiential learning; includes various health topics, program development, presentation and public speaking, communication, and group facilitation
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 303
title: Concepts in Health Education

description: Public health core knowledge address factors that pose risks and hazards in homes and workplaces; methods for defining environmental contamination; identifying contaminants, pathogens and toxins; assessing risks and causality; ameliorating hazards
prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification
title: The Environment and Public Health

description: Regulations and topics of relevance to occupational health professionals; includes legislation and regulations, workers’ compensation, accident investigation, industrial hygiene, ergonomics and fire prevention with an emphasis on the health professionals’ role
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Occupational Safety and Health I

description: Principles of accident investigation and how accidents happen in the workplace; integrates procedural, systematic, corrective and formative applications for the occupational health professional
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Accident Investigation

description: Exploration of in-depth racial, ethnic, and cultural dimensions that underlie health and health disparities; emphasis on culture, social economic status and governmental policies as they influence the adaptation of health practices
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Health Disparities and Diversity in Society

description: Many aspects of human sexuality; physiology and function of human reproductive system, factors involved in learning sex roles, biological and emotional motivations associated with the sexual aspects of life and their relationship to marriage and family planning
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Human Sexuality

description: Use and abuse of drugs in today's society; physiological, sociological and psychological factors involved
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in HLTH 210 or PHLT 302
title: Drugs and Society

description: Designed for students interested in pursuing a career in a health, medical, scientific or other helping profession; develop medical word power skills combined with related health and disease knowledge
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Medical Terminology for the Health Professions

description: A broad range of health issues that are either unique to women or of special importance to women; information for the health consumer; preparation as an advocate of healthy lifestyles; awareness of the role health plays in the life of all women
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Women's Health

description: Exploration of the relationship between spirituality, religion, health, health education and spiritual health; identification of techniques to measure spiritual health/wellness and enlighten healthcare professionals to the role spiritual health plays in healing; identification of spirituality topics important to health care professionals
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; School of Public Health majors
title: Spirituality and Health

description: International perspectives on public health and healthcare, comparative historical, political and cultural effects on public health; second course in the Broad Street Learning Community sequence
prerequisites: Grade of B or better in PHLT 270
title: Broad Street Learning Community II

description: Selection, evaluation and understanding of health information, medical services, advertising of products and sociocultural factors in consumer health protection
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Consumer Health

description: Issues facing rural health care; emphasis on understanding the geographical characteristics of rural communities and their affect on health care delivery
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; School of Public Health major
title: Rural Health

description: Careful examination of strategies to design, implement and evaluate exercise and health programs in worksites; including health risk assessment, marketing protocol, needs assessment, corporate culture issues, policy development and cost-benefit analysis
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in HLTH 210 or PHLT 302
title: Worksite Health Promotion

description: Exploration of different communication approaches for addressing public health challenges; basic concepts of public health-specific communication, including risk communication, the use of mass media and evaluation of public health communication programs
prerequisites: PHLT 310 ; public health major
title: Public Health Communication

description: Exploration of successful project management and administration in public health settings; includes project development, budgeting and implementation
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 303 ; public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Project Management in Public Health

description: Concepts of legal, ethical, economic and regulatory dimensions of public health policy; the roles, influences and responsibilities of the different agencies and branches of government; advocacy for the public’s health at all levels of society
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 313 ; public health major; junior or senior classification
title: Health Advocacy and Policy

description: Principles and practices of emergency management at the local, state, national and international levels; explores stages of emergency management such as preparedness, response and recovery; includes population health and the basic processes, approaches and interventions; emergency management systems in the United States; actors in emergency management
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Emergency Management in Public Health

description: Overview of major leadership and ethical theories, current leadership and ethical issues and their impact on public health practice
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Public Health Leadership and Ethics

description: Theory and practice in the development and use of creative and traditional health education strategies in secondary schools and community settings; emphasis is given to cognitive, affective and behavioral teaching strategies
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in HLTH 222 and HLTH 331 , or a grade of C or better in PHLT 441
title: Health Education Methodology

description: Theory and practice in evaluation of health programs in school and community; analysis of test results; evaluation of standardized health tests
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in HLTH 222 and HLTH 331 , or a grade of C or better in PHLT 441
title: Health Program Evaluation

description: Preparation for contributing to the healthcare system by gaining an understanding of selected business of healthcare topics such as the role of healthcare in the economy, the cost of healthcare, the patient experience, technology and ethics
prerequisites: Business and Public Health majors; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor
title: The Business of Healthcare

description: Principles of ergonomics including principles of anatomy, physiology, instrument design, and work environments; emphasis on ergonomic design, implementing ergonomic programs
prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification
title: Human Factors and Ergonomic Health and Safety

description: Estimation and management of project costs; emphasis on improving accuracy of cost projection, making better modifications to cost on work in-progress
prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor
title: Project Cost Benefit and Economics

description: Preparatory course for advanced students in the community health internship program
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in HLTH 222 , HLTH 231, HLTH 240 , HLTH 331 , BIOL 320 , and COMM 203 ; grade of C or better in ENGL 103 or ENGL 104 ; admission into internship program
title: Contemporary Issues for Community Health Interns

description: The three core functions of public health and strategies for improving population health; case studies exploring multiple types of interventions; engagement in class discussion, break-out groups and group assignments
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 322 or PHLT 411 ; public health major; junior or senior classification
title: Strategies for Population Health Improvement

description: Combines knowledge and skills related to public health experience and coursework to address public health issues; process of developing, implementing and evaluating public health interventions; role assignment and responsibilities in group assignments and presentations
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 441 ; public health major; junior or senior classification
title: Applications of Public Health

description: Study abroad experiences led by School of Public Health faculty in select countries; lectures prior to departing and lectures and classes in country; engage in public health practice and research activities in country; visit public health agencies and programs in country. May be taken for credit up to six hours
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor
title: Global Public Health Systems and Practice Experiences

description: Discussions of the transition from the college environment to professional school and/or career environments, including professional development. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 302 ; grade of C or better in ENGL 103 or ENGL 104 ; junior or senior classification
title: Seminar

description: Internship at a selected community, public, or private health agency; on-the-job training in the areas of public health studies industry; development of evaluations, objectives and goals determined based on the requirements of the degree program
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in public health coursework; instructor approval; Public Health major
title: Internship

description: Directed study of selected problems in the area of public health studies. May be taken four times for credit
prerequisites: Approval of instructor
title: Directed Studies

description: Selected topics in an identified area of public health
prerequisites: PHLT major; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Special Topics In

description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in public health studies. May be taken two times for credit
prerequisites: PHLT 485 ; junior or senior classification and approval of instructor; 3.0 TAMU GPA
title: Research

description: Critical thinking skills and problem solving in physics: time management and teaming skills
prerequisites: Physics majors; non-majors requires approval of instructor
title: Freshman Physics Orientation

description: Introduction to life as a physics major. Introduction to research in physics and astronomy. Student-led organizations and informal physics programs in the department. Development of career skills
prerequisites: First-semester transfer and change-of-major students
title: Physics Orientation

description: This team-taught, interdisciplinary course builds scientific literacy by examining contemporary issues — current questions, discoveries and challenges at the intersection of science and society. Topics may include the Big Bang, evolution, genetics, human reproduction and health, vaccines, drugs, artificial intelligence, cryptography and cybersecurity. Students will learn to evaluate scientific claims and critically analyze how science is presented in the news, on television and on social media
title: Contemporary Issues in Science - Cosmos, Earth and Humanity

description: Designed to give an intuitive understanding of the Big Bang and Black Holes, without mathematics, and de-mystify them for the non-scientist
title: Big Bang and Black Holes

description: Physics needed to be an effective policy maker or world leader but appropriate for any citizen, since all citizens need to understand the world in which they live and work; fundamental principles of physics made comprehensible and usable by those not in science- or math-related fields
prerequisites: Basic math skills; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Physics for Future Presidents

description: Modern physics in action with hands-on physics experience in simple experiments for non-physics majors; introduction to thermodynamics and soft matter physics; heat, temperature, thermodynamic efficiency, phase transitions, mechanical properties of soft matter, heat transfer mechanisms; physical measurements
title: Soft Matter Physics for Non-physicists

description: The basic level of concepts of quantum mechanics such as wave-particle duality, complementarity, quantum interference and entanglement, and their applications to fields such as quantum communication and quantum computing
prerequisites: High school physics and calculus
title: Introduction to Quantum Mechanics

description: Physics-oriented introductory programming; basics of programming and applications of programming for physics; programming in the context of physics, such as variables, expressions, flow control, functions and data visualization, applied to physics topics such as energy minimization, Newtonian dynamics and chaos
title: Introduction for Programming for Physics

description: (PHYS 1301 and 1101, 1401) College Physics. Fundamentals of classical mechanics, heat, and sound. Primarily for architecture, education, premedical, predental, and preveterinary medical students; also taught at Galveston campus
title: College Physics

description: (PHYS 1302 and 1102, 1402) College Physics. Continuation of PHYS 201 . Fundamentals of classical electricity and light; introduction to contemporary physics
prerequisites: PHYS 201 ; also taught at Galveston campus
title: College Physics

description: Preparation of grades 6-12 science teachers to teach physics by building understanding of motion, forces, energy, waves, electricity and atomic physics; inquiry-based teaching, addressing misconceptions, designing lessons and making abstract ideas clear; studio sessions combine lecture and lab to support both physics knowledge and teaching
title: Physics for Science Teachers

description: General survey physics course for K-8 preservice teachers integrating physics content and laboratory activities relevant to physics-related subject matter included in the current Texas and national standards for elementary school science; includes aspects of mechanics, waves, electricity, magnetism and modern physics
prerequisites: Major in interdisciplinary studies or interdisciplinary technology or approval of instructor
title: Concepts of Physics

description: (PHYS 2325, PHYS 2425*) Newtonian Mechanics for Engineering and Science. Calculus-based introductory Newtonian mechanics; laws of physical motion for solution of science and engineering problems
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 or MATH 171 , or equivalent; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Newtonian Mechanics for Engineering and Science

description: (PHYS 2326, PHYS 2426*) Electricity and Magnetism for Engineering and Science. Calculus-based electricity and magnetism; electromagnetic phenomena; basic laws of electricity and magnetism; science and engineering problems involving charges, electromagnetic fields, and electrical circuits
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHYS 206 ; grade of C or better in MATH 152 or MATH 172 or equivalent; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses
title: Electricity and Magnetism for Engineering and Science

description: Description and application of laws of physical motion to the solution of science and engineering problems; using sensing, control and actuation for experimental verification of physics concepts while solving engineering problems
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 or MATH 171 or equivalent; grade of C or better in ENGR 102 ; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Experimental Physics and Engineering Lab II - Mechanics

description: Electromagnetism and electromechanical systems; use of sensing, control and actuation to demonstrate key physical relationships through the transducer relationships linking pressure, temperature and other physical stimuli to changes in electric and magnetic fields
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 152 , MATH 172 , or equivalent; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 or equivalent; grade of C or better in PHYS 216/ENGR 216 or ENGR 216/PHYS 216 ; grade of C or better in PHYS 207 , or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements
prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification
title: The Mass Media and Politics

Through the analysis of real-world case studies and hands-on exercises utilizing Excel and practitioner-oriented workbooks, students will develop the technical skills necessary to manage organizational resources effectively. The course emphasizes technical proficiency in revenue forecasting, calculating budget variance and interpreting complex budgeting information to ensure the responsible stewardship of public resources. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, the course’s case studies and classroom discussions focus specifically on the public and nonprofit organizations, requiring students to propose administrative and policy solutions for complex management problems

Drawing on perspectives from performance studies, anthropology, philosophy and the health sciences, the course explores how creative practices have been used to restore balance, foster resilience and generate meaning across time and cultures, and how these practices inform today’s evidence-based models and professional standards. Through lectures, case studies, guest speakers and participatory activities, students will engage with both the enduring questions of art’s relationship to well-being and the current best practices, ethical considerations and research methods shaping the field. description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Introduction to Biblical Archaeology

description: CONTENT. Late-Antiquity; Pre-Islamic Arabia; the rise of Islam and a historical survey of the development of the Islamicate civilizations from c. 600 to the Mongol Conquests c. 1258. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Rise of Islam, 600-1258

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus
title: Anthropology of Religion

description: Political, social, cultural and religious histories of significant figures, groups, schools of thought and movements in western Afro-Eurasia from the rise of Islam to the Renaissance; developments in political theory, literature, sociology, arts, architecture, music, philosophy, law, sciences and education

description: Case studies of the sacred in varied times and regions; holy persons; holy places; holy objects; language and literature of the sacred; competing concepts of the holy within society; gender and the holy; institutions promoting holy people and places; the impact of social, political, cultural and intellectual developments on the relationship between the sacred and the profane

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence
prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436/RELS 436 or RELS 436/ANTH 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline

description: Analysis of the Holocaust as a challenge to previous theories of civics and civic engagement; investigation of theories developed in response to the Holocaust; exploration of comparisons of historical events following the Second World War to the Holocaust

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: Religious Communication

Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor
title: NATURE in the Classroom

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Basic knowledge from ichthyology, biology of fishes and limnology related to applied aspects of freshwater and marine fishery science; management techniques applicable to streams, ponds, reservoirs, estuaries and the oceans
prerequisites: BIOL 357 , or grade of C or better in ECCB 311 , ECCB 403 , or RWFM 404 , or approval of instructor
title: Principles of Fisheries Techniques and Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: ECCB 205 or equivalent; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; RWFM 406 and RWFM 407 and ECCB 320 preferred

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Management of various herbivorous large mammals, both game and non-game; development of knowledge on how to implement habitat and population management techniques to achieve management goals; history of modern wildlife management as it relates to the restoration and harvest of various species as game that once were imperiled; utilization of natural history information in the selection of the most the beneficial management techniques, and a survey of the techniques currently used in large mammal population management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

Students will examine the diversity of avian species, their habitats and the threats they face from habitat loss, climate change, invasive species and human activity. Emphasis is placed on conservation strategies, population monitoring techniques, habitat restoration and policy frameworks at local, national and global levels. Through lectures, fieldwork and case studies, students will gain practical skills in avian identification, data collection and management planning, preparing them for careers in wildlife conservation, environmental consulting or further academic study
prerequisites: RWFM majors; grade of C or better in ECCB 302 or approval of instructor

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Wetland Delineation

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Aquaculture Production and Hatchery Management

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Fish Health and Diseases

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Review of scientific perspectives on major aspects of nutrition, diet formulation and feeding of aquatic species in aquaculture; major disease-causing organisms encountered in aquaculture and means of disease prevention and control
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification
title: Aquatic Animal Nutrition, Diet Formulation and Feeding

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences
description: Integration and synthesis of the skills learned throughout the outdoor enterprise management curriculum as well as presentations from industry representatives and content experts; application of various material from previous courses to managing a diverse array of outdoor enterprises
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in RWFM 103 ; and junior or senior classification
title: Managing Outdoor Enterprises

college: College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor

prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor

title: World Food and Fiber Crops

prerequisites: SCSC 205 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor

Statistical methods used in evidence comparison

description: Introduction to Sociology. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the histories and theories regarding lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) identities and communities. description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course examines the field of queer theory as it emerged in the U.S. academy in the 1990s and grew and developed within and beyond U.S. borders in the early 21st century. The course includes scholarship on gender and sexual diversity and its overlaps with and divergences from feminist theories, while also highlighting the ways it functions as a critical practice that extends far beyond questions of gender and sexuality. Drawing on philosophy, literature, cultural studies and political theory, the course examines how “queer” operates as a challenge to systems of normalization — of identity, desire, embodiment and knowledge itself. The course considers foundational and contemporary texts in the field. TOPICS. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores journalistic reporting in Spanish and bilingual media environments. Covers foundational practices in newsgathering, interviewing, writing and/or audio storytelling conducted in both English and Spanish. Examines how bilingual journalists adapt style, tone and/or sourcing when communicating across cultural and linguistic audiences. Considers the distinct histories, media infrastructures and representational challenges associated with Latino/a and Spanish-language communities in the United States and around the globe. Coursework may include projects based on real-world local, national and/or international cases involving cultural identity, migration and/or public affairs. Spanish proficiency required. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds practical readiness for reporting roles in Spanish-language and bilingual media, as well as careers in public communication, community outreach, translation, podcasting and global media markets. Strengthens transferable communication skills valued in civic, nonprofit and governmental sectors that serve multilingual publics. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in journalism, Latino studies, global media or communication research. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how bilingual journalism involves more than translation; it requires cultural sensitivity, linguistic precision and ethical decision-making regarding representation and voice. Highlights differences in news values, sourcing practices and audience expectations between English-language and Spanish-language media. Informs reflection on how language choice can shift narrative emphasis, credibility and/or accessibility. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of bilingual interviewing; translation for journalistic accuracy; Spanish-language media history and market structures; ethics of reporting on immigration, identity, political conflict and cross-cultural communities; podcast scripting and audio editing; comparative analysis of Spanish and English newswriting conventions; trust-building and sourcing in marginalized or multilingual contexts; cross-national journalistic collaboration. Course content may include discussion of reporting on sensitive topics such as immigration, discrimination and political discord. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; SPAN 302 or approval of instructor
title: Bilingual Reporting

description: In the digital age, AI technologies are revolutionizing landscape architecture and urban planning, providing innovative solutions for complex design and planning challenges. This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the application of AI tools in these fields. Students will explore practical applications such as writing design statements, conducting research, creating and modifying images and generating high-quality renderings. The course integrates key aspects of landscape architecture design, such as site analysis, conceptual design and detailed planning, as well as urban planning processes including land-use planning, infrastructure management and smart city solutions. Through a practical, "learning by doing" approach, students will develop visual and textual communication skills essential for translating design concepts into various digital formats. They will gain hands-on experience with AI tools to enhance their ability to perform site analysis, generate design alternatives, optimize designs for sustainability and user experience, and simulate urban growth. Additionally, the course emphasizes ethical considerations, ensuring students understand the social impacts of AI and learn to use AI responsibly to create equitable and inclusive designs

description: This course introduces students to the essential creative, technical and analytical foundations of digital filmmaking. Emphasizing the integration of production craft and cinematic literacy, students engage in hands-on exercises in camera operation, lighting, sound recording and non-linear editing while critically analyzing how these techniques shape meaning, emotion and rhythm. Through the study of film form, aesthetics and visual storytelling, students develop the ability to translate abstract narrative ideas into concrete audiovisual expressions. The course positions filmmaking as both a practical craft and an interpretive art, an iterative process of seeing, composing, recording and refining, linking the expressive choices made on set and in post-production to the analytical understanding of cinematic form. By the end of the term, students will have completed a short digital project demonstrating technical fluency, aesthetic awareness and reflective critical insight

description: This course introduces students to the creative, analytical and technical techniques required to translate rich narrative ideas into innovative digital experiences across multiple media forms. Building from script analysis and visual storytelling fundamentals, students will explore how story structure, character and thematic intent transform when reimagined for screen, immersive and interactive contexts. The course spans linear and nonlinear modes of narrative, from short-form cinematic sequences and documentary hybrids to site-specific installations, augmented reality environments and online participatory works. Through both individual and collaborative exercises, students learn to adapt written and conceptual materials into digital storytelling prototypes that integrate visual, spatial and experiential design. Students will also examine the cultural and industrial frameworks surrounding intermedia and transmedia production, including intellectual property development, adaptation ethics and cross-platform authorship. By semester’s end, participants will have created a portfolio-ready project demonstrating their ability to translate complex textual or thematic material into a compelling, media-specific form of digital storytelling
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 305 or VIST 372 , or approval of instructor
title: Digital Storytelling - Narrative Design Across Media

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the art, theory and technical practice of film editing and the post-production pipeline. Anchored in a non-linear editing system the fundamental principles taught are applicable across all professional, leading, editing platforms. Students explore the history and theory of film montage, continuity editing and stylistic techniques across fiction and non-fiction cinema. Technical training covers the complete editorial workflow, from media management, assembly, rough and fine cuts, to post-processing stages that include sound design fundamentals, professional color correction and grading, and final delivery for multiple distribution formats. The primary goal is to teach students to think like editors, understanding post-production as both a technical discipline and a vital phase of cinematic storytelling where rhythm, structure and affect are refined into expressive coherence
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 200
title: Cinema Editing and Post-Production

college: College of Performance, Visualization and Fine Arts
description: This course explores the principles and practices of cinematography and lighting in the context of contemporary virtual production. Students engage with both the practical craft of image, making and the critical analysis of cinematic form, investigating how light, lens and movement operate as expressive, technical and interpretive tools. Through film analysis, design exercises and virtual simulation with a 3D real-time game and simulation development system, the course bridges the traditions of studio cinematography with emerging digital workflows. Students learn how to construct, evaluate and refine cinematic imagery, translating aesthetic and narrative intention into visual and spatial composition. The course emphasizes cinematography as a language of thought and emotion, uniting analytical insight with creative experimentation in both physical and virtual environments

The course emphasizes advanced project management, iterative content development (ICVFX/Unreal Engine asset creation), collaborative pre-visualization and the rigorous schedule of a physical virtual production shoot. The semester functions as a single, continuous production cycle culminating in post-production finishing and professional delivery, resulting in a portfolio-ready short film that demonstrates technical fluency, creative leadership and team-based collaboration

Emphasis is placed on diseases with population-level impacts to wildlife and those that are transmissible to humans or domestic animals and those found in Texas. For exams students should know common names of diseases, synonyms and the etiologic agent. They should be able to describe the agent and its basic history, its hosts and geographic distribution. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course explores the core concepts of the interdisciplinary field of women’s and gender studies, focusing on various perspectives, scholarship, theories and histories of sex, gender and sexuality; examines theories of intersectionality, analyzing the interplay among race/racism, class/classism, sex/sexism, disability/ableism, nation/nationalism, religion/religious bias among other factors in gendered experiences and systems; surveys feminist, queer, anti-racist, decolonial and/or global scholarship that examines how social institutions and control mechanisms enact power, privilege and bias; engages controversial material and historical and/or contemporary case studies that challenge and/or support conventional understandings of gender, sex, sexuality, identity and power as necessary to achieve course learning outcomes and proficiency in disciplinary concepts and ideas. TOPICS. Course may include and is not limited to discussions and descriptions of violence, sexual assault, homophobia, transphobia, femicide, genocide, familial/domestic abuse, forced sterilization and workplace harassment; investigations of political controversies centered on reproductive and gender healthcare, gender identity, policing and/or immigration; analysis of popular culture and creative expression, including but not limited to: performance, literature, drag, music, visual culture; examinations of primary texts from historical and/or contemporary social movements and activists across the United States and around the globe; investigations of contemporary and historical labor relations and globalization; analyses and descriptions of anatomy, physiology and psychology. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives
title: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the histories and theories regarding lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) identities and communities. The course focuses on current scholarship addressing the social construction of sex, sexuality and gender; institutional ways in which homophobia, biphobia and transphobia are systematically deployed; histories and examples of LGBTQ+ activism; evolution of desire and subjectivity; and the contributions of queer scholarship in understanding society. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings that address queer approaches to institutions; intersections of sexual and gender identity with race, class, ability/disability and/or nationality; digital activism; gender violence; controversies related to LGBTQ+ issues and politics, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives

description: Explore the historical, cultural, social, economic and political dimensions of gender; define and distinguish gender roles and norms and identify sociological theories important to the study of gender; examine ideas and expectations about gender including historical and contemporary norms; understanding of scholarship on this topic increases intercultural competence and effective cross-cultural communication for participation in civic contexts and public life. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise
title: Introduction to Gender and Society

Course may include discussions and readings related to intersectionality, traditions and genealogies of feminism, gender-based violence, performativity, domesticity, labor, Marxism, colonialism/postcolonialism/decolonialism, global capitalism, gender, sexuality and feminist and/or queer social movements, among others.
